levels.label: Community
levels.means: Found in an external source. Metadata captured, nothing checked.

levels.label: Reviewed
levels.means: Source, documentation and license have been checked by a curator.

levels.label: Tested
levels.means: Installation and the provided example have been run successfully.

levels.label: Verified
levels.means: The artifact was executed and its behaviour matched the documented expectation.

rules: A resource cannot skip a level.
verification is time-bounded: `last_verified` records the date, and the UI warns past a staleness threshold.
Listing is not endorsement: security posture is always displayed separately from verification.

states.label: Discovered

states.label: License checked
states.description: License identified and its terms recorded.

states.label: Deprecated
states.description: Superseded or unmaintained; kept for provenance.

scoring.scale: 0 = absent, 5 = exemplary. Components are averaged with equal weight; null components are excluded and reported.

resources.title: Author your first data contract
resources.description: Draft an enforceable contract for one real dataset by walking the six parts — owner, schema, semantics, SLA, breaking-change policy, enforcement — starting from the data-contract template, and finish with the CI test that makes it a contract instead of documentation.
when_to_use: A producer and its consumers keep arguing about what a column means

steps.text: Name an owner — a team, with an on-call.
Define the schema, typed and versioned.
Write the semantics: what each field means, units, nullability.
Set the SLA — freshness and completeness.
Agree the breaking-change policy — notice period and a deprecation path.
Wire enforcement: name the CI test that fails on violation.

what_you_need: A producer dataset with at least one consumer
check_yourself: The contract names a team with an on-call as owner, not a distribution list.
Renaming a promised field in a test branch fails the CI test named in part six.
gotchas: A contract with no enforcement is documentation. Documentation is not a contract.
The owner is a team with an on-call — a contract owned by nobody has no pager.
A rename + a new column with the old name looks compatible to a schema differ but breaks every consumer that read the old semantics — write the semantics section so the diff catches it.
production_notes: Enforcement is part six — the contract must name the CI test that fails on violation.
Keep contract.yaml, schema.avsc, ci/check-compat.sh and DEPRECATION.md together; the template ships all four.
resources.why: A contract with no enforcement is documentation, and documentation is not a contract — the sixth part is what makes the other five binding.

contract authoring
   |
   |- owner + schema --> semantics (units, nullability)
   |
   |- SLA (freshness, completeness) --> breaking-change policy
   |
   |- enforcement --> CI test fails on violation --> contract, not documentation

resources.title: Cut Athena bytes scanned with partitions and projection
resources.description: Walk one expensive Athena query through the Partition Advisor's levers in order: confirm the per-TB bill model, partition on the dominant filter column, replace MSCK REPAIR with partition projection, compact small files, and move to columnar compression. Every move is judged by a single number — bytes scanned.
when_to_use: Athena cost climbs with no change in query count
A partitioned table still scans everything because partition metadata relies on MSCK REPAIR
learning_objectives: Read the scanned-bytes metric per query
Apply partition projection for high-cardinality columns
Compact small files to cut per-request overhead

steps.text: Judge every recommendation by one question — does this reduce bytes scanned? You pay per TB scanned, and nothing else matters.
Partition on the dominant filter column (usually date).
Use partition projection instead of `MSCK REPAIR` for predictable layouts.
Compact small files — per-file overhead dominates at < 16 MB.
Go columnar + compression (Parquet + snappy/zstd) — 10-100x vs CSV.

what_you_need: An Athena workgroup and a table you can query
The scanned-bytes metric for recent queries
check_yourself: Re-running the expensive query after the levers land shows the scanned-bytes metric dropping to only the touched date partitions.
A table whose files average under 16 MB is compacted, and the per-query bill no longer carries per-file overhead.
gotchas: Every recommendation is judged by bytes scanned — a change that adds complexity without cutting scan is a no.
Per-file overhead dominates at < 16 MB — small files inflate the bill even when pruning works.
Partition projection replaces MSCK REPAIR only for predictable layouts.
production_notes: Track the scanned-bytes metric per query so layout regressions show up the day they land.
Write Parquet with snappy/zstd; CSV inputs scan 10-100x more bytes for the same data.
resources.why: Bytes scanned is the only thing Athena bills, so applying the advisor's four levers in order is the shortest path to a smaller invoice on the next run.
resources.diagram:
athena bytes pass
   |
   |- read scanned-bytes metric --> baseline per query
   |
   |- partition on dominant filter column --> projection replaces MSCK REPAIR
   |
   |- compact small files (< 16 MB overhead) --> parquet + snappy/zstd
   |
   --> re-run query --> bytes scanned drops

code.title: The four levers, in order
code.code:
## Levers, in order
1. Partition on the dominant filter column (usually date).
2. Partition projection instead of `MSCK REPAIR` for predictable layouts.
3. Compact small files — per-file overhead dominates at < 16 MB.
4. Columnar + compression (Parquet + snappy/zstd) — 10-100x vs CSV.

code.title: Bill model — you pay per TB scanned
code.code:
## Bill model
You pay per TB scanned. Every recommendation is judged by "does this reduce
bytes scanned?" — nothing else matters.

resources.title: Decide when a Delta table needs OPTIMIZE or Z-ORDER
resources.description: Apply the Delta Optimization Advisor's decision rules to one table: read file stats for the OPTIMIZE trigger, pick Z-ORDER columns from actual query predicates, weigh liquid clustering for high-cardinality write-heavy tables, and prove the choice by comparing numFiles and bytes scanned before and after.
when_to_use: A Delta table's reads slowed as micro-batch appends piled up
A choice between OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, and liquid clustering must be justified with data
learning_objectives: Decide if a table needs OPTIMIZE from file stats
Choose Z-ORDER columns from query predicates
Know when liquid clustering beats partitioning

steps.text: Decide: files < 32 MB and many -> run OPTIMIZE.
Decide: queries filter on 1-2 high-cardinality columns -> ZORDER BY those columns.
Decide: high-cardinality, many predicates, frequent writes -> liquid clustering.
Decide: predicate on one low-cardinality column (date) -> partition, or leave it; Delta handles pruning well already.
Measure — compare numFiles and query bytes scanned before and after; if scanning did not drop, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns.

what_you_need: A Delta table with file-stats and history access
The query predicates your consumers actually filter on
check_yourself: A table with thousands of sub-32 MB files is OPTIMIZEd and numFiles drops while the next query reports fewer bytes scanned.
A Z-ORDER on a column no query filters on is caught by the before/after measurement and reverted instead of shipped.
gotchas: If bytes scanned did not drop after Z-ORDER, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns — measure before and after.
A predicate on one low-cardinality column (date) rarely needs Z-ORDER — partition, or leave it; Delta handles pruning well already.
Liquid clustering is for high-cardinality, many-predicate, frequently written tables — not the default for every table.
production_notes: Track numFiles and bytes scanned per query as the standing success metric for layout changes.
Re-run the decision rules when write patterns change; frequent writes with many predicates move the answer to liquid clustering.
resources.why: OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER both rewrite storage, so the decision rules and the before/after measurement keep you from paying for the wrong one.
resources.diagram:
delta optimize decision
   |
   |- files < 32 MB and many --> OPTIMIZE
   |
   |- 1-2 high-cardinality predicates --> ZORDER BY those columns
   |
   |- many predicates + frequent writes --> liquid clustering
   |
   |- low-cardinality date predicate --> partition or leave it
   |
   --> measure numFiles + bytes scanned before/after

code.title: OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER (Delta)
code.code: OPTIMIZE db.tbl ZORDER BY (user_id);  -- Delta

code.title: Decision rules
code.code:
- Files < 32 MB and many → `OPTIMIZE`.
- Queries filter on 1-2 high-cardinality columns → `ZORDER BY` those columns.
- High-cardinality, many predicates, frequent writes → liquid clustering.
- Predicate on one low-cardinality column (date) → partition (or leave it; Delta
  handles pruning well already).

code.title: Measure before and after
code.code:
Compare `numFiles` and query `bytes scanned` before and after. If scanning
didn't drop, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns.

resources.title: Deduplicate records without rewriting the table
resources.description: Row counts are inflated and revenue double-counted after a retry or a fan-out join. Work the duplicate-records runbook: find the first duplicate date, correlate it with a deploy, dedupe on the business key, and rewrite only the affected partitions.
when_to_use: Row counts are inflated and metrics double-counted
A unique-key test starts failing after a retry, join change or backfill
learning_objectives: Count duplicates per key with one GROUP BY query
Correlate the first duplicate date with a deploy
Rewrite affected partitions instead of the whole table

steps.text: Identify the duplicate key and count duplicates per key.
Run: `SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 20;`
Determine the earliest date duplicates appeared → correlate with a deploy.
Check whether the write is append vs merge/overwrite.
Deduplicate on the business key, keeping the latest by event time.
Rewrite the affected partitions (overwrite), not the whole table.

what_you_need: The inflated table and its business (grain) key
Warehouse SQL access to run the grouping queries
check_yourself: After the fix, the duplicates query returns zero rows for the rewritten partitions: `SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1` is empty.
Duplicate-rate per key is back to 0 and row count vs source count reconciles.
gotchas: Fix the destination partitions, not the whole table — a full rewrite is both slow and a new risk.
An append instead of overwrite on retry is the classic maker of duplicates.
A non-unique 'one' side in a join fans out silently; test the grain, not the totals.
production_notes: Idempotent writes: partition overwrite or MERGE on the business key.
Run a unique test on the grain key in CI and in production.
resources.why: Duplicates corrupt every metric quietly; finding the first duplicate date and the deploy that introduced it is the whole diagnosis.
resources.diagram:
duplicates
   |
   |- count per key --> top duplicated keys
   |
   |- min duplicate date --> correlate with deploy --> fix write mode
   |
   |- dedupe by business key --> keep latest by event time --> overwrite affected partitions

code.title: Count duplicates per key
code.code: SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 20;

code.title: Find the first and last duplicate dates
code.code: SELECT min(dt), max(dt) FROM (SELECT dt, k, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY dt, k HAVING count(*)>1);

code.title: Dedupe keeping latest event time, overwrite affected partitions
code.code:
Deduplicate on the business key, keeping the latest by event time.
Rewrite the affected partitions (overwrite), not the whole table.

Prevention: idempotent writes (partition overwrite or MERGE on the key);
a `unique` test on the grain key in CI and in production.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Enforce contracts in CI with the schema change check
resources.description: Install the Schema Change Check as a pre-commit gate over staged schema files so a breaking change exits non-zero unless a migration plan or deprecation annotation rides along with it — the producer-CI placement that catches breakage before merge.
when_to_use: Shared assets across teams
Regulated or SLA-bearing data
learning_objectives: Configure a pre-commit check over staged schema files
State what lets a breaking change pass — MIGRATION.md or a deprecated_at annotation
Explain why the gate belongs in the producer's CI, not the consumer's runtime

steps.text: Run the check on staged schema files: *.avsc, *.sql DDL, dbt schema.yml.
Diff the staged files against HEAD and classify the change.
Exit non-zero on a breaking change — failure_behavior is block.
Allow the commit only when a MIGRATION.md or a `deprecated_at` annotation is present.
Keep the gate in the producer's CI, where the change is made — the cheapest place to catch it is before merge.
Verify with the documented case: a commit narrowing `amount` from decimal(18,2) to decimal(10,2) is blocked with an explanation and a suggested migration.

what_you_need: A repo carrying schema files (*.avsc, *.sql DDL, dbt schema.yml)
A pre-commit hook setup in the producer repo
The consumer list for the covered datasets
check_yourself: A commit narrowing `amount` from decimal(18,2) to decimal(10,2) is blocked with an explanation and a suggested migration.
The same commit passes once MIGRATION.md or a `deprecated_at` annotation is present.
gotchas: The check only sees staged schema files (*.avsc, *.sql DDL, dbt schema.yml) — schema changes elsewhere never reach it.
Producers carry process overhead; the gate needs buy-in, or it gets bypassed.
A rename + a new column with the old name looks compatible to a schema differ — always diff semantics, not just names.
production_notes: Wire it as a pre-commit trigger so classification happens before the change leaves the branch.
Additive changes pass; breaking changes require a dated deprecation plan.
resources.why: A pre-commit gate blocks breaking schema changes at the producer, where catching them is cheapest.
resources.diagram:
producer commit
   |
   |- staged schema files --> diff vs HEAD --> classify
   |
   |- compatible --> pass
   |
   |- breaking --> MIGRATION.md or deprecated_at? --> yes --> pass
                                                 --> no --> block (exit non-zero)

code.title: Pre-commit gate over staged schema files
code.code:
Runs on staged schema files (*.avsc, *.sql DDL, dbt schema.yml).
Diffs against HEAD, classifies the change, and exits non-zero on a breaking
change unless a MIGRATION.md or a `deprecated_at` annotation is present.

code.title: Documented case — decimal narrowing blocked
code.code:
A commit narrowing `amount` from decimal(18,2) to decimal(10,2) is blocked
with an explanation and a suggested migration.

code.title: Gate placement — producer CI, before merge
code.code:
producer change ─▶ [contract CI] ─┬─ compatible ─▶ deploy
                                  └─ breaking ─▶ blocked + plan required

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: First hands-on — a correct SELECT with a justified join
resources.description: Stand up a local DuckDB through the DuckDB MCP server, inspect before you query with list_tables and describe_table, and write one SELECT with a join whose cardinality you can justify. You read CSV and Parquet straight into the engine, state the grain of the result, and finish by proving the join cannot fan out — the habit the sql-review skill demands.
when_to_use: First query against a new local dataset
Teaching a new analyst the inspect-then-query habit
learning_objectives: Inspect a database with list_tables and describe_table before writing SQL
Write a SELECT with a join whose cardinality is stated and justified
Prove a join cannot fan out before writing it

steps.text: Run DuckDB locally through the DuckDB MCP server, which queries DuckDB databases and MotherDuck, including reading Parquet/CSV directly from object storage.
Inspect before you query — list_tables and describe_table, then query, are the three tools the server exposes.
The DuckDB documentation covers the embedded analytics SQL engine, Parquet and CSV readers, and in-process query execution.
Every join states its cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) and justifies it.
Prove a join cannot fan out before writing it.
Close by writing a grain statement for each SELECT — the artifact the SQL Reviewer emits for every result set.

what_you_need: DuckDB via the MCP server — uvx mcp-server-motherduck --db-path /data/warehouse.duckdb
A CSV or Parquet file to load
check_yourself: describe_table names every column and key you used in the join, and you can say which side is the many side.
Your join's cardinality is written down (1:1, N:1, N:N) with a one-line justification.
Counting rows before and after the join shows no inflation — the join cannot fan out.
gotchas: SELECT * hides which columns the join keys came from — name them.
Parquet and CSV readers mean no import step — point the query at the file.
A join that cannot fan out on today's data can fan out tomorrow — state the cardinality, not the current counts.
production_notes: Keep the MCP server pointed at a local file (mcp-server-motherduck --db-path) so experiments never touch shared data.
Read the DuckDB documentation's Parquet and SQL pages — they cover what the review skill checks.
resources.why: The inspect-then-query habit plus a justified join is the smallest complete unit of correct SQL.
resources.diagram:
first correct SELECT
   |
   |- start mcp-server-motherduck --> local DuckDB
   |
   |- list_tables --> describe_table --> keys and columns
   |
   |- SELECT with join --> cardinality stated (1:1, N:1, N:N)
   |
   |- row count before/after --> no inflation --> grain statement

code.title: Start the DuckDB MCP server on a local database
code.code: uvx mcp-server-motherduck --db-path /data/warehouse.duckdb

code.title: Register the server with your agent
code.code:
mcpServers:
  duckdb:
    command: uvx
    args:
      - mcp-server-motherduck
      - --db-path
      - /data/warehouse.duckdb

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Fix SQL lint with the SQLFluff core rule pack
resources.description: Install the SQLFluff core rule pack, point it at your warehouse dialect, and lint a fixture that fails on purpose: indentation, keyword capitalisation, SELECT star, and unused CTEs. You fix each finding while the passing fixture stays green, then wire the same lint run into CI.
when_to_use: Team SQL style drifts and review time burns on formatting
Legacy SQL debt needs fixing incrementally instead of one big reformat
learning_objectives: Configure SQLFluff for your warehouse dialect
Fix L003, L010, L030, and L057 findings in real SQL
Integrate SQLFluff into CI/CD pipelines

steps.text: Configure SQLFluff for your warehouse dialect.
L003 — Consistent indentation.
L010 — Keywords capitalisation policy (UPPER).
L030 — SELECT star usage.
L057 — Unused CTE detection.
Integrate SQLFluff into CI/CD pipelines.

what_you_need: Python >= 3.8 with pip
pip install sqlfluff==3.0.0 sqlfluff-templater-dbt
A .sql file or dbt project to lint
check_yourself: sqlfluff lint flags the seeded violations in the failing fixture and returns nothing on the passing one.
CI fails on style-severity findings and stays green on the passing fixture.
gotchas: The pack defaults to the dbt templater and the snowflake dialect — set both to your project or findings mislead.
L014 and L030 are warnings, not style errors — severity decides what blocks CI.
Fix legacy SQL debt incrementally; a whole-repo reformat buries the real diff.
production_notes: Pin sqlfluff==3.0.0 with sqlfluff-templater-dbt so CI and local runs agree.
Exclude rules deliberately via exclude_rules rather than ignoring findings inline.
resources.why: Mechanical lint rules settle formatting and naming so review time goes to correctness.
resources.diagram:
sqlfluff pass
   |
   |- install sqlfluff==3.0.0 + dbt templater
   |
   |- set dialect + templater --> lint fixture
   |
   |- L003 --> L010 --> L030 --> L057 --> fix each finding
   |
   |- lint in CI --> passing fixture stays green

code.title: Install SQLFluff 3.0.0 with the dbt templater
code.code:
pip install sqlfluff==3.0.0 sqlfluff-templater-dbt
sqlfluff --version

code.title: Set dialect and templater for your project (.sqlfluff)
code.code:
[sqlfluff]
dialect = snowflake   # pack default - set to your warehouse dialect
templater = dbt       # pack default - or jinja for plain SQL

code.title: Lint the failing fixture and keep the passing one green
code.code:
sqlfluff lint tests/fixtures/style_fail.sql   # flags the seeded violations
sqlfluff lint tests/fixtures/style_pass.sql   # returns nothing

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Hold the cloud data stack mental model — storage, catalog, compute, IAM
resources.description: Build the map before opening a console: object storage holds the bytes, a managed catalog describes them, and serverless compute bills for what a query scans. Walk the same shape through five managed engines — Glue, Athena, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks — and note the IAM surface each one needs before the first query.
when_to_use: You are about to open a cloud console for the first time and need the map before the menus
A stack mixes engines (Glue, Athena, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks) and one vocabulary has to cover all of them
learning_objectives: Explain storage/compute separation with one managed example per layer
Name the IAM surface each managed service needs before the first query
Map any cloud data stack into one data flow — storage, catalog, compute, serve

steps.text: See the stack as Terraform sees it — S3 buckets with lifecycle + encryption, a Glue catalogue, IAM roles scoped to least privilege, and Athena workgroups with query limits.

Read the flow in one line — Parquet in S3 (Hive layout, dt=..) into the Glue Data Catalog, queried by Athena serverless SQL, with Terraform provisioning buckets, catalog, and a workgroup with a bytes limit.
Learn the managed Glue surfaces — jobs, crawlers, the Data Catalog, job bookmarks, DPU configuration, and Ray integration are what every Glue pipeline touches.
Know where the surprises live — job bookmarks and the catalogue's behaviour are the source of the most common Glue surprises.

See storage/compute separation in BigQuery — partitioning, clustering, slot management, and the query optimizer's behavior are the levers, and the partitioning/clustering pages are the exact levers for cost control.

See it again in Snowflake — virtual warehouses, micro-partitions, clustering keys, and zero-copy cloning are the managed primitives; the performance and cost sections are the reference for clustering-key and warehouse-sizing decisions.
Close the map with Databricks — Delta Live Tables, Unity Catalog, liquid clustering, and the Photon engine are platform-specific and only documented there.

what_you_need: No cloud account required — this is a concepts lesson
The AWS Glue, BigQuery, and Snowflake documentation pages open beside you
check_yourself: You can draw the S3 → Glue Data Catalog → Athena flow from memory and say which layer stores bytes, which describes them, and which bills for scanning.
Asked what each engine bills for compute, you name the unit — DPU configuration for Glue, slot management for BigQuery, credits/hour warehouse size for Snowflake — without opening a pricing page.
For each managed service you can name the IAM surface — the least-privilege role or profile the job or agent assumes.
gotchas: Job bookmarks and the catalogue's behaviour are the source of the most common Glue surprises — read those doc sections before your first job.
Liquid clustering and Unity Catalog are platform-specific and only documented in the Databricks docs — engine assumptions do not transfer.
IAM roles scoped to least privilege are part of the stack definition, not a bolt-on after the first query.
production_notes: Keep the Terraform template's shape as your baseline — buckets with lifecycle + encryption, catalog, least-privilege roles, workgroup with query limits.
Re-read each engine's performance and cost doc section when a sizing decision stalls; the levers are documented.
resources.why: Every managed service rents you the same shape — storage, catalog, compute, IAM — so learn the shape once and every console becomes familiar.
resources.diagram:
cloud data stack (one shape, five engines)
   |
   |- storage: object storage (S3) holds bytes; lifecycle + encryption live here
   |
   |- catalog: Glue Data Catalog describes the bytes
   |
   |- compute: DPUs (Glue) | scanned bytes (Athena) | slots (BigQuery) | credits/hour (Snowflake)
   |
   |- IAM: least-privilege roles/profiles gate every layer
   |
    --> map services to one data flow before judging any of it

code.title: The stack in one line
code.code:
Parquet in S3 (Hive layout: dt=..) ─▶ Glue Data Catalog ─▶ Athena (serverless SQL)
          ▲                                                    │
[Terraform: buckets, catalog, workgroup with bytes limit]    └─▶ BI

code.title: Cost levers in BigQuery
code.code:
BigQuery levers: partitioning, clustering, slot management, query optimizer
behavior. The partitioning/clustering pages are the exact levers for cost
control; the query optimizer section explains slot utilization.

code.title: The IaC baseline
code.code:
S3 buckets with lifecycle + encryption, Glue catalogue, IAM roles scoped to
least privilege, and Athena workgroups with query limits.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Hold the streaming mental model: events, partitions, delivery semantics
resources.description: Build the vocabulary before touching a cluster: events instead of rows, partitions instead of tables, at-least-once delivery instead of exactly-once, and the lambda/kappa decision for speed versus correctness. Every later lesson in this series leans on these four ideas.
when_to_use: You are new to streaming and need the vocabulary before touching a cluster
A team debate between lambda and kappa needs a decision framework
learning_objectives: Explain why ordering and partitions behave the way they do
Treat at-least-once delivery and replays as the normal case
Choose between lambda, kappa, and plain batch for a latency and reprocessing need

steps.text: Read the map first — the docs cover architecture and design, delivery semantics, the protocol, consumer groups and offsets, operations, and security.
The design section explains why ordering and partitions behave the way they do; the operations section is the runbook companion.
Set your expectations for delivery — at-least-once delivery is the norm, replays happen after failure, and consumers must not see duplicates.
Name the core tradeoff — streaming is fast but hard; batch is simple but slow; you need both speed and correctness.

Learn the two architectures — Lambda runs a batch layer (authoritative, reprocessable) plus a speed layer (approximate, low-latency), merged at query time; Kappa is one streaming path where reprocessing means replaying the log, which requires long log retention and replay safety.
Carry one health probe into every cluster — is lag rising, flat, or falling? Flat at a high number is fine; rising is not.

what_you_need: No cluster required — this is a concepts lesson
The Apache Kafka documentation open beside you
check_yourself: You can say why a partition gives per-key ordering and why the design section of the docs is where that behavior is explained.
Asked whether a nightly batch needs lambda or kappa, you answer with the pattern's own exit — neither, if a nightly batch genuinely meets the SLA.
gotchas: At-least-once is the norm — replays happen after failure, so consumers must tolerate duplicates from day one.
Flat lag at a high number is fine; rising is not — do not alert on an absolute lag number.
Lambda means two code paths and two bugs — the speed layer must stay consistent with the batch layer.
production_notes: Keep raw immutable so history is always reprocessable — the modern default is a single lakehouse path with replayable streams, a pragmatic kappa.
Neither pattern if a nightly batch genuinely meets the SLA — keep it simple.
resources.why: Every streaming incident traces back to a violated assumption about ordering, delivery, or replay — hold the model before holding the tools.
resources.diagram:
streaming mental model
   |
   |- events, not rows --> append-only log, ordered per partition
   |
   |- at-least-once --> replays happen after failure --> consumers dedupe
   |
   |- batch: simple + slow | stream: fast + hard
   |
   |- lambda --> batch (authoritative) + speed (approx) --> serve
   |- kappa  --> one path; reprocess = replay the log
   |
    --> probe every cluster: is lag rising, flat, or falling?

code.title: Lambda vs Kappa in one view
code.code:
Lambda:  source ─┬─ batch (authoritative) ─┐
                 └─ speed (approx)       ─┴─▶ serve
Kappa:   source ─▶ stream ─▶ table ─▶ serve   (reprocess = replay)

code.title: The delivery contract
code.code:
- At-least-once delivery is the norm
- Replays happen after failure
- Consumers must not see duplicates

code.title: The three questions
code.code:
1. Is lag rising, flat, or falling? Flat at a high number is fine; rising is not.
2. Is lag even across partitions? Skew means a hot key, not capacity.
3. Is the consumer group stable? Frequent `PreparingRebalance` is the real bug.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Inspect Kafka topics and groups with the Kafka MCP server
resources.description: Connect an agent to a Kafka cluster through the Kafka MCP server and work through its four tools: list_topics for inventory, describe_topic for a single topic, describe_consumer_group for lag, and consume_messages for sampling — stream debugging from an agent, with the sampling risks called out up front.
when_to_use: An agent needs read access to topic inventory, lag, and message samples
Stream debugging should happen from the agent's context instead of ad hoc CLI sessions
learning_objectives: Configure the Kafka MCP server against a broker list
Inventory topics and read group lag with the four tools
Sample messages without leaking production PII

steps.text: Point the server at the cluster — KAFKA_BROKERS holds the comma-separated broker list, and KAFKA_SASL_USER / KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD are set if the cluster requires it.
Run list_topics for a topic inventory.
Run describe_topic and describe_consumer_group to inspect one topic and its consumer-group lag.
Use consume_messages to sample messages when the debugging needs content, not just offsets.

Before sampling, know the risk — it can expose production PII in the agent's context; grant a read-only principal, prefer a topic allow-list, and never sample topics containing personal data without masking.

what_you_need: KAFKA_BROKERS (comma-separated broker list), optionally SASL credentials
An agent host with kafka-mcp-server installed
A read-only principal scoped to an allow-listed topic
check_yourself: describe_consumer_group on the suspect group returns the same per-partition offsets the CLI kafka-consumer-groups describe shows.
consume_messages runs only against an allow-listed topic with a read-only principal, and no personal data reaches the agent context unmasked.
gotchas: consume_messages can expose production PII in the agent's context — never sample topics containing personal data without masking.
Grant a read-only principal and prefer a topic allow-list before handing the server to an agent.
The server's licensing is ambiguous — MIT badge in the README but no LICENSE file — verify before commercial use.
production_notes: Give the server its own KAFKA_CLIENT_ID and stdio transport so its connections are identifiable.
Keep SASL credentials in the environment, scoped to a read-only principal.
resources.why: The server puts topic inventory, consumer-group lag, and message sampling behind four tools, so an agent can debug a stream without cluster write access.
resources.diagram:
kafka mcp exploration
   |
   |- KAFKA_BROKERS + optional SASL --> server connects (stdio)
   |
   |- list_topics --> topic inventory
   |
   |- describe_topic + describe_consumer_group --> topic detail + lag
   |
    |- consume_messages --> samples (read-only principal, allow-list, mask PII)

code.title: Register the server with the agent
code.code:
mcpServers:
  kafka:
    command: kafka-mcp-server
    args: []
    env:
      KAFKA_BROKERS: localhost:9092
      KAFKA_CLIENT_ID: kafka-mcp-server
      MCP_TRANSPORT: stdio

code.title: Server environment variables
code.code:
KAFKA_BROKERS       (required) Comma-separated broker list.
KAFKA_CLIENT_ID     (optional) Kafka client id for connections.
KAFKA_SASL_USER     (optional) SASL user, if the cluster requires it.
KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD (optional) SASL password, if required.

code.title: Sampling risk — security requirements
code.code:
Sampling messages can expose production PII in the agent's context. Grant a
read-only principal, prefer a topic allow-list, and never sample topics
containing personal data without masking.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Install cost guardrails before the invoice
resources.description: Instrument, attribute, then guard: the Cost Guardrails pattern in four moves — a unit metric per pipeline, a baseline of the last N runs, CI failing on regression, and hard caps. It ends with a build that fails on a 3.9x shuffle jump instead of a surprise invoice.
when_to_use: Any pipeline with variable compute cost
Multi-team platforms
learning_objectives: Define a unit metric per pipeline
Baseline the last N runs and fail CI past a threshold
Add hard caps on top of CI guards

steps.text: Define a unit metric per pipeline ($ per run, per 1M rows).
Baseline the last N runs.
Fail CI on regression > threshold.
Add hard caps (warehouse resource monitors, quota limits).
Alert on the unit metric, never on total spend, so healthy growth doesn't page anyone and a regression does.
Verify the guard — shuffle write grows 3.9x after a join change → the build fails with the stage id.

what_you_need: Cost-relevant metrics per run (shuffle/spill/scan)
CI where a build can fail on a metric check
check_yourself: A change that grows any metric > 25% vs the baseline fails CI with the offending stage and metric named.
Healthy growth (more data, same cost per run) does not page anyone.
gotchas: Spend varies with data growth and regressions hide in growth — total-spend dashboards cannot see them.
Guardrails need metrics plumbing and a baseline to be maintained — skip the baseline and the guard has nothing to compare.
Needs prior runs to build its 5-run baseline, so a cold start has nothing to compare against.
production_notes: Keep the baseline as the median of the last 5 runs.
Gate deploys on shuffle/scan metrics, and keep resource monitors as the hard cap.
resources.why: Alert on the unit metric, never on total spend, so healthy growth doesn't page anyone and a regression does.
resources.diagram:
run
   |
   |- metrics --> unit metric ($ per run / per 1M rows)
   |
   |- baseline last N runs --> within baseline --> pass
   |                          > regressed --> fail CI / alert
   |
   |- hard caps --> resource monitors + quotas --> invoice backstop

code.title: The four moves — instrument, attribute, guard, cap
code.code:
Instrument, attribute, then guard.
  1. unit metric per pipeline ($ per run, per 1M rows)
  2. baseline the last N runs
  3. fail CI on regression > threshold
  4. hard caps (warehouse resource monitors, quota limits)
Alert on the *unit* metric, never on total spend, so healthy growth doesn't page
anyone and a regression does.

code.title: Metrics worth baselining
code.code:
shuffle read/write bytes, spill (disk) bytes, task count, max task duration,
input bytes. These predict cost far better than wall-clock time.

code.title: The guard in CI — 25% vs the median of the last 5 runs
code.code:
After the job's test run, read shuffle/spill/scan metrics from the event log,
compare against the stored baseline (median of last 5), and fail if any metric
grew by more than 25%. Emit the offending stage and metric.

Example: shuffle write grows 3.9x after a join change → build fails with the stage id.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Keep an agent read-only until a human approves
resources.description: Coding agents can do real data-engineering work, but can also ship a schema change or drop a table. Walk the Agent-in-the-Loop Review pattern: separate read/recommend from write/execute, put a human gate before anything irreversible, and encode the policy as hooks.
when_to_use: Any agent touching production data
Regulated environments
learning_objectives: Separate agent read/recommend from write/execute
Encode the safety policy as hooks
Keep a human gate on anything irreversible

steps.text: Separate read/recommend from write/execute.
Constrain the agent with read-only credentials plus MCP servers limited to the needed tools.
Encode the safety policy as hooks (destructive SQL guard, prod write confirmation).
Keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible.
Test the policy — `DROP TABLE prod.orders` from an agent is denied and surfaced for confirmation.

what_you_need: An agent working against a real data repository
Read-only credentials for the agent
The destructive SQL guard and prod write confirmation hooks available
check_yourself: A write against a production target is suspended pending a human 'approve once' token scoped to the single call.
A destructive statement is denied by default, and a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied.
gotchas: Blast radius can be production — an agent with write credentials is one prompt away from a drop.
The human gate adds friction; it requires a real permission model, not a convention.
A DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied — there is no flag for it.
production_notes: Grant read-only credentials by default; write only through the scoped, logged execute path.
Encode the safety policy as hooks so it holds even when the agent is prompted otherwise.
resources.why: Trust must be earned per action — the pattern keeps agent velocity while bounding the blast radius to what a human approved.
resources.diagram:
agent
   |
   |- read tools --> analysis --> proposal
   |
   |- proposal --> human gate --> approved --> scoped write (logged)
   |                  > rejected --> no write
   |
   |- hooks --> destructive SQL guard + prod write confirm --> policy enforced

code.title: Separate read/recommend from write/execute
code.code:
read ─▶ recommend ─▶ human approves ─▶ execute (scoped, logged)

Constrain the agent with read-only credentials plus MCP servers limited to the
needed tools. Encode the safety policy as hooks (destructive SQL guard, prod
write confirmation), and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible.

code.title: Destructive SQL guard — what gets denied
code.code:
Destructive statements are denied by default; a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE
clause is always denied. Statements on a non-production target can be allowed
with a `--allow-destructive` flag that requires a human confirmation token.

Example: `DROP TABLE prod.orders` from an agent is denied and surfaced for confirmation.

code.title: Prod write confirmation — approve once, per call
code.code:
Classify the tool target as production by connection string, project or
catalogue tag. Any write-class tool against a production target is suspended
and surfaced for a human "approve once" token scoped to the single call.

Example: an agent asked to run a MERGE on prod.sales is suspended pending approval.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Name the four dimensions of data quality
resources.description: Build the mental model before writing a single test: freshness, completeness, validity, consistency. See each dimension in a real registry artifact — the SLA part of a contract, the profiling workflow of the data-quality reviewer, the rule vocabulary of the quarantine starter — and leave able to name the dimension behind any "the data is bad" complaint.
when_to_use: You are about to write quality tests and need to decide what to test first
A stakeholder asks 'is the data good?' and you want to answer with a named dimension, not a shrug
learning_objectives: Name the four dimensions of data quality — freshness, completeness, validity, consistency
Map each dimension to a concrete signal — SLA, null rate, range, uniqueness
Rank failure modes by blast radius before writing any test

steps.text: The SLA part of a contract states freshness and completeness — the first two dimensions, with numbers.
Semantics is next — what each field means, units, nullability — the validity a consumer was promised.
Profile key columns (null rate, uniqueness, ranges) — the measurements that turn each dimension into a check.
Rank failure modes by blast radius before writing a single test.
The starter's rule vocabulary covers the dimensions — not_null, unique, range, enum.
Monitor the three signals that watch the dimensions in production — expectation pass rate, quarantine row counts, freshness.

what_you_need: No installation — this lesson reads registry artifacts, it does not run them

resources.title: The batch processing mental model
resources.description: Batch processing in partition terms. Learn what a partition, a shuffle and a spill are, why "the job is slow" resolves into four named causes — skew, partition count, spill, over-scan — and why the write side carries one invariant: same date twice, same output.
when_to_use: Starting with batch processing on Spark
Turning 'the job is slow' into a named cause
learning_objectives: Name the four causes of a slow batch job: skew, partition count, spill, over-scan
Explain what a shuffle does to a hot key
State the idempotent-write invariant for re-runnable batch jobs

steps.text: Batch processing recomputes per logical partition: `INSERT OVERWRITE partition(dt=...)` or Delta/Iceberg replace-where replace that partition atomically.
Never append to a partition you can recompute — the invariant is that running the same date twice yields identical output.
A shuffle moves data by key, and key skew on a join or group-by key is the first cause of a slow stage.
The second cause is partition count: too few partitions after a filter, or too many after a shuffle.
The third cause is spill to disk from an oversized partition.
The fourth cause is reading far more data than needed (missing partition filter).
When a job skews or slows, check the config reference and the tuning guide before changing code.

what_you_need: A Spark job to inspect — its Spark UI stage view or event log
The output table's partition layout (dt=... or equivalent)
check_yourself: You can name the four causes of a slow batch job: key skew, partition count, spill, over-scan.
A re-run for dt=2026-09-01 overwrites that partition and produces identical output.
gotchas: Too few partitions after a filter, or too many after a shuffle: both look like 'Spark is slow'.
Spill shows up as slow tasks, not failures — check spill bytes before paying for bigger executors.
An empty partition and an absent partition both read as 'no data' downstream.
production_notes: Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics per run so regressions are visible before users feel them.
Store the logical date explicitly as a partition column, not derived at read time.
resources.why: Batch failures cluster into four named causes — skew, partition count, spill, over-scan — and the write side has one invariant, so the mental model turns vague slowdowns into diagnoses.
resources.diagram:
batch job
   |
   |- read --> partitions (unit of parallelism)
   |
   |- shuffle by key --> hot key --> skew
   |        > oversized partition --> spill to disk
   |
   |- scan --> missing partition filter --> over-scan
   |
   |- write --> INSERT OVERWRITE dt=... --> same date twice = same output

code.title: The four causes of a slow batch job
code.code:
- Key skew on a join or group-by key
- Too few partitions after a filter, or too many after a shuffle
- Spill to disk from an oversized partition
- Reading far more data than needed (missing partition filter)

code.title: The idempotent batch write
code.code:
INSERT OVERWRITE partition(dt=...)   # or Delta/Iceberg replace-where

The invariant: running the same date twice yields identical output.

code.title: Where the exact semantics live
code.code:
Spark SQL, the DataFrame API, tuning and the configuration catalogue,
versioned per Spark release. The config reference alone resolves most
tuning debates.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: The data reliability mental model — freshness, completeness, correctness
resources.description: Build the map before writing a single check: a consumer experiences a table as three properties — freshness, completeness, correctness — declared as an SLA in a data contract, enforced by a CI test, and spent like an error budget when failures land.
when_to_use: Onboarding onto a table or pipeline your team depends on
Deciding what 'reliable' means before writing a single check
learning_objectives: Name the three properties a consumer experiences — freshness, completeness, correctness
Read a data contract's SLA section as the table's reliability promise
Explain why an unenforced SLA is documentation, not a contract

steps.text: Reliability is the first word in DDIA's list of what data systems must balance — reliability, scalability, replication, partitioning, consistency — and every chapter maps directly to patterns in this registry.
A contract has six parts — owner, schema, semantics, SLA, breaking-change policy, enforcement — and part four is the SLA (freshness, completeness).
Specify a freshness and completeness SLA — the two promises consumers experience first.
Freshness is computed, not felt — compare the schedule/cron with the source's declared freshness SLA, and when a change can produce data older than the SLA, warn with the computed worst-case lag.
Correctness needs a written definition before anyone re-runs anything — what should the values be, and how will you check?
Design for the forces that never go away — retries are inevitable, backfills are routine, consumers must see stable values.
A contract with no enforcement is documentation. Documentation is not a contract.

what_you_need: A table your team's consumers depend on
The pipeline's schedule and the source's declared freshness SLA
check_yourself: You can name freshness, completeness and correctness for a table you consume, and say where each is declared.
Given a cron change, you can compute the worst-case lag and say whether it violates the declared freshness SLA.
gotchas: A contract with no enforcement is documentation. Documentation is not a contract.
The SLA miss cascades — downstream tasks sit skipped/upstream_failed until the failure is classified and recovered.
Retries are inevitable and backfills are routine — design for them instead of hoping.
production_notes: Put freshness and completeness in the contract's SLA section, with the CI test that enforces each.
Compute the worst-case lag when a schedule changes instead of trusting the cron.
resources.why: Reliability is three promises a consumer experiences — freshness, completeness, correctness — and a promise nobody enforces is documentation, not a contract.
resources.diagram:
data reliability mental model
   |
   |- freshness --> declared SLA --> worst-case lag computed on schedule change
   |
   |- completeness --> SLA section of the contract
   |
   |- correctness --> written definition: what should the values be?
   |
   |- enforcement --> a CI test that fails on violation, or it is not a contract

code.title: A contract has six parts
code.code:
1. Owner (a team, with an on-call).
2. Schema (typed, versioned).
3. Semantics (what each field *means*, units, nullability).
4. SLA (freshness, completeness).
5. Breaking-change policy (notice period, deprecation path).
6. Enforcement (which CI test fails on violation).

code.title: The freshness check
code.code:
Compare the schedule/cron in the diff with the source's declared freshness SLA.
If the new schedule can produce data older than the SLA (e.g. daily when the
SLA is 6h), warn with the computed worst-case lag.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: The lakehouse mental model — lake vs warehouse vs table formats vs zones
resources.description: Build the map before touching a table: object storage is files with no structure for trust or ownership, a table format (Iceberg or Delta) adds snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning, ACID, and evolution, and medallion zones make trust legible from raw to serving. Multi-catalog means the formats coexist — pick each one deliberately.
when_to_use: Before laying out a new lakehouse or admitting a new table format to one
Onboarding onto a team where many teams write and read the same storage
learning_objectives: Contrast lake, warehouse, and lakehouse by what each does to raw files
Name the table format's jobs — snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning, schema evolution
Place the medallion zones over a lakehouse and say who owns each zone

steps.text: Start from the gap: object storage gives you a place to put files but no structure for trust or ownership.
Name the setting: a lake or lakehouse where many teams write and read, and consumers need to know how far to trust a table.

The table format is what turns the lake into a lakehouse: Iceberg's spec covers the table format, snapshots and manifests, hidden partitioning, schema and partition evolution, and maintenance procedures like compaction and snapshot expiry.

Delta is the other major format: its official docs cover ACID transactions on object storage, time travel, OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER clustering — and the registry says compare with a Delta vs Iceberg decision guide before committing to a format.
Multi-format is normal, not a compromise: Amazon EMR's multi-catalog queries Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, and Hive tables through a single catalog and joins data across AWS accounts without copying it.

Give the house its zones: raw/ is immutable, exactly as received, never edited, schema-on-read; curated/ is cleaned, typed, deduplicated, quality-gated; serving/ is modelled marts optimised for consumption, SLA-bearing — and promotion between zones is a pipeline step with a gate, not a copy.

what_you_need: An object-storage lake or lakehouse you can point at
The Iceberg spec and Delta docs — both are in the DE//AGENT registry
No installs — this lesson is the map, not the tools
check_yourself: You can say what object storage lacks — structure for trust or ownership — and which zone supplies it for a given consumer.

check_yourself.You can name four things the Iceberg spe: snapshots and manifests, hidden partitioning, schema and partition evolution, maintenance procedures.

check_yourself: You can explain why promotion between zones is a gated pipeline step, not a copy.
gotchas: Object storage alone gives no structure for trust or ownership — zones and formats are what turn a lake into a lakehouse.
The table format is a specification; the spec is the ground truth when tools disagree.
Do not let curated become a dumping ground; enforce the gate.
production_notes: The spec is essential reading for multi-engine shops where Spark, Trino, and warehouses share tables — start there, not at engine docs.
Cross-account joins without copying are possible through multi-catalog; every extra copy is extra storage and another pipeline to run.
resources.why: A lakehouse is two decisions — a table format and a zoning contract — and both are cheap to make deliberately now and expensive to reverse later.
resources.diagram:
lakehouse mental model
   |
   |- object storage --> files, no structure for trust or ownership
   |
   |- table format (Iceberg | Delta) --> ACID, snapshots, manifests, evolution
   |
   |- raw (immutable) --> curated (quality gate) --> serving (SLA)
   |
   |- multi-catalog --> Iceberg + Delta + Hudi + Hive through one catalog

code.title: The medallion contract
code.code:
raw/       — immutable, exactly as received; never edited; schema-on-read.
curated/   — cleaned, typed, deduplicated; partitioned; quality-gated.
serving/   — modelled marts optimised for consumption; SLA-bearing.
Each zone has a different retention, quality bar and owner. Promotion
between zones is a pipeline step with a gate, not a copy.

code.title: One catalog, many formats
code.code:
Query Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, and Hive tables through a single
catalog and join data across AWS accounts without copying it.

resources.title: The orchestration mental model — DAGs, schedules, idempotency, backfills
resources.description: Build the map before touching code: a DAG plus its schedule decides when runs happen, the idempotency test decides whether re-runs are safe, catchup decides what happens to missed intervals, and a backfill decides how history gets fixed — four decisions every later lesson sharpens.
when_to_use: Designing your first recurring pipeline
Onboarding onto a codebase full of scheduled DAGs
learning_objectives: Name the four decisions orchestration makes — schedule, catchup, idempotency, backfill
Apply the idempotency test to a task before running anything
Say what a backfill is for and why it is dangerous

steps.text: Airflow's documentation covers DAG authoring, scheduling semantics and timetables, backfills and catchup, task state and retries, dynamic task mapping, and best practices — that list is the map of orchestration.
Read the scheduling and best-practices pages before designing any recurring pipeline — they answer the idempotency and backfill questions the skills only sketch.
Set `catchup` as a deliberate choice, not a default.
Hold every task to the idempotency test — "If this task runs twice for the same logical date, is the output the same?"
If no, fix it before anything else — retries will happen.
A backfill exists because historical output is wrong or missing and must be recomputed safely, without breaking production.
Respect its blast radius — backfills corrupt production or take down the daily run.

what_you_need: An Airflow project to reason about — real or planned
The pipeline's schedule and SLA
The Airflow documentation at airflow.apache.org/docs
check_yourself: You can say what a DAG, a logical date, `catchup` and a backfill each decide about a pipeline.
Asked whether a task is safe to re-run, you reach for the idempotency test instead of a guess.
Given a wrong historical date range, you name the backfill runbook before touching anything.
gotchas: `catchup` is a deliberate choice, not a default.
Retries will happen — fix a task that is not idempotent before anything else.
Backfills corrupt production or take down the daily run when run unmanaged.
production_notes: The scheduling and best-practices pages answer the idempotency and backfill questions the skills only sketch.
Keep pipelines idempotent so a backfill is a routine operation.
resources.why: Orchestration is four decisions — what runs, when it runs, whether re-runs are safe, and how history gets fixed — and every later lesson sharpens one of them.
resources.diagram:
orchestration mental model
   |
   |- DAG + schedule + catchup --> when runs happen
   |
   |- idempotency test --> whether re-runs are safe
   |
   |- backfill + shadow swap --> how history gets fixed

code.title: The idempotency test
code.code:
"If this task runs twice for the same logical date, is the output the same?"
If no, fix it before anything else — retries will happen.

code.title: What the Airflow docs cover
code.code:
DAG authoring, scheduling semantics and timetables, backfills and catchup,
task state and retries, dynamic task mapping, and best practices.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: The relational mental model — sets, grain, and NULL
resources.description: Before the first SELECT, build the model every later lesson uses: a query returns a set with a stated grain, a join changes that grain by its cardinality, and NULL never compares as you expect. You learn the first question every SQL review asks, the five rules that follow from it, and the failure modes — fan-out joins, NULL-unsafe predicates, implicit casts, non-deterministic ordering, functions that silently change grain — the rest of the series attacks.
when_to_use: Before writing your first production query
Onboarding onto a team that reviews SQL with the sql-review skill
learning_objectives: State the grain of a result set in one sentence
Explain how a join's cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) changes the row count of the result
Name the five correctness failure modes the SQL review rules target

steps.text: Start every query with the review skill's first question: what is the grain of this result? If the author can't answer, stop.
State the grain of a result set in one sentence.
A query returns a set — and every join states its cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) and justifies it, because cardinality is what changes the grain.
NULL is part of the model and it never compares as you think — learn to spot NULL-unsafe `NOT IN` and `=` predicates.
The failure modes the series attacks — fan-out joins, NULL-unsafe predicates, implicit casts, non-deterministic ordering, and functions that silently change grain.
The artifact of the mental model is a grain statement for each SELECT.

what_you_need: No engine required — this is a concepts lesson
A query from your own team to state the grain of
check_yourself: You can answer the first question — the grain of a given result set — in one sentence.
Given a join, you can say whether it is 1:1, N:1, or N:N and what that does to the row count.
You can explain why NOT IN over a nullable subquery column is banned.
gotchas: NOT IN with a nullable column never compares as you think; use NOT EXISTS.
A result set can be technically correct and still wrong — if the grain is wrong, the numbers are wrong.
Grain is a property of the result, not of the tables — the same join can be N:1 or N:N depending on the keys.
production_notes: Make a grain statement part of every SQL PR description.
The five review rules come from the sql-review skill — keep them next to the mental model.
resources.why: Sets, grain, and NULL semantics are the three ideas every later lesson — joins, windows, plans, review — keeps returning to.
resources.diagram:
relational mental model
   |
   |- query = set --> state the grain in one sentence
   |
   |- join cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) --> what happens to the row count
   |
   |- NULL --> never compares as you think --> NOT EXISTS over NOT IN
   |
   |- failure modes --> fan-out, NULL-unsafe, casts, ordering, grain-changing functions

code.title: The first question, and the rules that follow from it
code.code:
The first question: what is the grain of this result?
If the author can't answer, stop.

1. Every join states its cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) and justifies it.
2. NOT IN (subquery) is banned where the subquery can return NULL — use NOT EXISTS.
3. Comparisons across types must be explicit casts, not implicit.
4. ORDER BY without LIMIT in a view is meaningless — drop it.
5. SELECT * in a persisted model freezes an unstable schema.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: The warehouse mental model — micro-partitions, clustering, scan vs compute
resources.description: Build the map before tuning anything: a table is a set of micro-partitions, every query is described by bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, and queue time, a clustering key decides how much gets pruned, and a slow query is either a scan problem or a compute problem — never both at once.
when_to_use: Before tuning anything on a warehouse
Onboarding onto a team that shares one warehouse
learning_objectives: Name the three numbers that describe a warehouse query — bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, queue time
Explain why a table is a set of micro-partitions and what a clustering key prunes
Separate a scan problem from a compute problem before touching any knob

steps.text: The advisor's scope is the mental model's table of contents: clustering keys, warehouse sizing, result caching, and the difference between a scan problem and a compute problem.
Describe any warehouse query with the three numbers on the runbook's monitoring list — bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, queue time.
A table is physically a set of micro-partitions; the runbook lists data volume growth crossing a micro-partition threshold as a cause — a query can go slow with no change at all.
Diagnose first: a query that scans far more partitions than it needs is a clustering/partition problem; a scan that is optimal but still waits is a warehouse sizing or concurrency problem.
The clustering key is picked from workload shape — the column that appears in the WHERE clause of the most expensive queries, with reasonable cardinality, most selective first.
Compute is elastic and separate from storage — if queue time is far above execution time for short queries, scale out (more clusters), not up (bigger warehouse).
Under the engine sits the logical layer the lesson arc builds — the star schema that stops analysts re-deriving the same joins and disagreeing on metric definitions.

what_you_need: A warehouse to reason about — Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift
Install: npx de-agent-platform add warehouse-clustering-advisor
One slow query and one fast query from your own history to compare
check_yourself: You can read a query's bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, and queue time and say which side is sick.
Asked why a query got slow when nothing changed, you answer micro-partition thresholds before blaming code.
You can name the clustering key you would pick for your most expensive query and why.
gotchas: Bytes scanned and queue time are different diseases — fix the predicate vs add clusters; sizing up a scan-bound query buys nothing.
Clustering on a low-selectivity key stops pruning entirely.
Data volume growth silently crosses micro-partition thresholds — a query can go slow with no change at all.
production_notes: Alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio from day one.
Scale out for queue time on short queries; scale up never fixes a scan-bound query.
resources.why: Every warehousing decision later in the series is a choice about partitions, clustering, or compute — and this is the map of all three.
resources.diagram:
warehouse mental model
   |
   |- table = micro-partitions --> volume growth crosses thresholds silently
   |
   |- scan side --> bytes + partitions scanned --> clustering key / predicate
   |
   |- compute side --> queue time --> scale out (more clusters), not up
   |
   |- logical layer --> star schema under the engine

code.title: The three numbers for any query, from query history
code.code:
-- Snowflake
SELECT query_id, partitions_scanned, partitions_total, bytes_scanned
FROM table(information_schema.query_history_by_session())
ORDER BY start_time DESC LIMIT 10;

code.title: Install the clustering advisor skill
code.code: npx de-agent-platform add warehouse-clustering-advisor

resources.title: Troubleshoot a lagging group with the Kafka Troubleshooter
resources.description: Hand the Kafka Troubleshooter agent the consumer-group describe output, per-partition offsets, and consumer logs, then follow its four-step workflow from lag trend to the least destructive fix. The agent works read-only against the cluster, never resets offsets, and ships every fix with a risk rating.
when_to_use: An incident needs a diagnosis with evidence, not a guess
A fix must be the least destructive option with its risk stated
learning_objectives: Feed an incident agent the inputs it needs — group describe, offsets, logs
Follow a diagnosis, evidence, fix, prevention loop
Keep destructive shortcuts like offset resets off the table

steps.text: Check lag trend and per-partition distribution.
Check group state history for rebalances.
Identify poison messages from retry counts.
Recommend the least destructive fix.
Expect four outputs — diagnosis, evidence, fix with risk rating, prevention measure.
Hold the guardrails — never resets offsets, read-only against the cluster.

what_you_need: Consumer-group describe output
Per-partition offsets
Consumer application logs
check_yourself: The verdict on "lag on partitions 3 and 7 only, others flat" is to re-key the offending key, not scale the fleet — the agent's own worked example.
The final recommendation includes a risk rating and a prevention measure, and no offset reset was proposed at any step.
gotchas: The agent never resets offsets — treat any offset-reset suggestion as out of bounds.
It stays read-only against the cluster; it will not mutate group state.
Lag on a few partitions only is key skew, not a capacity problem — the fix is re-keying, not fleet scaling.
production_notes: Attach consumer-group describe output and application logs to the incident so the diagnosis is evidence-backed.
File the prevention measure from each diagnosis as a follow-up action so the same lag signature does not recur.
resources.why: Triage under pressure drifts toward the most destructive shortcut, and a fixed workflow with guardrails keeps the fix reversible and evidenced.
resources.diagram:
kafka troubleshooter
   |
   |- inputs: describe output + offsets + logs
   |
   |- lag trend + per-partition distribution
   |
   |- group state history --> rebalances
   |
   |- retry counts --> poison messages
   |
   |- least destructive fix --> risk rating + prevention
   |
    --> guardrails: read-only, never reset offsets

code.title: Collect the group describe evidence
code.code:
kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group $G
kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group $G --state

code.title: Four-step workflow
code.code:
- Check lag trend and per-partition distribution.
- Check group state history for rebalances.
- Identify poison messages from retry counts.
- Recommend the least destructive fix.

code.title: Outputs and guardrails
code.code:
Outputs: Diagnosis, Evidence, Fix with risk rating, Prevention measure

Guardrails:
- Never resets offsets
- Read-only against the cluster

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: What makes an agent — model, tools, loop, guardrails
resources.description: Build the map before touching anything: an agent is a model that reasons, tools that act, a loop that iterates, and guardrails that bound it. Meet a real data-engineering agent from the registry, point at each of the four parts, and see where the guardrails come from — hooks and the human gate.
when_to_use: Before your first hands-on lesson
Deciding whether a task needs an agent at all
learning_objectives: Name the four parts of an agent — model, tools, loop, guardrails
Identify each part in a real registry agent
Say where DE agents fit — review, triage and planning under guardrails

steps.text: Start from a concrete one — agent-sql-reviewer reviews SQL before it merges, catching correctness bugs and fan-out joins.
Its tools are read_file and git_diff_unstaged — the file and diff access the task needs, nothing more.
The rules it applies live in a skill it loads — skill-sql-review.
A skill is a SKILL.md file with front-matter (name, description, version), plus references/, scripts/, and examples/ directories that an agent loads on demand.
The loop is its workflow — read the diff and the file context, establish the grain of every result set, apply the review rules, emit findings.
Guardrails bound it — read-only, never executes SQL, does not modify files without explicit approval.
Guardrails scale up to a pattern — separate read/recommend from write/execute, and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible.

what_you_need: A registry agent to inspect — agent-sql-reviewer is the example throughout
The Agent Skills format reference
No installation — this lesson reads, it does not run
check_yourself: Given agent-sql-reviewer, you can point at its tools, its skill, its workflow loop and its guardrails.
You can say which part of an agent would execute a DROP TABLE — and which parts are supposed to stop it.
gotchas: An agent is a loop, not a function — it keeps calling tools until the model decides it is done.
A guardrails list is a promise; hooks are what enforce it.
Read-only tools still reach real data — review what they can read.
production_notes: Prefer agents whose tool list is the minimum the task needs.
Encode the safety policy as hooks so it holds even when the agent is prompted otherwise.
resources.why: Every later lesson sharpens one of the four parts — tools, skills, hooks or the human gate — so name them once, here.
resources.diagram:
agent anatomy
   |
   |- model --> reasons about the task
   |
   |- tools --> read_file, git_diff_unstaged --> act in scope
   |
   |- skills --> SKILL.md loaded on demand
   |
   |- loop --> read diff -> grain -> rules -> findings
   |
   |- guardrails --> read-only, no unapproved writes, human gate

code.title: One agent, four parts
code.code:
tools:      read_file, git_diff_unstaged
skills:     skill-sql-review
workflow:   Read the diff and the file context. Establish the grain of
            every result set. Apply the SQL review rules; stop at the
            first fan-out. Emit findings with file:line and a rewritten clause.
guardrails: Read-only: never executes SQL. Does not modify files
            without explicit approval.

code.title: The skill format
code.code:
A SKILL.md file with front-matter (name, description, version), plus
references/, scripts/, and examples/ directories that an agent loads
on demand.

resources.title: Wire cloud tooling — registry skills, MCP servers, and one review workflow
resources.description: Wire the registry's cloud tooling into one agent workflow: install the Glue and Athena review skills, bind the AWS MCP server to a least-privilege profile, and compose both skills plus the MCP server into the architecture reviewer. The same pattern covers GCP with the BigQuery server.
when_to_use: You are setting up an agent to review or operate a cloud data platform
A team shares one admin role for agents and needs the least-privilege pattern
learning_objectives: Install a registry skill and bind an MCP server with least-privilege credentials
Compose skills and MCP servers into a single review workflow
Keep agent access read-only by default

steps.text: Add the Athena advisor to your agent — the install command is npx de-agent-platform add athena-partition-advisor.
Give the agent the Glue checklist — it reviews Glue/Spark jobs for worker sizing, job bookmarks, partition pruning, and the catalogue/schema pitfalls that cause silent full reprocessing.
Give it the Athena lever — the advisor recommends partition projection, bucketing or file-layout changes to reduce bytes-scanned, and writes the projection DDL.
Bind the AWS MCP server — uvx awslabs.core-mcp-server@latest, with AWS_PROFILE supplied through the environment.
Know the AWS tool surface — aws_documentation_search, read_documentation, recommend, and run_iac_generation.
Compose the reviewer — it ships with the Glue reviewer and Athena advisor skills attached, plus mcp-aws among its MCP servers.
Same pattern for GCP — the BigQuery server exposes execute_query, list_datasets, list_tables, and describe_table.

what_you_need: An AWS named profile with least-privilege permissions
check_yourself: npx de-agent-platform add athena-partition-advisor succeeds and the skill appears in the agent's list.
The AWS MCP server starts with AWS_PROFILE pointing at a dedicated least-privilege profile, not an admin role.
The architecture reviewer lists skill-aws-glue-reviewer and skill-athena-partition-advisor among its skills, and mcp-aws among its MCP servers.
gotchas: Server capabilities vary widely; some AWS MCP servers can create resources — treat resource-creating tools as requiring human confirmation.
The BigQuery server needs GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS pointing at a service-account key with BigQuery roles — scope those roles down before binding.
AWS_PROFILE is required for the AWS MCP server — the named profile's IAM permissions define what is reachable.
production_notes: Bind each MCP server to a dedicated profile with short-lived SSO credentials; never attach an admin role.
Prefer key-pair auth over passwords for service users on warehouse MCP servers.
resources.why: An agent is only as safe and useful as the skills and credentials bound to it — least-privilege profiles and curated checklists beat a general-purpose admin role.
resources.diagram:
cloud agent tooling
   |
   |- npx de-agent-platform add aws-glue-job-reviewer   --> Glue checklist
   |- npx de-agent-platform add athena-partition-advisor --> bytes-scanned levers
   |
   |- mcp-aws: uvx awslabs.core-mcp-server@latest + AWS_PROFILE --> least privilege
   |
   |- agent-aws-architecture-reviewer: skills + mcp-aws composed
   |
    --> GCP same pattern: mcp-server-bigquery (execute_query, list_datasets, ...)

    command: uvx

    command: uvx
    args: [mcp-server-bigquery, --project, my-project]

resources.title: Wire the core MCP servers for a data repo
resources.description: Wire the three reference MCP servers a data repo needs: filesystem for the working directory, git for history and commits, and GitHub for issues and pull requests. Each connection is scoped — one directory, one repository, one fine-grained token.
when_to_use: Setting up an agent for a data repository
Giving an agent repo access without broad credentials
learning_objectives: Configure the filesystem, git and GitHub MCP servers
Scope each server to the minimum it needs
Know what each server can and cannot do

steps.text: Add the filesystem server: `npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /path/to/allowed/dir`.
Scope it to a single working directory; never pass a home directory or a mount containing secrets.
Add the git server: `uvx mcp-server-git --repository /path/to/repo`.
Note its limits — it can commit and create branches in the scoped repository, but cannot push unless credentials are also present in the environment.
Add the GitHub server with a token: `docker run -i --rm -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server`.
Use a fine-grained token limited to the target repositories and read-only unless the task must open PRs; never grant org-wide admin.

what_you_need: A repository to work in
Node/npx and uvx available
A fine-grained GitHub token (read-only unless the task must open PRs)
check_yourself: The agent reads files in the allowed directory and commits on the scoped repository, but has no push path and no access outside the directory.
The GitHub token is fine-grained, repository-scoped and read-only; its permission list shows no org-wide scopes.
gotchas: Never pass a home directory or a mount containing secrets to the filesystem server.
The git server cannot push unless credentials are also present in the environment.
Never grant org-wide admin on the GitHub token — scope it to the target repositories.
production_notes: Keep the filesystem allowlist to the working directory the task needs.
Prefer fine-grained, read-only GitHub tokens; widen only when the task must open PRs.
resources.why: Each server is scoped at connection time — one directory, one repository, one fine-grained token — so blast radius is a configuration choice, not an accident.
resources.diagram:
agent config
   |
   |- mcp-filesystem --> one allowed dir --> read/write in scope only
   |
   |- mcp-git --> one repository --> status/diff/log/commit, no push
   |
   |- mcp-github --> fine-grained token --> read-only unless PRs required

Git server — one scoped repository
GitHub server — fine-grained token via env

resources.title: Write the minimum dbt test set for a model
resources.description: Start from the model's grain, then rank dbt tests by the cost of the failure they prevent: uniqueness and not-null on the grain key, relationships on foreign keys, accepted values on enums, and freshness on sources. You add one custom singular test, wire freshness on a source, and finish by running the set in data-aware CI against a staging schema.
when_to_use: A model's test set does not protect its grain key
A source has no freshness check while the extractor can stall silently
learning_objectives: Rank dbt tests by blast radius instead of by effort
Add a singular test for a rule schema.yml cannot express
Wire freshness on a source and read its result

steps.text: State a model's grain and match it to its unique key test.
Rank tests by the cost of the failure they prevent.
Write a custom singular test.
Wire freshness on a source.
Run data-aware CI against a staging schema.

what_you_need: A dbt project with at least one model
models/schema.yml for generic tests
check_yourself: schema.yml has unique + not_null on the declared grain key, and dbt test passes on the dev target.
The source block carries freshness thresholds, and dbt source freshness runs green.
gotchas: Row-count equality tests on raw sources: they flake.
Testing a column nobody reads.
`warn` severity on a correctness test nobody will see.
production_notes: Freshness on sources catches a stalled extractor, the #1 silent outage — run it on a schedule.
Keep warn severity off correctness tests nobody will see.

resources.diagram:
dbt test set
   |
   |- state grain --> unique + not_null on grain key
   |
   |- rank by blast radius --> relationships --> accepted_values --> freshness
   |
   |- singular test --> run in data-aware CI on staging schema

code.title: Install the dbt-test-writer skill
code.code: npx de-agent-platform add dbt-test-writer

code.title: Test set ranked by blast radius in schema.yml
code.code:
# Rank by blast radius, not by effort
models:
  - name: <model>
    columns:
      - name: <grain key>      # 1. unique + not_null - the model is meaningless without it
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: <foreign key>    # 2. relationships - catches broken joins upstream
        tests:
          - relationships:
              to: ref('<dimension model>')
      - name: <enum column>    # 3. accepted_values - catches upstream renames
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: [<allowed values>]

code.title: Run the test set with dbt build on the dev target
code.code:
dbt deps && dbt seed
dbt build --target dev
