resources.title: Your first lakehouse table — create, query, measure, compact
resources.description: Run the whole loop in one sitting on a scratch table: create and query a first Delta or Iceberg table from the official docs, read its health from the files metadata table with one SQL query, run a first OPTIMIZE or rewrite_data_files, and prove it worked by comparing numFiles and bytes scanned before and after.
when_to_use: First contact with a Delta or Iceberg table — yours to create, query, and break safely
You want the create → query → measure → compact loop demonstrated end to end before touching production tables
learning_objectives: Create and query a first table on a real table format using the official docs
Read a table's file health from the metadata table with one SQL query
Run a first compaction and prove it with before/after numbers

steps.text: Create and query your first Delta table following the official docs — the definitive source for ACID transactions on object storage, time travel, OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER clustering.

Prefer Iceberg? The spec and docs cover the table format, snapshots and manifests, hidden partitioning, and maintenance procedures like compaction and snapshot expiry — read them before writing the first table.
Before adding data, learn the one health query: SELECT count(*), avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 FROM db.tbl.files;

Write like production does — streaming or high-frequency writes without compaction, over-partitioning (partition per hour, per user), or many small appends from a micro-batch job — and watch the health query report the damage.
Interpret the numbers with the skill's rule: avg_mb < 32 and a growing count means compact.
Run your first maintenance call: OPTIMIZE db.tbl ZORDER BY (user_id); on Delta, or CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files('db.tbl'); on Iceberg.
Close the loop: compare numFiles and query bytes scanned before and after. If scanning didn't drop, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns.

what_you_need: A lakehouse with Delta or Iceberg available (Spark, Trino, or a warehouse that reads the format)
Permission to create one scratch table
check_yourself: The health query runs on your table and returns a count and an average file size you can write down.
After OPTIMIZE or rewrite_data_files, numFiles drops and the next query reports fewer bytes scanned.
You can state the compact trigger — avg_mb < 32 and a growing count — without looking it up.
gotchas: The compact trigger is avg_mb < 32 and a growing count — measure, do not guess.
If bytes scanned did not drop after Z-ORDER, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns.
One scratch table is the whole exercise — do not point OPTIMIZE at a shared table.
production_notes: Keep the health query standing — SELECT count(*), avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 FROM db.tbl.files is the check on every table you own.
Install the Iceberg maintenance skill once and reuse its plan on every table: npx de-agent-platform add iceberg-table-maintenance.
resources.why: The whole lakehouse discipline — metadata, file health, compaction, before/after measurement — fits on one first table, and practicing the loop on a scratch table makes every later lesson concrete.

first lakehouse table

   |- create + query (Delta docs | Iceberg spec)
   |
   |- SELECT count(*), avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 FROM db.tbl.files
   |
   |- avg_mb < 32 and growing --> compact
   |
   |- OPTIMIZE (Delta) | rewrite_data_files (Iceberg)
   |
   --> numFiles + bytes scanned before/after

code.title: The health query
code.code: SELECT count(*), avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 FROM db.tbl.files;

code.title: First compaction on each format
code.code:
OPTIMIZE db.tbl ZORDER BY (user_id);  -- Delta
CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files('db.tbl');  -- Iceberg

code.title: The measure rule
code.code:
Compare `numFiles` and query `bytes scanned` before and after. If
scanning didn't drop, the Z-ORDER was on the wrong columns.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: ACID and concurrent writes — why compaction and ingestion collide
resources.description: What ACID on object storage actually guards, and where it stops: Delta commits transactions on files, but compaction is also a writer, and the two meet in the ingestion window. Learn the schedule rule, the write-path/layout-path separation, and how a guardrail blocks maintenance from running in the wrong window.
when_to_use: Compaction and ingestion keep colliding on one table
You are writing the maintenance calendar and need the rules written down
learning_objectives: Say what ACID transactions on object storage guarantee concurrent writers
Schedule compaction outside the ingestion window and explain the contention
Handle a contending OPTIMIZE — compaction is additive, so halt it, no rollback

steps.text: Ground truth first: Delta's official docs cover ACID transactions on object storage, time travel, OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER clustering, Delta Live Tables, and Unity Catalog integration.
The classic conflict: do not run compaction during peak ingestion — it conflicts with concurrent writers.
The schedule rule: compact after the ingestion window, never during it.

The pattern behind the rule: separate the write path from the layout path — writes make many small files, scheduled compaction makes 128-256 MB files — and do it outside the ingestion window so compaction and writers don't contend.
When contention happens anyway: compaction is additive, so there is nothing to roll back — halt any concurrent OPTIMIZE that contends with the ingestion window.
Guardrail it: Lakehouse Guard is a Delta/Iceberg table maintenance advisor plus a guard that blocks compaction or snapshot expiry during peak ingestion windows.

what_you_need: A Delta or Iceberg table with real ingestion traffic
An ingestion window you can schedule around
check_yourself: You can point at the ingestion window on a calendar and say when compaction may run.
A compaction plan issued during peak ingestion is blocked by the guard instead of executing.
You can explain why halting a contending OPTIMIZE needs no rollback.
gotchas: Compaction during peak ingestion conflicts with concurrent writers — schedule it after the window.
ZORDER rewrites the whole table — only worth it on a real query predicate.
Compaction is additive: halt the contending OPTIMIZE, do not attempt a rollback.
production_notes: Separate the write path from the layout path: let writers be small and fast, and let scheduled compaction own file size.
Enforce the window with a guardrail (Lakehouse Guard) rather than a calendar reminder.
resources.why: ACID protects writers from each other, but maintenance is also a writer — the ingestion window is the contract that keeps them apart.
resources.diagram:
acid + concurrent writes
   |
   |- writes --> many small files --> peak window: writers only
   |
   |- after the window --> [compaction] --> 128-256 MB files
   |
   |- contending OPTIMIZE? --> halt it (additive, no rollback)
   |
   |- guard --> blocks compaction/expiry during peak ingestion

code.title: The do-not that ends most contention stories
code.code:
Do not run compaction during peak ingestion; it conflicts with
concurrent writers.

code.title: Write path vs layout path
code.code:
writes ─▶ many small files ─▶ [scheduled compaction] ─▶ 128-256 MB files
Compact on a schedule (or auto-compact), targeting a file size that
matches your read pattern. Do it outside the ingestion window so
compaction and writers don't contend.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Aggregations and windows without the skew
resources.description: Aggregations and windows are shuffles in disguise. Treat the group-by key as a skew suspect, read p50 vs p99 and the spill bytes, then apply the matching fix — a salted two-stage aggregate, more partitions, or a partition predicate — and never repartition(1).
when_to_use: A group-by or window stage has one or a few tasks that dominate
An aggregation slows down as the table grows
learning_objectives: Read p50 vs p99 task durations to confirm an aggregation is skewed
Salt a hot key and aggregate twice
Right-size partitions when an oversized aggregate spills

steps.text: Treat the group-by (and any window over the same key) as a shuffle — key skew on a join or group-by key is the first cause to check.
Check shuffle read/write bytes and spill (disk) bytes per task.
Skew if p99 >> p50 (10x+). Uniform slowness if p50 is high.
If a hot key skews the aggregate, salt the hot key on both sides and aggregate twice.
Spill → increase partition count or raise executor memory.
AQE skew-join healing does not fix over-scan; check bytes scanned separately.

what_you_need: A Spark job with a group-by or window stage, and its Spark UI or event log
check_yourself: The evidence is attached: task-duration histogram, shuffle read/write bytes, top-10 keys by row count.
A skewed aggregate is fixed by AQE skew join or the salted two-stage aggregate — not by repartition(1).
gotchas: p99 much greater than p50 means skew; uniformly high p50 means capacity. Salting helps the first, not the second.
Spill shows up as slow tasks, not failures — check spill bytes before paying for bigger executors.
`repartition(1)` serialises the stage — never reach for it to 'fix' slowness.
production_notes: Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics and fail CI on regression.
Monitor task duration p99/p50 ratio, shuffle read/write bytes per run, spill bytes per stage.
resources.why: The same key that groups your rows concentrates your shuffle, so the skew playbook applies to every aggregate before you buy bigger executors.
resources.diagram:
aggregation / window stage
   |
   |- shuffle by key
   |     |- p99 >> p50 --> key skew --> salt hot key, aggregate twice
   |     |- spill bytes high --> more partitions / executor memory
   |     |- all tasks slow, huge shuffle read --> partition/scan, not skew
   |     |- bytes scanned >> table size --> add partition predicate

code.title: Evidence to attach to any aggregation fix
code.code:
The task-duration histogram, the shuffle read/write bytes, and the top-10 keys
by row count — the review is not complete without them.

code.title: Fixes by cause
code.code:
Skew → enable AQE skew join; else salt the hot key and aggregate twice.
Spill → increase partition count or raise executor memory.
Over-scan → add the partition predicate; confirm with bytes scanned.
Never repartition(1); it serialises the stage.

code.title: Monitor the aggregate stage
code.code:
- task duration p99/p50 ratio
- shuffle read/write bytes per run
- spill bytes per stage

resources.title: Attribute a 4x Spark cost regression
resources.description: One job's compute cost quadrupled overnight with no functional change. Run the 4x runbook: diff shuffle and input bytes run-over-run, find the guilty stage, reverse the regression — then wire hook-spark-cost-check so the next one fails CI before the invoice.
when_to_use: Compute spend for one job multiplied without a functional change
A cost-per-run alarm fired right after a deploy
learning_objectives: Diff shuffle write and input bytes run-over-run
Attribute a cost regression to one stage
Gate deploys on shuffle/scan metrics

steps.text: Diff shuffle write bytes and input bytes for the job run-over-run.
Compare output row counts before/after the join, per stage.
Check whether the partition predicate still prunes (bytes scanned).
Fan-out → dedupe the many-side on the join key before joining.
Lost filter → restore the partition predicate and re-run.
Read shuffle/spill/scan metrics from the event log, compare against the stored baseline (median of last 5), and fail if any metric grew by more than 25%.

what_you_need: The event log or job metrics for two runs (before and after the cost jump)
The job source
check_yourself: Output rows from the join stage greatly exceed source rows → fan-out confirmed; after deduping the many-side, output rows match and cost returns to baseline.
A deliberate join change grows shuffle write 3.9x → the build fails with the stage id.
gotchas: Autoscaling masks the cause: a slow stage widens the cluster and buys speed while the fan-out stays.
Compare run-over-run, not day-over-day — traffic deltas will fool the diff.
A dropped partition filter reads full history: the join looks right, the input bytes don't.
production_notes: Track cost per run as a unit metric with a 25% regression alarm.
Gate deploys on shuffle/scan metrics (hook-spark-cost-check).
resources.why: Silent cost regressions compound — a 4x job running hourly is a new invoice line within a day; run-over-run byte diffs find the guilty stage fast.
resources.diagram:
cost 4x
   |
   |- diff bytes run-over-run --> shuffle write + input bytes
   |
   |- output rows >> source rows --> join fan-out --> dedupe the many-side
   |
   |- input bytes >> usual --> lost partition filter --> restore predicate
   |
   |- baseline (median of last 5) --> >25% growth --> fail CI with stage id

code.title: Diff shuffle write and input bytes from the event log
code.code:
# from the event log
grep -E 'Shuffle Write|Input Size' spark.log | tail -40

code.title: Compare join output rows to the source count
code.code: SELECT count(*) FROM stage_output_pre JOIN ... -- compare to source count

code.title: Guard — fail CI when a metric grows > 25% vs the 5-run baseline
code.code:
After the job's test run, read shuffle/spill/scan metrics from the event log,
compare against the stored baseline (median of last 5), and fail if any metric
grew by more than 25%. Emit the offending stage and metric.

Example: shuffle write grows 3.9x after a join change → build fails with the stage id.

resources.title: Audit an MCP server's tool contracts
resources.description: Before connecting an MCP server, audit its tools for blast radius. Read each tool schema, classify every tool as Read, Write, Destructive, Spend or Exfiltrate, and produce a least-privilege connection config that grants only what the task needs.
when_to_use: Before connecting a new MCP server
Writing the least-privilege config for an agent

Classify tools by blast radius
Write a least-privilege MCP configuration

Classify every tool — Read, Write, Destructive, Spend, Exfiltrate.
Treat Destructive tools (delete/drop/truncate) as requiring human confirmation.
Produce a table of tools by class, then a config that grants only the Read/Write tools the task needs.
Never connect an unvetted server with broad credentials.

The task the agent must perform

resources.title: Capstone — the batch pipeline checklist
resources.description: Bring the API → S3 → Spark → Parquet starter up end to end, then audit it: offline transform tests, idempotent partition-scoped writes, complete partitions, replay-safe extraction, and baseline metrics with a CI guard. One pipeline that exercises every lesson in the series.
when_to_use: You finished the series and want one pipeline that exercises every lesson
A new batch pipeline needs a production checklist before its first real run
learning_objectives: Run a batch pipeline end to end with offline tests
Prove idempotency with a two-run row-count check
Ship the completeness, hardening, and baseline guards

steps.text: The pipeline — REST API → extract (paginate + retry) → S3 raw/ (JSON, immutable) → PySpark transform (type, dedupe, partition) → S3 curated/ (Parquet, dt=.., Hive layout).
Bring it up — `make up` starts MinIO + a local Spark, `make seed` uploads sample raw JSON, `make test` runs the transform tests offline.
The tests that matter — row count stable across two runs (idempotency), no nulls in the business key, and partition dt matches the logical date, not the wall clock.
A re-run for the same date must not duplicate rows — the overwrite is partition-scoped.
The invariant — running the same date twice yields identical output.
Harden — retry with jittered exponential backoff, alert on extract lag and on null business keys, checksum raw files, and store the API's cursor for replay.
A completeness check asserts every expected partition exists, and the logical date is stored explicitly as a partition column, not derived at read time.

what_you_need: Docker (the starter runs MinIO + a local Spark)
An API endpoint to extract from, or the seeded sample data
check_yourself: Two consecutive runs produce the same row count, and dt equals the logical date.
Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics exist and CI fails on a regression.
The overwrite is partition-scoped — a re-run for the same date does not duplicate rows.
gotchas: A re-run for the same date duplicates rows → the overwrite is not partition-scoped.
An API returns 429 → backoff then resume from the last cursor, not from page 1.
An empty partition and an absent partition both read as 'no data' downstream.
production_notes: Checksum raw files; store the API's cursor for replay.
Store the logical date explicitly as a partition column, not derived at read time.
resources.why: A pipeline is done when re-runs are safe, partitions are complete, and the metrics that would catch today's failure are baselined.
resources.diagram:
capstone checklist
   |
   |- run --> make up / seed / test (offline, MinIO + local Spark)
   |
   |- idempotency --> row count stable across two runs
   |
   |- completeness --> every expected dt partition exists
   |
   |- hardening --> backoff, cursor replay, raw checksums
   |
   |- guard --> baseline shuffle/spill/scan, CI fails on regression

code.title: Bring the pipeline up
code.code:
make up    # starts MinIO + a local Spark
make seed  # uploads sample raw JSON
make test  # runs the transform tests offline

code.title: The pipeline under test
code.code:
REST API ─▶ [extract: paginate + retry] ─▶ S3 raw/ (JSON, immutable)
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                [PySpark transform: type, dedupe, partition]
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                S3 curated/ (Parquet, dt=.., Hive layout)

code.title: Failure scenarios to drill
code.code:
- API returns 429 → backoff then resume from the last cursor, not from page 1
- A page arrives with a changed field type → quarantine the page, alert
- A re-run for the same date duplicates rows → the overwrite is not partition-scoped

resources.title: Capstone — the checklist that decides whether a DAG ships
resources.description: Close the series by running the full review pass over your own pipeline: the idempotency test per task, partitioned or MERGE writes, deliberate catchup, backoff retries, reschedule sensors, bounded concurrency — and a documented runbook for the day history needs fixing.
when_to_use: Signing off a DAG before it merges or takes production traffic
Auditing an inherited DAG for the first time
learning_objectives: Run the full four-step review pass end to end
Confirm every checklist item on your own pipeline
Leave behind a runbook so the next backfill is routine

steps.text: Apply the idempotency test to every task.
Every task writes to a partition keyed by the logical date, or uses MERGE.
Set `catchup` as a deliberate choice, not a default.
Retries have a backoff; a task that retries instantly will hammer a downstream.
Cap max_active_runs and pool limits so a backfill cannot starve the daily run.
Sensors use `reschedule`, not `poke`, so they don't hold a worker slot.
Keep pipelines idempotent so a backfill is a routine operation.

what_you_need: The DAG you built across this series
The pipeline's schedule, SLA and lineage
check_yourself: The four-step review pass — idempotency, retry/timeout/concurrency, backfill prediction, missing tests — runs clean over the capstone DAG.
A documented backfill runbook exists for the pipeline, with its idle window and resource budget.
gotchas: A task that appends without a partition key will duplicate rows on retry.
Never overlap the production window; never backfill without a rollback path.
Backfilling without a written definition of correctness just relocates the bug.
production_notes: Document a backfill runbook per pipeline, with its idle window and resource budget.
Keep the fixture of 8 DAGs with seeded non-idempotency bugs in CI so regressions resurface.
resources.why: Ten lessons reduce to one list — if the checklist passes, the DAG survives retries, catchup and the next backfill.
resources.diagram:
capstone checklist
   |
   |- idempotency test --> partition or MERGE writes
   |
   |- deliberate catchup --> backoff retries --> reschedule sensors
   |
   |- bounded concurrency --> backfill runbook --> ship

code.title: The full DAG review checklist
code.code:
1. Every task writes to a partition keyed by the logical date, or uses MERGE.
2. `catchup` is a deliberate choice, not a default.
3. Retries have a backoff; a task that retries instantly will hammer a downstream.
4. `max_active_runs` and pool limits prevent a backfill from starving the daily run.
5. Sensors use `reschedule`, not `poke`, so they don't hold a worker slot.

code.title: The four-step review pass
code.code:
1. Apply the idempotency test to every task.
2. Check retry, timeout and concurrency settings.
3. Predict backfill behaviour.
4. Propose missing integration tests.

resources.title: Capstone — the cloud guardrail checklist
resources.description: Close the series by turning nine lessons into one standing checklist: workgroup bytes limits and compaction on storage, sized workers and stable bookmarks on compute, resource monitors and unit-metric alerts on spend, and least-privilege IAM everywhere — then produce the four review outputs as evidence.
when_to_use: A platform just left the build phase and needs its guardrails inventoried
A quarterly review needs one page that covers the whole cloud series
learning_objectives: Run the full cloud guardrail checklist on your own platform
Turn each series lesson into a standing check with an owner
Produce the four review outputs as evidence

steps.text: Storage and query guardrails — an Athena workgroup with a per-query bytes-scanned limit, a nightly compaction job, and CloudWatch alarms on scanned bytes per hour.
IaC baseline — S3 buckets with lifecycle + encryption, a Glue catalogue, IAM roles scoped to least privilege, and Athena workgroups with query limits.
Compute guardrails — size Glue workers from data volume, not habit, use job bookmarks correctly, and avoid full-table reprocessing from catalogue mistakes.
Scan guardrails — read the scanned-bytes metric per query, apply partition projection for high-cardinality columns, and compact small files to cut per-request overhead.
Warehouse guardrails — configure warehouses for different workloads, set up resource monitors for budget enforcement, and optimize auto-scaling for cost/performance.
Spend guardrails — attribute compute cost to a pipeline run, define a unit metric that resists regressions, and alert on cost-per-run rather than total spend.
Evidence — collect the four review outputs: architecture diagram (text), IAM findings, cost drivers, and reliability risks.

what_you_need: Your platform's IaC or an architecture description
The series lessons 1-9 completed
check_yourself: Every guardrail family has a live check — bytes-scanned limit and compaction on storage, task histograms on compute, credit caps and cost-per-run alarms on spend, least-privilege roles on IAM.
The four review outputs (diagram, IAM findings, cost drivers, reliability risks) exist as artifacts from your last review pass.
No agent or job in the account holds an admin role.
gotchas: A checklist without an owner rots — assign each guardrail family to a person or a pipeline.
The reviewer never creates resources and requires human approval for any IAM recommendation — keep it that way.
Guardrails are per environment — dev XSMALL with 100 credits is not a production config.
production_notes: Score each review against the 30-anti-pattern checklist so passes are comparable over time.
Re-run the checklist quarterly and every time a new service joins the stack.
resources.why: A cloud platform is production-ready when each guardrail in this series is a standing check with an owner, not a memory.

resources.title: Capstone — the reliability checklist for a pipeline you can page on
resources.description: Close the series by running the reliability checklist over your own pipeline: a declared and enforced SLA, idempotent tasks with backoff retries, a documented backfill runbook — then drill the incident path from alert to blameless postmortem with dated, owned action items.
when_to_use: Signing off a pipeline for on-call
Running a quarterly reliability drill
learning_objectives: Run the reliability checklist over your own pipeline end to end
Drill the incident path — match the alert, walk the runbook, capture the timeline
Close with a blameless postmortem with dated, owned action items

steps.text: Declare the SLA — freshness and completeness — with the CI test that enforces it, because a contract with no enforcement is documentation.
Make every task idempotent so a re-run is always safe, and retry with backoff with a clear failure classification in the alert.
Keep a documented backfill runbook per pipeline.
When the alert fires, load the production playbooks into the agent, match the alert to a runbook, and walk the operator through diagnosis and mitigation step by step.
The incident workflow — establish impact and start time; check for a correlated deploy; walk the matching runbook; capture the timeline for the postmortem.

The postmortem structure — impact in business terms with a duration; a timestamped, factual, no-blame timeline; how we found out, because if a human told us that's a gap; contributing factors, plural; action items each with an owner, a date and a "done" definition.
"Be more careful" is not an action item — change the system so a careful mistake is harmless.

what_you_need: The pipeline you built across this series
Its SLA, runbook and alert routing
check_yourself: The checklist passes — SLA declared and enforced, tasks idempotent with backoff retries, backfill runbook documented, failure class in the alert text.
A tabletop incident produces a rolling timeline and a draft postmortem with dated, owned action items.
gotchas: "Be more careful" is not an action item — change the system so a careful mistake is harmless.
If a human told you about the incident, detection is a gap.
Incidents are rarely single-cause — contributing factors are plural.
production_notes: Capture the timeline as the incident happens, not from memory afterwards.
The incident assistant suggests, never executes, production changes — it escalates to a human before any destructive step.
resources.why: Ten lessons reduce to one page — a declared SLA, idempotent tasks, a backfill runbook, classified alerts, and a postmortem that changes the system.
resources.diagram:
reliability capstone
   |
   |- SLA declared + enforced --> freshness, completeness in CI
   |
   |- idempotent tasks + backoff retries --> reruns safe by construction
   |
   |- backfill runbook documented --> history fixable without fear
   |
   |- alert --> match runbook --> walk diagnosis --> capture timeline
   |
   |- postmortem --> impact, timeline, detection, factors, owned actions

code.title: The postmortem structure
code.code:
1. **Impact** — who/what, in business terms, with a duration.
2. **Timeline** — timestamped, factual, no blame.
3. **Detection** — how we found out; if a human told us, that's a gap.
4. **Contributing factors** — plural; incidents are rarely single-cause.
5. **Action items** — each with an owner and a date, and a "done" definition.

code.code:

Check for a correlated deploy.
Walk the matching runbook.
Capture the timeline for the postmortem.

/match-alert

resources.title: Capstone — the SQL correctness checklist
resources.description: Close the series by turning nine lessons into one standing checklist: a grain statement for every SELECT, a cardinality justification for every join, NULL-safe anti-joins, explicit casts, lint in CI, and one decision rule for slow queries. Each line cites the lesson that earned it, and the checklist ends where the review agent ends — with findings that cite severity, location, rule, and fix.
when_to_use: A new query, model, or PR needs one pass that covers the whole series
A quarterly review needs one page that covers the whole python-sql series
learning_objectives: Assemble the series' rules into one checklist you can run on any query
Turn each checklist line into a standing check with an owner
Emit findings with severity, location, rule, and fix

steps.text: Line one, from lesson 1 — ask the first question: what is the grain of this result? If the author can't answer, stop.
Line two, from lesson 3 — every join states its cardinality (1:1, N:1, N:N) and justifies it.
Line three, from lessons 3 and 4 — prove a join cannot fan out before writing it.
Line four, from lesson 8 — NOT IN where the subquery can return NULL is banned; use NOT EXISTS.
Line five, from lesson 8 — comparisons across types must be explicit casts, not implicit.
Line six, from lesson 5 — integrate SQLFluff into CI/CD pipelines so the structure rules hold without review time.
Line seven, from lesson 6 — for the slow query, decide between an index, a rewrite, or a stats refresh.
The standing output — a findings list (severity, location, rule, fix) and a grain statement for each SELECT.

what_you_need: The series lessons 1-9 completed
check_yourself: You can run the whole checklist on a query you have never seen and produce findings with severity, location, rule, and fix.
Each checklist line names the lesson and the rule that backs it.
The checklist is wired into CI — lint and review rules run without a human remembering them.
gotchas: A checklist that lives in a doc rots — wire the lint and review rules into CI instead.
Stop at the first violation; five findings at once hide which fix worked.
The checklist checks correctness first — the plan reading comes after the query is right.
production_notes: Assign an owner to each line — an unowned check is a wish.
Keep the 12-case evaluation fixture in CI so the review rules stay honest.
resources.why: Nine lessons become production-ready when each rule on this checklist is a standing check with an owner, not a memory.

   |

   |
   |- sqlfluff in CI --> structure (lesson 5)
   |
   |- one fix per slow query --> index, rewrite, or stats refresh (lesson 6)
   |
   |- findings --> severity, location, rule, fix

resources.description: Close the series by running the full checklist on one table you own: zones with gates, a deliberately chosen format, the three standing monitors, the four-part maintenance plan as a scheduled job, guardrail-enforced windows, and the escalation line that decides when it pages.

Turn the four-part maintenance plan into a scheduled job with alerts
Apply the escalation line — page only on a freshness-SLA threat

steps.text: Check the zones: raw/ is immutable, exactly as received, never edited, schema-on-read; curated/ is cleaned, typed, deduplicated, quality-gated; serving/ is SLA-bearing — and each zone has a different retention, quality bar and owner, with promotion between zones a pipeline step with a gate, not a copy.

Check the format decision: Delta's docs are the definitive source for Delta features and the maintenance operations the lakehouse skills reference — compare with a Delta vs Iceberg decision guide before committing to a format.
Check the monitors: file count, avg file size, planning time.

Check the maintenance plan: rewrite_data_files with a target size (128-256 MB), rewrite_manifests when the manifest list is huge, expire_snapshots within retention keeping one full snapshot for time travel, remove_orphan_files on a schedule with a safety margin.
Check the automation: enable Delta auto-compaction or schedule Iceberg rewrite_data_files; target 128-256 MB files and alert on file-count growth.
Check the guardrails: /table-health for a status read, /plan-compaction for the maintenance plan, /expire-snapshots for the expiry plan — plans first, not ad hoc runs.
Check the escalation line: no page — schedule compaction; escalate only if planning time threatens a critical dashboard's freshness SLA.

check_yourself: Every zone has a named owner, a quality bar, and a gate — and curated is not a dumping ground.
The three monitors (file count, avg file size, planning time) have alerts, and 128-256 MB is the recorded target.
A /plan-compaction during peak ingestion is blocked; the same plan after the window runs.
gotchas: Compaction and snapshot expiry never run during peak ingestion — the guard blocks them, and so should you.
Curated becomes a dumping ground without an enforced gate — promotion is a pipeline step, not a copy.
Escalate only when planning time threatens a critical dashboard's freshness SLA — otherwise schedule, do not page.
production_notes: The four-part plan (data files, manifests, snapshots, orphans) is one scheduled job with a safety margin — never four ad hoc commands.

resources.title: Capstone — the warehousing checklist, end to end
resources.description: Close the series by auditing one warehouse project against everything it taught: models with tests and docs, layered staging to marts with a declared grain, incremental loads with a lookback, CI on a staging schema, monitored query history, and a repo structure a new joiner can read.
when_to_use: Closing out a warehouse build before handover
Quarterly review of an existing warehouse project
learning_objectives: Audit a warehouse project against the model-tests-docs triad
Verify layering, grain, incremental lookback, and CI staging on one project
Leave a repo whose structure a new joiner can read

steps.text: Audit the triad — every model is code with three faces: model (SQL) + tests (schema.yml) + docs (descriptions); ref() builds the DAG, tests encode the invariants, and materialisation is a deliberate choice per model.
Check the layers and the load — staging, intermediate, and marts with the grain declared, and incremental on fct_orders with a 3-day lookback.
Check the test set — unique + not_null on the fct grain key, relationships from fct to dims, and accepted_values on status.
Check the production gate — CI builds to a per-PR staging schema and runs full tests, source freshness checks on raw, and exposures declared for dashboards.
Check the watchtower — alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio and review query history weekly for the top cost queries.
Check the team constraints — logic must be reviewable, changes must be testable, and new joiners need to understand the lineage.
Check the repo reads clean — models/staging, models/intermediate, models/marts, schema.yml with tests and descriptions, singular tests, macros, and the CI workflow.

what_you_need: A warehouse project you own or review — the dbt-warehouse-tests starter works
The project's query history and CI configuration
One afternoon to run the checklist for real

CI green but prod differs → CI ran on a different target/schema.

production_notes: Keep tests and descriptions on every node; CI on a staging schema with source freshness on raw.
Keep the partitions-ratio alert and the weekly top-cost review on the calendar.

resources.title: Capstone — wire a dataset's quality gates end to end
resources.description: Close the series by walking one SLA-bearing dataset through every gate the series taught — six-part contract, CI compatibility check, staged quality suite, quarantine split, quarantine-rate alerts — and finish with the monitoring signals and incident paths that keep the gates honest.
when_to_use: A dataset is about to become SLA-bearing and needs its gates wired in one pass
Auditing an existing pipeline for missing quality gates
learning_objectives: Run the full checklist — contract, CI gate, promotion gate, quarantine, alerts — against one dataset
Point at the registry artifact that enforces each gate
Name the monitoring signals and prevention paths that keep the gates honest

steps.text: Write the six-part contract — owner, schema, semantics, SLA, breaking-change policy, enforcement.
Run the contract as code in the producer's CI — compatibility check, then build, then publish.
After a pipeline writes to the staging namespace, run the model's dbt/GE tests against the staged output; promote only if all critical tests pass.
Split every batch into publish and quarantine on a quality contract — a row never disappears.
Alert when quarantine rate > 1% for 2 consecutive runs, and ship a reprocess command that re-runs the quarantined rows after a fix.
Watch the signals — expectation pass rate, quarantine row counts, freshness.
Close the loop with consumer-driven contract tests in the producer's pipeline.

what_you_need: The eight earlier lessons of this series, or their registry artifacts
A dataset with a consumer and an SLA worth defending
check_yourself: The checklist names the CI test that fails on violation — enforcement, part six of the contract.
A not-null test failing on 412 rows in staging blocks promotion and leaves the previous production data in place.
The quarantine alert fires on rate — 1% for 2 consecutive runs — not only on a hard failure.
gotchas: Tier the expectations: critical (block) vs warning (alert only) — blocking on a warning-tier expectation turns small blips into outages.
Quarantine never reviewed → add a scheduled review and a reprocess path.
The gate lives where the change is made (producer CI), not in the consumer's runtime — the cheapest place to catch it is before merge.
production_notes: Alert when quarantine rate > 1% for 2 consecutive runs.
Contracts get CI enforcement and a dated deprecation path.
resources.why: A quality gate you cannot point at in the registry is a hope, not a gate — the capstone makes every gate concrete, named and enforced.
resources.diagram:
capstone checklist
   |
   |- contract (six parts) --> CI compatibility check --> build --> publish
   |
   |- staged run --> dbt/GE tests --> all critical pass --> promote
   |                                  any critical fail --> block --> production untouched
   |
   |- batch --> pass --> published
   |             fail --> quarantine (+reason) --> rate > 1% x2 runs --> alert --> review --> reprocess
   |
   |- signals: expectation pass rate, quarantine row counts, freshness
   |
   |- consumer-driven contract tests in the producer's pipeline

code.title: The six-part contract
code.code:
1. Owner (a team, with an on-call).
2. Schema (typed, versioned).
3. Semantics (what each field *means*, units, nullability).
4. SLA (freshness, completeness).
5. Breaking-change policy (notice period, deprecation path).
6. Enforcement (which CI test fails on violation).

purpose: Run the quality suite against a staged run before promoting to production.
failure_behavior: block

resources.title: Diagnose a skewed Spark stage
resources.description: One Spark stage hangs while other executors idle. Open the stage view, read the p50-vs-p99 task durations, and follow the skew skill's decision order: AQE skew join first, salting second, broadcast only under a size budget — and never repartition(1).
when_to_use: A batch job's runtime jumped and no code changed
Executors idle while a few tasks run long
learning_objectives: Read task-level duration histograms to confirm skew
Choose between AQE skew join, salting and broadcast
Attach the evidence a skew review requires

steps.text: Open the Spark UI stage view; compare p50 vs p99 task duration.
Skew if p99 >> p50 (10x+). Uniform slowness if p50 is high.
Check shuffle read/write bytes and spill (disk) bytes per task.
Confirm with `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true` — if it fixes it, ship that.
If not, salt the hot key on both sides and aggregate twice.
Broadcast only if the small side is < 100 MB *after* filtering; never `repartition(1)` to 'fix' skew — it serialises the stage.

what_you_need: Spark UI access or the job's event log
The job source
check_yourself: Re-running with `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true` removes the straggler; if it does not, the salted two-stage aggregate does.
The task-duration histogram, the shuffle read/write bytes, and the top-10 keys by row count are attached — the review is not complete without them.
gotchas: repartition(1) serialises the stage — never reach for it to 'fix' slowness.
p99 much greater than p50 means skew; uniformly high p50 means capacity. Salting helps the first, not the second.
Spill shows up as slow tasks, not failures — check spill bytes before paying for bigger executors.
production_notes: Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics so CI can fail a regression before users feel it.
Keep AQE on, and confirm broadcast vs sort-merge plans with explain('formatted') before shipping.
resources.why: Slow jobs miss SLAs and burn executor-hours — attributing between skew, spill and over-scan is the difference between a 10-minute and a 10-hour incident.
resources.diagram:
stage slow
   |
   |- p99 >> p50 --> key skew --> AQE skew join --> fixed? ship
   |                                          > not fixed --> salt hot key, aggregate twice
   |
   |- spill bytes high --> oversized partitions --> more partitions / memory
   |
   |- all tasks slow (high p50) --> capacity, not skew --> do not salt

code.title: Confirm the diagnosis — AQE on, event log, plan
code.code:
spark-submit --conf spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true ...
# inspect the event log: grep 'TaskSetManager' spark.log | tail
df.explain('formatted')  # confirm broadcast vs sort-merge join

code.title: Skew signals
code.code:
- Median task duration ~p50, but p99 is 30x+ → key skew.
- All tasks slow and shuffle read is huge → partition/scan problem, not skew.
- One executor at 100% while others idle → hot partition.

code.title: Decision order — AQE, salt, broadcast, never repartition(1)
code.code:
1. Confirm with `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true` — if it fixes it, ship that.
2. If not, salt the hot key on both sides and aggregate twice.
3. Broadcast only if the small side is < 100 MB *after* filtering.
4. Never `repartition(1)` to "fix" skew; it serialises the stage.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Diagnose a small-files explosion
resources.description: Follow the small-files runbook from symptom to prevention: confirm the tens-of-thousands-of-tiny-files signature, query the metadata tables for the average file size, compact to a 128-256 MB target, coarsen an over-partitioned layout, and schedule compaction outside the ingestion window. The fix follows the small-files compaction pattern — separate the write path from the layout path.
when_to_use: Planning or listing time dominates query time on one table
Metadata operations (OPTIMIZE/REPAIR) have become very slow
learning_objectives: Recognize the small-files signature from file sizes and planning time
Query metadata tables to quantify fragmentation
Fix the layout, not just the symptoms

steps.text: Confirm the symptoms: tens of thousands of tiny files, query planning and listing dominating query time, metadata operations (OPTIMIZE/REPAIR) very slow.
List file sizes; avg < 32 MB and a growing count is the signature.
For Iceberg/Delta, query the metadata tables (`files`, `history`).
Compact to a 128-256 MB target; rewrite manifests if huge.
Reduce partition granularity if the layout over-partitions.
Auto-compaction on the table (Delta) or a scheduled maintenance job; partition by date, not by hour/user, unless access patterns demand it.

what_you_need: A table whose queries spend more time planning than scanning
Metadata-table access (Iceberg files, Delta history)
An ingestion window you can schedule compaction around
check_yourself: The metadata query shows an average file size under 32 MB before the fix and inside the 128-256 MB target after compaction.
Planning time no longer dominates — the same query's planning phase shrinks below scan time after compaction and layout coarsening.
gotchas: Compact after the ingestion window, never during it.
ZORDER rewrites the whole table — only worth it on a real query predicate.
Over-partitioning is often the root cause; coarsening the layout beats compacting harder.
production_notes: Enable Delta auto-compaction or schedule Iceberg rewrite_data_files.
Target 128-256 MB files and alert on file-count growth.
resources.why: Fragmentation turns every read into a metadata crawl; compaction restores predictable latency without touching consumers.
resources.diagram:
small files diagnosis
   |
   |- planning dominates query time --> list file sizes
   |
   |- avg < 32 MB + growing count --> metadata tables (files/history)
   |
   |- compact to 128-256 MB --> rewrite manifests if huge
   |
   |- over-partitioned? --> coarsen layout (date, not hour/user)
   |
    |- schedule compaction after ingestion window --> prevent regrowth

code.title: Quantify fragmentation from the metadata tables
code.code: SELECT count(*), avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 FROM db.tbl.files;

code.title: Compaction commands (Delta and Iceberg)
code.code:
OPTIMIZE db.tbl ZORDER BY (user_id);  -- Delta
CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files('db.tbl');  -- Iceberg

code.title: Fix and prevention
code.code:
Fix:
- Compact to a 128-256 MB target; rewrite manifests if huge.
- Reduce partition granularity if the layout over-partitions.
- Schedule compaction after the ingestion window, never during it.

Prevention:
- Auto-compaction on the table (Delta) or a scheduled maintenance job.
- Partition by date, not by hour/user, unless access patterns demand it.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: DR and replication — design the recovery path before you need it
resources.description: Disaster recovery for data systems starts before the outage: DDIA's replication and consistency chapters name the mechanisms, and the registry's runbooks name the recovery paths — code rollback for deterministic failures, quarantine-then-retry for data errors, shadow-then-swap for recomputes.
when_to_use: Deciding which tables need replication, snapshots or both
Writing the recovery section of a pipeline's runbook
learning_objectives: Map replication and consistency from DDIA to mechanisms in your own stack
Keep the old data until the new data is validated — shadow-then-swap as rollback
Classify recovery per failure class — code rollback vs quarantine-then-retry vs recompute

steps.text: DDIA's chapters map directly to patterns in this registry — replication to CDC, partitioning to lakehouse, consistency to transaction semantics.
A recovery design must satisfy three forces — correctness must be verifiable, production must stay available, rollback must be possible.
Keep the old data until validated — shadow-then-swap keeps rollback in reach: delete the shadow, never the production table; swap only after sample validation passes.
Classify the recovery by failure class — roll back the code deploy if the class is deterministic and new; data errors get quarantine-then-retry, not rollback.
Recovery is when destructive SQL is most dangerous — destructive statements are denied by default, and a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied.
Any write-class tool against a production target is suspended and surfaced for a human "approve once" token scoped to the single call.

what_you_need: The tables your consumers cannot lose
The deploy/revert mechanism for pipeline code
A recovery drill scheduled with the platform owner
check_yourself: Every critical table has a named recovery path — code rollback, quarantine-then-retry, or shadow-then-swap recompute.
The old data still exists until the replacement is validated — you have never deleted production to fix production.
gotchas: Roll back the code deploy if the class is deterministic and new — data errors get quarantine-then-retry, not rollback.
Delete the shadow, never the production table; swap only after sample validation passes.
A DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied — recovery scripts are not exempt.
production_notes: Map replication to CDC and consistency to transaction semantics when choosing the mechanism for each critical table.
Suspend write-class tools against production targets during recovery — a human approve-once token scoped to a single call.
resources.why: Rollback must be possible — a recovery path that starts with "delete production" is not a path, and replication is the principle that keeps one open.
resources.diagram:
recovery paths
   |
   |- deterministic (new code) --> roll back the deploy
   |
   |- data error --> quarantine input --> re-run idempotently
   |
   |- recompute --> shadow-then-swap --> old data kept until validated
   |
   |- destructive SQL during recovery --> denied by default

code.title: Recovery classification
code.code:
Roll back the code deploy if the class is deterministic and new; data errors
get quarantine-then-retry, not rollback.

code.title: The three forces a recovery design satisfies
code.code:
- Correctness must be verifiable
- Production must stay available
- Rollback must be possible

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Fan out over date batches with dynamic task mapping
resources.description: Run one task definition over many date batches with dynamic task mapping — the docs' mapping feature applied the way the backfill material demands: batched ranges, smallest first, a validated sample after each batch.
when_to_use: The same transformation must run over many dates or partitions
A single large range would starve the cluster
learning_objectives: Map one task over many date batches with dynamic task mapping
Scope the fan-out by date and by dependency
Validate a sample after each batch before continuing

steps.text: Use dynamic task mapping — one of the topics Airflow's documentation covers — to run one task definition over many inputs.
Scope a backfill by date and by dependency.
Prefer batched date ranges over one large range.
One huge date range starves the cluster; batch it and validate a sample per batch.
Backfill in date batches, smallest first, validating a sample after each batch.
Stage a backfill gradually with validation between batches.

what_you_need: A date range to recompute or process
The cluster's idle window and resource budget
check_yourself: The DAG maps the task over weekly date batches, smallest first, instead of one 90-day range.
Each batch instance validates a sample before the next batch starts.
gotchas: One huge date range starves the cluster; batch it and validate a sample per batch.
Backfill in date batches, smallest first, validating a sample after each batch.
production_notes: Detect which downstream tables must also be rebuilt before fanning out.
Monitor backfill progress, resource contention and validation pass rate.
resources.why: Dynamic task mapping turns 'run this over N dates' into N checked instances — the batched, validated shape the backfill material demands.
resources.diagram:
dynamic mapping over date batches
   |
   |- date range --> batch into ranges, smallest first
   |
   |- map task over batches --> N instances
   |
   |- validate sample per batch --> proceed or stop

code.title: Batched range command
code.code:
airflow dags backfill --start-date YYYY-MM-DD --end-date YYYY-MM-DD --reset-dagruns dag_id
# prefer batched date ranges over one large range

code.title: Execution rule
code.code: Backfill in date batches, smallest first, validating a sample after each batch.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Gate backfills with the safety check hook
resources.description: Wire the Backfill Safety Check as a pre-run gate that refuses any backfill lacking an explicit date range, a shadow or snapshotted target, and a window clear of the scheduled production run — and watch it block the bare backfill command that would otherwise corrupt the target.
when_to_use: Any historical recompute of a production table
A backfill trigger lacks a rollback path or overlaps the daily run
learning_objectives: Install a pre-run gate that intercepts backfill triggers
State the three requirements the hook enforces before any backfill
Recognize a denied bare backfill command and what it was missing

steps.text: Set the trigger to pre-run so the check intercepts a backfill trigger.
Require an explicit date range.
Require a target that is either a shadow table or snapshotted.
Require a window that does not overlap the scheduled production run.
Deny the trigger otherwise — failure behavior is block.
Confirm the gate: a bare `airflow dags backfill --start-date 2024-01-01` is denied for missing a range and rollback.

what_you_need: A scheduler or wrapper that triggers backfills
The daily production schedule for the target DAG
A shadow table or snapshot procedure for the target
check_yourself: A bare `airflow dags backfill --start-date 2024-01-01` is denied for missing a range and rollback.
A trigger with an explicit range, a snapshotted target and an off-peak window passes the pre-run check.
gotchas: Never overlap the production window; never backfill without a rollback path.
An explicit date range alone is not enough — the target must be a shadow table or snapshotted.
Passing the gate is not the finish line — backfill in date batches, smallest first, validating a sample after each batch.
production_notes: failure_behavior is block — the hook denies the trigger instead of warning.
Document a backfill runbook per pipeline, with its idle window and resource budget.
resources.why: The cheapest backfill incident is the one denied before it starts — a pre-run block costs seconds, a corrupted target costs days.
resources.diagram:
backfill trigger
   |
   |- pre-run gate --> explicit date range? --> no --> block
   |
   |- shadow or snapshotted target? --> no --> block
   |
   |- window clear of daily run? --> yes --> run batches, validate samples

code.title: Pre-run gate requirements
code.code:
Intercepts a backfill trigger. Requires: an explicit date range, a target that
is either a shadow table or snapshotted, and a window that does not overlap the
scheduled production run. Denies otherwise.

code.title: Bare backfill command the gate denies
code.code: airflow dags backfill --start-date 2024-01-01

code.title: Compliant trigger with an explicit range
code.code: airflow dags backfill --start-date YYYY-MM-DD --end-date YYYY-MM-DD --reset-dagruns dag_id

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Gate promotion with a pre-deploy DQ check
resources.description: Wire the pre-deployment DQ check so a pipeline is only promoted when its quality suite passes against staged output. You attach the pre-deploy trigger, run dbt/GE tests on the staging namespace, and prove a failed expectation leaves production untouched.
when_to_use: A staged run must pass its quality suite before promotion to production
Bad data must never reach consumers, even under a urgent deploy
learning_objectives: Attach the DQ suite to a pre-deploy trigger
Promote only when critical tests pass on staged output
Block promotion while keeping the previous production data

steps.text: Wire the check to the pre-deploy trigger, before promotion to production.
After a pipeline writes to the staging namespace, run the model's dbt/GE tests against the staged output.
Promote only if all critical tests pass.
Otherwise leave the previous production data in place and report the failed expectations.
Confirm the failure behavior is block — a not-null test failing on 412 rows in staging blocks promotion, production untouched.

what_you_need: A pipeline that writes to a staging namespace before production
A dbt or Great Expectations test suite for the model
A deployment workflow with a pre-deploy stage to register the hook

check_yourself.Stage a run with a not-null violation: promotion is blocked and the previous production data is still in place.

check_yourself: The hook's failure_behavior is block — an all-green critical suite is the only path to promotion.
gotchas: The check runs after the pipeline writes to staging — an empty or stale staging namespace has nothing to test.
Tier the expectations: critical (block) vs warning (alert only) — blocking on a warning-tier expectation turns small blips into outages.
When the gate blocks, production still serves the previous data — say so in the report instead of assuming the deploy partially landed.
production_notes: Promote only on an all-green critical suite; anything else leaves the previous production data in place.
Report the failed expectations with the block — the operator needs the column, rule and row count.
resources.why: Promotion is the last chance to stop a bad batch — this hook turns the quality suite into that last gate.
resources.diagram:
deploy
   |
   |- pipeline writes --> staging namespace
   |
   |- pre-deploy hook --> run dbt/GE tests on staged output
   |
   |- all critical pass --> promote --> production
   |
   |- any critical fail --> block --> production untouched --> report failures

code.title: Hook contract — pre-deploy trigger, block on failure
code.code:
# hook-pre-deployment-dq-check
trigger: pre-deploy
purpose: Run the quality suite against a staged run before promoting to production.
failure_behavior: block

code.title: Run the quality suite against the staged output
code.code:
After a pipeline writes to the staging namespace, run the model's dbt/GE tests
against the staged output. Promote only if all critical tests pass; otherwise
leave the previous production data in place and report the failed expectations.

code.title: What a blocked promotion looks like
code.code: A not-null test fails on 412 rows in staging → promotion blocked, production untouched.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Govern cloud spend — right-sizing, resource monitors, and unit economics
resources.description: Govern cloud spend the way you govern data quality: right-size each warehouse per environment, put a resource monitor between the workload and the invoice, and alert on cost-per-run instead of total spend. Ends with the unit-economics rule that turns a 4x regression into a number, not a surprise.
when_to_use: Warehouse spend grows with no change in workload
A team debates warehouse sizing with no documented per-environment defaults
Cost alerts fire on total spend and everyone ignores them
learning_objectives: Right-size warehouses per environment instead of one size for all
Enforce budgets with resource monitors and hard credit caps
Alert on cost-per-run, not on total spend

steps.text: Start from a template that covers warehouse sizing, auto-suspend/resume, resource monitors for cost control, query acceleration, and multi-cluster settings — with dev, staging, and production defaults.
Right-size per environment — dev runs XSMALL with a 60-second auto-suspend and 100 monitor credits; staging runs MEDIUM with 500; production runs LARGE with 5,000 credits and 2-5 clusters.

Know the parameters that carry money — warehouse_size is compute (credits/hour), auto_suspend is seconds of inactivity before suspend (0 = never), and resource_monitor_credits is the monthly credit quota.
Turn billing into unit economics — cost per 1M rows, per run, per model — so a 4x regression shows up as a number, not a surprise invoice.
Learn why total spend is the wrong alert — total spend rises with growth and hides regressions, while cost-per-unit is flat when growth is healthy and spikes the day a join starts fanning out.
Back the budget with a hard cap — any principal that can run billable queries gets a resource monitor with a hard credit cap and a read-only role by default.
When a sizing debate stalls, go to the source — the performance and cost sections are the reference for clustering-key and warehouse-sizing decisions.

what_you_need: A Snowflake account where you can create warehouses and resource monitors
check_yourself: The dev warehouse auto-suspends after 60 seconds and carries 100 monitor credits while production runs LARGE with 5,000 — and you can say why they differ.
Your alert fires on $ per pipeline run with a regression threshold, not on the month's total bill.
Every principal that can run billable queries sits behind a resource monitor with a hard credit cap.
gotchas: auto_suspend = 0 means never suspend — an idle warehouse bills credits until you change it.
Total spend rises with growth and hides regressions — cost-per-unit is the metric that spikes the day a join starts fanning out.
Resource monitor credits must be positive (at least 1) — a zero quota is not a budget.
production_notes: Ship the dev/staging/production defaults from the template and change them by review, not by hand.
Alert on cost-per-run, not total spend, and keep the unit metric beside the pipeline's SLA.
resources.why: Total spend rises with growth and hides regressions — a unit metric behind a resource monitor catches the regression the day it lands.
resources.diagram:
cost governance
   |
   |- warehouse sizing per env --> dev XSMALL / staging MEDIUM / prod LARGE
   |
   |- auto-suspend --> seconds of inactivity --> 0 = never (bills forever)
   |
   |- resource monitor --> monthly credit quota --> hard credit cap
   |
   |- unit metric --> $ per run, per 1M rows, per model build
   |
    --> alert on cost-per-unit; total spend hides regressions

code.title: Environment defaults from the template
code.code:
dev:        XSMALL, auto_suspend 60,  1 cluster,     ECONOMY,  monitor_credits 100
staging:    MEDIUM, auto_suspend 300, 1-2 clusters,  STANDARD, monitor_credits 500
production: LARGE,  auto_suspend 600, 2-5 clusters,  STANDARD, monitor_credits 5000

code.title: Unit metrics that don't lie
code.code:
- $ per pipeline run (stable denominator)
- $ per 1M rows processed
- DBU/credits per model build

code.title: Warehouse parameters that matter
code.code:
warehouse_size:            compute size (credits/hour)
auto_suspend:              seconds of inactivity before suspend (0 = never)
resource_monitor_credits:  monthly credit quota for resource monitor

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Hooks — deterministic gates around an agent
resources.description: The model can be talked into anything; a hook is code on the tool path. Walk the four safety hooks every data repo should know — destructive-SQL guard, prod write confirmation, secret scan, backfill safety check — and wire the two the starter plugin ships.
when_to_use: Any agent that can call database, git or backfill tools
Encoding a safety policy that must not depend on the prompt
learning_objectives: Explain where hooks run — on tool-call and pre-run events, outside the model
Match each safety hook to the failure it prevents
Wire the two starter hooks every agent repo should have

steps.text: A hook is a deterministic gate — the destructive SQL guard intercepts DROP / TRUNCATE / DELETE-without-WHERE before an agent executes it.

Its policy — destructive statements are denied by default; a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied; non-production targets can be allowed with a --allow-destructive flag that requires a human confirmation token.

Production writes get a human gate — any write-class tool against a production target, classified by connection string, project or catalogue tag, is suspended for an approve-once token scoped to the single call.

Secrets never reach the repo — staged diffs are scanned for high-confidence secret patterns (AWS keys, private key headers, connection strings with passwords, JWTs); entropy-based detection warns, pattern matches block the commit.
Gates also run before a job starts — the backfill safety check refuses to start a backfill that lacks a rollback path or overlaps the daily run.
The starter plugin wires two of them for you — hook-destructive-sql-guard and hook-secret-scan-commit.
Encode the whole safety policy as hooks — destructive SQL guard, prod write confirmation — so it holds even when the agent is prompted otherwise.

what_you_need: An agent host with hook support
A data repository and a non-production database target
The DE Data Toolkit plugin, which wires the destructive-SQL guard and the secret scanner
check_yourself: A `DROP TABLE prod.orders` from the agent is denied and surfaced for confirmation — before any database call.
A write against prod.sales is suspended until a human issues an approve-once token scoped to that single call.
gotchas: Destructive statements are denied by default — there is no flag that lets a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE through.
Entropy-based secret detection warns; pattern matches block — a warning is not a pass.
The guard's failure behavior is block — when it matches, the tool call does not proceed.
production_notes: Keep hook-destructive-sql-guard and hook-secret-scan-commit active on every repo agents commit to.
The approve-once token is scoped to the single call — no standing write approvals.
resources.why: The model can be talked into anything — a hook is code on the tool path, so the policy holds even when the agent is prompted otherwise.
resources.diagram:
agent tool call
   |
   |- on-tool-call --> destructive SQL guard --> DROP/TRUNCATE/DELETE-no-WHERE --> block
   |
   |- write-class tool --> prod target --> suspend --> approve-once token
   |
   |- pre-commit --> secret scan --> pattern match --> block
   |
   |- pre-run --> backfill safety --> rollback path + no daily-run overlap

code.title: Destructive SQL guard — the policy
code.code:
Matches the SQL string passed to a database/MCP tool. Destructive statements
are denied by default; a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied.
Statements on a non-production target can be allowed with a `--allow-destructive`
flag that requires a human confirmation token.

Failure behavior: block.

code.title: Prod write confirmation — approve once
code.code:
Classify the tool target as production by connection string, project or
catalogue tag. Any write-class tool against a production target is suspended
and surfaced for a human "approve once" token scoped to the single call.

code.title: Secret scan on commit
code.code:
Scan staged diffs for high-confidence secret patterns (AWS keys, private key
headers, connection strings with passwords, JWTs). Entropy-based detection runs
as a warning; pattern matches block the commit.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Idempotency and reruns — make every task safe to run twice
resources.description: Retries are inevitable, so a task that appends duplicates rows every time it is cleared: hold each task to the idempotency test, replace its partition atomically instead of appending, and assert the invariant in CI with a test that runs the same date twice.
when_to_use: Wiring retries onto any task that writes
Preparing a pipeline you will need to backfill
learning_objectives: Apply the idempotency test to every task before trusting retries
Replace appends with atomic partition overwrites keyed by the logical date, or MERGE
Assert idempotency in CI with an invariant test on row counts

steps.text: Retries and backfills duplicate or corrupt data because writes are appends.
Hold every task to the idempotency test — "If this task runs twice for the same logical date, is the output the same?" If no, fix it before anything else — retries will happen.

Make each run write the complete result for its logical partition and replace that partition atomically — `INSERT OVERWRITE partition(dt=...)` or Delta/Iceberg replace-where. The invariant — running the same date twice yields identical output.
Every task writes to a partition keyed by the logical date, or uses MERGE.
A re-run is only safe if the task is idempotent — check before clearing.
Make every task idempotent so a re-run is always safe, and retry with backoff.
Assert invariants, not snapshots — count(*) is stable across a re-run (idempotency), no nulls in the grain key, sum(revenue) equals the source sum within tolerance.

what_you_need: A batch job that can be cleared and retried
A logical date or partition key per run
check_yourself: Running the same logical date twice yields identical output — proven by a CI test that asserts count(*) is stable across a re-run.
No task appends to a partition it can recompute.
gotchas: Retries and backfills duplicate or corrupt data because writes are appends.
A re-run is only safe if the task is idempotent — check before clearing.
Idempotency costs an upsert/overwrite pattern on every write — pay it once and retries become routine.
production_notes: Idempotent tasks turn incidents into routine re-runs.
If a test needs the network or a running warehouse, it is not a unit test — keep the invariant harness offline.
resources.why: Retries are inevitable, so a task that is not idempotent turns every retry into a duplicate — make each run replace its partition atomically instead of appending.
resources.diagram:
idempotent reruns
   |
   |- idempotency test --> "same logical date twice, same output?"
   |
   |- append --> duplicates on retry   (the bug)
   |- INSERT OVERWRITE partition / MERGE --> atomic replace  (the fix)
   |
   |- CI invariant --> count(*) stable across re-run

code.title: The idempotency test
code.code:
"If this task runs twice for the same logical date, is the output the same?"
If no, fix it before anything else — retries will happen.

code.title: The invariant list for the harness
code.code:
- `count(*)` is stable across a re-run (idempotency)
- no nulls in the grain key
- sum(revenue) equals the source sum within tolerance
- a quarantined row never appears in the published table

code.title: The atomic overwrite
code.code:
Make each run write the complete result for its logical partition and replace
that partition atomically. Never append to a partition you can recompute.
`INSERT OVERWRITE partition(dt=...)` or Delta/Iceberg replace-where do this.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Incident — the dashboard query that went slow
resources.description: Run the slow-query runbook as an incident: confirm the regression, split scan cost from compute contention, pull partitions_scanned and bytes from query history as evidence, apply the matched fix, and escalate on the shared-warehouse SLA before the queue takes other teams down with it.
when_to_use: A dashboard that used to take seconds now takes minutes
Queue times rising on a shared warehouse
learning_objectives: Confirm a query regression from symptoms and query history
Collect the evidence packet — query_id, partitions ratio, bytes, queue split
Apply the fix that matches the disease and escalate on the SLA

steps.text: Confirm the regression — a dashboard or model query that used to take seconds now takes minutes, or queue times rising on a shared warehouse.
Name the two candidate diseases before touching anything — separate scan inefficiency from compute inefficiency.
Diagnose — separate scan cost from compute time (bytes/partitions scanned vs queue time) and compare the plan against the clustering/partition key.
Pull the evidence — query_id, partitions_scanned, partitions_total, and bytes_scanned from query history, ordered by start time.
Complete the evidence packet — the query_id with its partitions ratio and bytes, the plan compared against the clustering/partition key, and the queue-time vs execution-time split.

Fix what the evidence says — over-scan means fixing the predicate or adding/adjusting the clustering key; compute-bound with high queue time means adding clusters, not size; rebuild clustering on a low-selectivity key.
Escalate to the warehouse admin when queue time breaches the shared-warehouse SLA; otherwise the query owner fixes the predicate.

what_you_need: A regressed query and access to its query history
Install: npx de-agent-platform add warehouse-clustering-advisor
The shared warehouse's queue-time SLA
check_yourself: Your incident notes contain a query_id with its partitions ratio, bytes scanned, and a queue-vs-execution split.
The fix you applied matches the disease — predicate/key for over-scan, clusters for queue time.
Escalation happened on the SLA breach, not on feelings.
gotchas: Bytes scanned and queue time are different diseases — fix the predicate vs add clusters; sizing up a scan-bound query buys nothing.
Clustering on a low-selectivity key stops pruning entirely.
Data volume growth silently crosses micro-partition thresholds — a query can go slow with no change at all.
production_notes: Monitor bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, and queue time on the shared warehouse.
Alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio; review weekly query history for the top-cost queries.
resources.why: A regressed dashboard erodes trust quietly, and a scan-bound query melts everyone else's queue too.
resources.diagram:
slow-query incident
   |
   |- symptom confirmed --> scan vs compute split
   |
   |- evidence --> query_id + partitions ratio + bytes + queue/execution
   |
   |- over-scan --> predicate / clustering key
   |- queue-bound --> add clusters, not size
   |
   |- SLA breach --> escalate to warehouse admin

code.title: Pull the evidence from query history
code.code:
-- Snowflake
SELECT query_id, partitions_scanned, partitions_total, bytes_scanned
FROM table(information_schema.query_history_by_session())
ORDER BY start_time DESC LIMIT 10;

code.title: What the runbook monitors
code.code: bytes scanned, partitions scanned ratio, queue time

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Incident — the job that quadrupled in cost overnight
resources.description: An invoice alert or a cost-per-run dashboard spike lands: one job's compute cost quadrupled with no functional change. Work the runbook — diff shuffle write and input bytes run-over-run, rank the four usual suspects, fix per cause, and cap the damage with a resource monitor while you diagnose.
when_to_use: Cluster or warehouse spend for one job quadrupled overnight
An invoice alert fired with no functional change in the pipeline
learning_objectives: Attribute a cost spike to a stage with run-over-run byte diffs
Tell apart fan-out, lost filters, and small-file regressions
Cap the damage with resource monitors and unit-metric alarms

steps.text: Name the incident — one job's compute cost quadrupled without an obvious functional change; attribute it and reverse the regression.
Diagnose run-over-run — diff shuffle write bytes and input bytes, compare output row counts per stage, and check whether the partition predicate still prunes.

Rank the four usual suspects — a join fanning out, a dropped partition filter re-reading full history, a small-file explosion after a partitioning change, autoscaling widened because a stage became slow.

Read the masking trap — autoscaling hides the cause because a slow stage widens the cluster and buys speed while the fan-out stays; compare run-over-run, not day-over-day, or traffic deltas will fool the diff.
Fix per cause — dedupe the many-side on the join key, restore the partition predicate and re-run, or OPTIMIZE/compact and re-run.
Make the alarm precise — $ per pipeline run is a stable denominator, and cost-per-unit spikes the day a join starts fanning out.
Prevent the repeat — a cost-per-run unit metric with a 25% regression alarm and a CI guard on shuffle/scan metrics (hook-spark-cost-check).

what_you_need: Spark event logs or job metrics for the run before and the run during the spike
check_yourself: The run-over-run diff of shuffle write bytes identifies the guilty stage, and the fix brings cost-per-run back to baseline.
A cost-per-run alarm with a regression threshold exists, so the next spike pages within one run instead of one month.
Warehouses touched by agents sit behind a resource monitor with a hard credit cap.
gotchas: Autoscaling masks the cause — a slow stage widens the cluster and buys speed while the fan-out stays.
Compare run-over-run, not day-over-day — traffic deltas will fool the diff.
A dropped partition filter reads full history — the join looks right, the input bytes don't.
production_notes: Monitor $ per run, shuffle write bytes, input bytes, and output rows together.
Add a CI guard on shuffle/scan metrics (hook-spark-cost-check) so cost regressions fail before deploy.
resources.why: Silent cost regressions compound — a 4x job running hourly is a new invoice line within a day, so the rollback is the incident response.

cost spike incident
   |
   |- invoice alert / $-per-run spike --> name the incident
   |
   |- diff run-over-run: shuffle write bytes, input bytes
   |
   |- suspects: fan-out | dropped partition filter | small files | autoscaling loop
   |
   |- fix per cause: dedupe many-side | restore predicate | OPTIMIZE/compact
   |
   |- resource monitor with hard credit cap --> blast radius bounded
   |
    --> revert the suspect deploy first; diagnose on the reverted baseline

grep -E 'Shuffle Write|Input Size' spark.log | tail -40
SELECT count(*) FROM stage_output_pre JOIN ... -- compare to source count

resources.title: Incident — the numbers doubled and no alarm fired
resources.description: Row counts are inflated and metrics double-counted after a retry, a fan-out join or a backfill — the incident signature of a silent fan-out. You work the duplicate-records runbook end to end: count duplicates per key with one query, correlate the first duplicate date with a deploy, check whether the write is append or merge/overwrite, then dedupe on the business key and rewrite only the affected partitions.
when_to_use: Metrics double-counted and no alarm fired
Row counts jumped after a retry, a fan-out join, or a backfill
learning_objectives: Recognize inflated row counts and double-counted metrics as the fan-out signature
Count duplicates per key and correlate the first duplicate date with a deploy
Rewrite affected partitions instead of the whole table

steps.text: Name the incident — row counts are inflated and metrics double-counted after a retry, a fan-out join or a backfill.
Identify the duplicate key and count duplicates per key.
Run: SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 20;
Determine the earliest date duplicates appeared → correlate with a deploy.
Check whether the write is append vs merge/overwrite.
Deduplicate on the business key, keeping the latest by event time.
Rewrite the affected partitions (overwrite), not the whole table.

what_you_need: A table whose counts jumped and the pipeline that wrote it
Write access to rewrite the affected partitions
check_yourself: The GROUP BY duplicate count returns zero rows after the fix, on the affected partitions.
You can name the deploy that introduced the duplicates and the date it landed.
The rewrite touched only the partitions with duplicates — the rest of the table is untouched.
gotchas: The earliest duplicate date, not the loudest metric, points at the causing deploy.
Append vs merge/overwrite decides whether the fix is a dedupe or a re-run.
Rewriting the whole table for one bad day widens the blast radius.
production_notes: Alert on duplicates per key, not just on row-count deltas.
Prevent the recurrence with the review rule: prove a join cannot fan out before writing it.
resources.why: A silent fan-out ships wrong numbers with green dashboards — the runbook turns the blast into a dated, partitioned, deduped fix.
resources.diagram:
silent fan-out incident
   |
   |- signature --> counts inflated, metrics double-counted
   |
   |- GROUP BY HAVING --> duplicates per key
   |
   |- earliest duplicate date --> correlate with deploy
   |
   |- append vs merge/overwrite --> dedupe on business key
   |
   |- rewrite affected partitions --> verify duplicate count returns to zero

code.title: Count duplicates per key, and bound the damage window
code.code:
SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT min(dt), max(dt) FROM (SELECT dt, k, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY dt, k HAVING count(*)>1);
