resources.title: Incremental processing with a watermark
resources.description: Full reloads stop scaling once a table grows past millions of rows. Process a bounded window instead: a watermark ends it, a lookback absorbs late files, and an idempotent write (partition overwrite or MERGE) makes every re-run safe — including re-processing a late window.
when_to_use: Append-mostly sources
Cost-sensitive pipelines
Deterministic event/updated timestamps
learning_objectives: Bound incremental work with a watermark and a lookback window
Write incremental output idempotently so a re-run is safe
Absorb late-arriving files without re-running history

steps.text: Process a window that ends at a watermark and starts a lookback before it: scan from (max(watermark) - lookback) to now.
The lookback absorbs late arrivals; the watermark bounds the work.
Write idempotently (partition overwrite or MERGE) so a re-run is safe.
Handle deletes explicitly (soft-delete or periodic full refresh) — they don't arrive in an append-only stream.
Watch a naive is_incremental() without a lookback — it silently drops late data.
Files arrive after the daily job already ran, so yesterday's numbers change the next morning.
Re-process the late window idempotently (partition overwrite or MERGE), and widen the reprocessing window to cover observed lateness.

what_you_need: An append-mostly source with deterministic event or updated timestamps
A table past millions of rows where full reloads cost too much
check_yourself: A re-run for the same window produces identical output — partition overwrite or MERGE, no appends.
Yesterday's late files are absorbed by the lookback, and no full reload ran.
gotchas: A naive is_incremental() without a lookback silently drops late data.
Re-running the whole partition for one late file is wasteful — overwrite windows, not history.
Timezone mismatch between partner and pipeline shifts lateness by hours — measure arrival times in UTC.
production_notes: Adopt a watermark policy: reprocess the last N days every run.
Use idempotent writes keyed by business date so a re-run is safe.
resources.why: Incremental only pays off if it is safe to re-run — the watermark bounds the cost and the idempotent write bounds the blast radius.
resources.diagram:
incremental run
   |
   |- watermark --> window = [max(watermark) - lookback, now]
   |
   |- lookback --> late files absorbed, no full reload
   |
   |- write --> OVERWRITE dt=... / MERGE --> re-run safe
   |
   |- deletes --> soft-delete or periodic full refresh

resources.title: Make queries prune — clustering keys and scan diagnosis
resources.description: Choose a clustering key from the predicates of your most expensive queries, prove the prune with partitions_scanned versus partitions_total, and fix the disease you actually have — a lost predicate or a low-selectivity key on the scan side, or queue time on the compute side.
when_to_use: A dashboard or model scans far more partitions than it needs
Choosing the first clustering key for a large fact table
learning_objectives: Choose a clustering key from predicate selectivity
Prove pruning with partitions_scanned versus partitions_total
Fix the scan or compute problem you actually measured

steps.text: Pick the clustering column from the workload — the one that appears in the WHERE clause of the most expensive queries, with reasonable cardinality; order matters, so put the most selective first.
Know the failure mode — clustering on a low-selectivity key stops pruning entirely.
Diagnose before changing anything — separate scan cost from compute time (bytes/partitions scanned vs queue time) and compare the plan against the clustering/partition key.
Measure the prune directly — query_id, partitions_scanned, partitions_total, and bytes_scanned from the session's query history.
Match the fix to the finding — over-scan means fixing the predicate or adding/adjusting the clustering key; rebuilding clustering on a low-selectivity key.
Keep it fixed — alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio and review query history weekly for the top cost queries.

what_you_need: A shared warehouse with a query history you can read
Install: npx de-agent-platform add warehouse-clustering-advisor
Your top-cost queries and their WHERE clauses
check_yourself: Your clustering key's first column is the most selective predicate of your costliest queries.
You can quote partitions_scanned/partitions_total for a query before and after the change.
Scan-bound and queue-bound queries get different fixes, and you can name which yours is.
gotchas: Clustering on a low-selectivity key stops pruning entirely.
Scan is optimal but the query waits → warehouse sizing or concurrency problem.
Bytes scanned and queue time are different diseases — fix the predicate vs add clusters; sizing up a scan-bound query buys nothing.
production_notes: Alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio.
Review weekly query history for the top-cost queries.

FROM table(information_schema.query_history_by_session())
ORDER BY start_time DESC LIMIT 10;

resources.title: Make the sink idempotent so replays never duplicate rows
resources.description: The core producer-side reliability skill for streams: you cannot stop replays, so the sink must converge. Deduplicate by a business key and event time within the watermark, MERGE on the key, and rank change events by (lsn, ts_ms) — never by arrival time.
when_to_use: Kafka → Delta/Iceberg/warehouse
Any replay-prone stream
learning_objectives: Make the sink idempotent rather than trying to make the source exactly-once
Deduplicate by a business key + event time within the watermark
Rank change events deterministically by (lsn, ts_ms), never by arrival time

steps.text: Name the failure mode — streaming sinks either duplicate on replay or lose rows on failure.
Make the sink idempotent rather than trying to make the source exactly-once.
Deduplicate by a business key + event time within the watermark, then MERGE (upsert) on the key — a replay recomputes the same rows and merges to the same state, idempotent by construction.
Order by event time, not arrival time.
For change streams, rank by `(lsn, ts_ms)` — never by ingestion time; ranking by LSN makes re-running the same micro-batch produce the same table.
Deduplicate before merging — keep the latest event per primary key with a window function, then merge once.
Plan for checkpoint loss — checkpoint lost means duplicates, and the fix is making the sink idempotent.

what_you_need: A stream writing into Delta/Iceberg or a warehouse table with a stable business key
check_yourself: Replaying the same micro-batch twice produces an identical table — the merge is idempotent by construction.
The dedupe key is a business key plus event time within the watermark, not an offset and not an arrival timestamp.
gotchas: Ranking by arrival time breaks idempotency — rank by (lsn, ts_ms) or event time.
The pattern requires a stable business key and event time; state cost is the price.
A pure append-only event log with no dedup need does not need this pattern.
production_notes: Correct under replay with no reliance on perfect exactly-once — that is the goal, and it is achievable.
MERGE aggregates on the window key so replays converge.
resources.why: You cannot stop replays, so the sink must converge to the same state no matter how many times a batch arrives.
resources.diagram:
idempotent sink
   |
   |- stream arrives (at-least-once, replays included)
   |
   |- windowed dedupe by business key + event time
   |
   |- MERGE (upsert on key) --> table converges
   |
    --> replay the same batch --> same rows --> same state

code.title: The pattern in one line
code.code: stream ─▶ [windowed dedupe by key] ─▶ MERGE (upsert on key) ─▶ table

code.title: Ordering and idempotency rules
code.code:
Events arrive out of order. Rank by `(lsn, ts_ms)` — never by ingestion time.

Re-running the same micro-batch must produce the same table. Ranking by LSN
guarantees this; ranking by arrival time does not.

resources.title: Own the consumer side — offsets, rebalances, and the KIP-848 protocol
resources.description: Consumer reliability is where streams quietly break: a rebalance loop looks like slowness, consumers past the partition count buy nothing, and stop-the-world rebalances pause consumption. Read group state, fix the timeouts, and know what the next-generation protocol changes.
when_to_use: Consumers restart or rebalance more often than the workload explains
You need to reason about offsets before changing consumer configs
learning_objectives: Explain how consumer groups and offsets decide who reads what
Detect a rebalance loop from consumer-group state history
Know what the KIP-848 protocol changes about rebalancing

steps.text: Ground yourself in the mechanics — consumer groups and offsets are what decide who reads what, and delivery semantics decide what a restart means.
Get per-partition lag — uniform vs skewed tells you capacity vs key skew.
Check the consumer-group state history for `PreparingRebalance`.
Read the signature — lag resets to zero then climbs means a rebalance loop; check `session.timeout.ms`.
Know where the protocol is going — the KIP-848 consumer protocol in Apache Kafka 4.0 redesigns consumer group rebalancing to eliminate stop-the-world pauses.
When a rebalance loop is the bug — raise session.timeout.ms / max.poll.interval.ms.
Before scaling the fleet — adding consumers past the partition count buys nothing.

what_you_need: kafka-consumer-groups CLI access to the cluster
check_yourself: Frequent `PreparingRebalance` in the group state history, with lag that resets to zero then climbs, is a rebalance loop — not a slow consumer.
A 13th consumer on a 12-partition topic changes nothing — partitions cap parallelism.
gotchas: A rebalance loop can look like slowness: check the group state history for PreparingRebalance.
Adding consumers past the partition count buys nothing.
Stop-the-world pauses are the problem the next-generation protocol eliminates — older protocols pause all consumption during a rebalance.
production_notes: Alert on lag slope, not on an absolute lag number.
Rebalance count belongs in monitoring next to consumer lag per partition and DLQ depth.
resources.why: A rebalance loop steals consumption time and can look like slowness, so the consumer side is where streaming reliability is usually lost first.
resources.diagram:
consumer reliability
   |
   |- group subscribes --> partitions split across members
   |
   |- offsets committed per partition --> restart resumes, not re-reads
   |
   |- PreparingRebalance looping --> raise session.timeout.ms / max.poll.interval.ms
   |
   |- consumers > partitions --> idle members, no gain
   |
    --> KIP-848 (Kafka 4.0): rebalancing without stop-the-world pauses

kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group $G
kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group $G --state

resources.title: Plan and execute a backfill that doesn't break production
resources.description: Historical output is wrong or missing, and the fix touches a production table: define correct first, map the blast radius from lineage, then shadow-write in date batches smallest-first, validate a sample per batch, and swap atomically — behind a gate that demands a rollback path.
when_to_use: A past date range is wrong or missing
A logic fix or new column must be applied historically
learning_objectives: Scope a backfill by date, dependency and blast radius before running anything
Shadow-write in date batches, smallest first, validating a sample per batch
Gate the backfill on an explicit range and a rollback path

steps.text: Historical output is wrong or missing and must be recomputed safely, without breaking production.

Before running anything — which dates are wrong and what does "correct" look like; every downstream model/table that reads the target; will this run beside the daily job and at what hour the cluster is idle; can each date be re-run safely; snapshot the target or write to a shadow table first.
Define correctness first — what should the values be, and how will you check? Then compute the downstream impact set from lineage.

Treat a backfill as a controlled migration — 1. shadow target (or snapshot), 2. batched date ranges smallest first, 3. validate a sample after each batch, 4. swap atomically, 5. keep the old data until validated.
The safety gate requires an explicit date range, a target that is either a shadow table or snapshotted, and a window that does not overlap the scheduled production run — it denies otherwise.
Never run a backfill concurrently with the daily production run; one huge date range starves the cluster — batch it and validate a sample per batch.
Shadow-then-swap keeps rollback in reach — delete the shadow, never the production table; swap only after sample validation passes.

what_you_need: A past date range in a production table that is wrong or missing
The pipeline's idle window and resource budget
check_yourself: The plan names the wrong dates, the written definition of correct, the downstream blast radius and the rollback path before anything runs.
The run writes to a shadow target in date batches, smallest first, and the swap happens only after sample validation passes.
gotchas: Never run a backfill concurrently with the daily production run.
One huge date range starves the cluster; batch it and validate a sample per batch.
Backfilling without a written definition of correctness just relocates the bug.
production_notes: Idempotent pipelines make a backfill a routine operation.
Document a backfill runbook per pipeline, with its idle window and resource budget.
resources.why: A backfill is production work with a bigger blast radius than the original pipeline — shadow-write, sample-validate, then swap.
resources.diagram:
safe backfill
   |
   |- define correct + lineage impact --> blast radius known
   |
   |- shadow target (or snapshot) --> batched ranges, smallest first
   |
   |- validate sample per batch --> pass --> swap atomically
   |                              fail --> delete the shadow, never prod

code.title: The batched backfill command
code.code:
airflow dags backfill --start-date YYYY-MM-DD --end-date YYYY-MM-DD --reset-dagruns dag_id
# prefer batched date ranges over one large range

code.title: What the safety gate requires
code.code:
Intercepts a backfill trigger. Requires: an explicit date range, a target that
is either a shadow table or snapshotted, and a window that does not overlap the
scheduled production run. Denies otherwise.

code.title: The five-step controlled migration
code.code:
1. shadow target (or snapshot)
2. batched date ranges, smallest first
3. validate a sample after each batch
4. swap atomically
5. keep the old data until validated

resources.title: Production gotchas — NULL traps, implicit casts, silent drift
resources.description: The bugs that survive testing compare wrong instead of failing loud: NOT IN over a nullable subquery, a comparison across types left to an implicit cast, and a schema change that silently turns a column to NULLs. You walk the review rules that ban each pattern, then use the schema-drift runbook to tell a hard failure from a silent one and to decide between an explicit cast and a quarantine.
when_to_use: Before merging SQL with NOT IN, cross-type comparisons, or a changed source schema
A pipeline went quiet instead of failing — checking for silent nulls
learning_objectives: Spot NULL-unsafe `NOT IN` and `=` predicates and rewrite them with NOT EXISTS
Make every cross-type comparison an explicit cast, not an implicit one
Classify a schema drift failure as hard (job error) or silent (nulls)

steps.text: `NOT IN (subquery)` is banned where the subquery can return NULL — use `NOT EXISTS`.
Spot NULL-unsafe `NOT IN` and `=` predicates.
Comparisons across types must be explicit casts, not implicit.
A drift can be silent — determine whether the failure is hard (job error) or silent (nulls).
A type change gets cast explicitly, or reject and quarantine.
Audit the quiet ones together — non-deterministic ordering is in the same review pass as the NULL and cast traps.

what_you_need: A query with a cross-type comparison or a NOT IN to audit
The schema-drift runbook for the silent-null cases
check_yourself: Every NOT IN in the query has a nullable-column story — or is rewritten as NOT EXISTS.
Every cross-type comparison shows an explicit CAST.
For the last schema change on the source, you can say whether it failed hard or silently.
gotchas: NOT IN with a nullable column never compares as you think; use NOT EXISTS.
An implicit cast that works in dev can flip semantics when the source type changes.
Silent nulls pass green pipelines — diff the source schema, not just the row counts.
production_notes: Quarantine type-change rejections instead of letting the cast decide.
Run the sql-review rules in CI so the NULL and cast traps are caught before merge.
resources.why: NULL traps and implicit casts compare wrong without erroring — the only defense is a rule you apply before the query runs.
resources.diagram:
production gotchas
   |
   |- NOT IN vs NULL --> never compares as expected --> NOT EXISTS
   |
   |- cross-type comparison --> explicit cast, not implicit
   |
   |- schema drift --> hard (job error) vs silent (nulls)
   |
   |- type change --> cast explicitly, or reject and quarantine

code.title: The two review rules this lesson enforces
code.code:
2. NOT IN (subquery) is banned where the subquery can return NULL — use NOT EXISTS.
3. Comparisons across types must be explicit casts, not implicit.

code.title: What the schema-drift runbook does with a type change
code.code: Type change → cast explicitly, or reject and quarantine.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Production gotchas — silent failures and partial writes
resources.description: The failures that become pages are the ones nobody was watching: a regression hiding in growth, a cron change that silently widens the freshness SLA, and appends that duplicate on retry — cap each with a guard, a computed worst-case lag, and an atomic partition replace.
when_to_use: Hardening pipelines that already serve consumers
After an incident caused by a silent failure or a partial write
learning_objectives: Catch silent failures — hidden cost regressions and silently widened freshness SLAs
Stop partial writes — no appends to recomputable partitions, no unguarded prod writes
Put the failure class in the alert text so on-call can triage before touching anything

steps.text: A working pipeline silently becomes expensive and nobody notices until the invoice.
A change can silently widen the freshness SLA of a source — compare the schedule/cron in the diff with the source's declared freshness SLA and warn with the computed worst-case lag.
Partial writes come from appends — retries and backfills duplicate or corrupt data because writes are appends; replace the partition atomically instead.
Read the first real error in the log, not the last — and retrying a data error re-runs the same failure; fix or quarantine the input first.
Guard every production write — any write-class tool against a production target is suspended and surfaced for a human "approve once" token scoped to the single call.
`DROP TABLE prod.orders` from an agent is denied and surfaced for confirmation.
Retry with backoff, and put the failure class in the alert text.

what_you_need: The pipelines currently in production
An alerting channel wired to task failure rate and SLA misses
CI where a hook can warn or block a merge
check_yourself: A cron change that would violate the freshness SLA warns at pre-merge with the computed worst-case lag.
No production write path exists that a hook does not classify, confirm or block.
gotchas: Read the first real error in the log, not the last.
Retrying a data error re-runs the same failure; fix or quarantine the input first.
Spend varies with data growth and regressions hide in growth — total-spend dashboards cannot see them.
production_notes: Retry with backoff, and put the failure class in the alert text.
Make every task idempotent so a re-run is always safe.
resources.why: The failures that page you are the ones no dashboard was watching — silent regressions, silently widened SLAs and appends that duplicate on retry.
resources.diagram:
silent failures + partial writes
   |
   |- regression hides in growth --> unit metric + baseline catches it
   |
   |- cron change --> freshness SLA widened silently --> warn with worst-case lag
   |
   |- append on retry --> duplicated rows --> atomic partition replace
   |
   |- prod write --> classified + confirmed or blocked

code.title: The silent widening example
code.code:
Changing a source cron from hourly to daily warns that the 6h freshness SLA
will be violated.

code.title: The production write suspension
code.code:
Classify the tool target as production by connection string, project or
catalogue tag. Any write-class tool against a production target is suspended
and surfaced for a human "approve once" token scoped to the single call.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Production gotchas — surprise bills, region defaults, and IAM overreach
resources.description: The surprises that turn into invoices: workers sized by habit, a renamed prefix that silently resets a bookmark, thousands of small files, an agent holding an admin role, and a query that scans everything because the predicate missed the partition column. Each gotcha names the metric that catches it early.
when_to_use: A Glue job's bill grew without any change in data volume
An agent was granted broad credentials as a temporary measure
A new region or profile default may be silently routing resources
learning_objectives: Catch the Glue cost leaks before the invoice — oversized workers, reset bookmarks, drifted catalogues
Keep small files and repeated metadata repairs out of the bill
Bind agents to least-privilege profiles so IAM overreach and region drift stay impossible

steps.text: Watch for the most common Glue cost leak — over-provisioned workers; size from data volume, not habit.
Check the input path layout before every bookmark-dependent run — a renamed prefix silently resets the bookmark into a full reprocess.
Compact small files — per-file overhead dominates at under 16 MB, so small files inflate the bill even when pruning works.
Recognize the classic combo the reviewer flags — a Glue job running with an admin role and no bookmark, causing nightly full reprocessing.
Never attach an admin role to an agent — bind to a dedicated AWS profile with least privilege and short-lived SSO credentials.
Set AWS_REGION deliberately — it is the default region for the AWS MCP servers, while AWS_PROFILE decides what is reachable.
Treat every BigQuery MCP query as billable — grant bigquery.dataViewer + bigquery.jobUser only, set a custom quota, and consider maximum_bytes_billed on every job.

what_you_need: Recent Glue task histograms and Athena scanned-bytes metrics
check_yourself: The task histogram shows balanced tasks after re-sizing, and no Glue job in the account runs with an admin role and no bookmark.
Tables averaging under 16 MB per file are compacted, and the per-query bill no longer carries per-file overhead.
Agents bind to a dedicated least-privilege profile with short-lived SSO credentials and an explicit AWS_REGION.
gotchas: A renamed prefix under the input path silently resets the bookmark into a full reprocess.
Per-file overhead dominates at under 16 MB — small files inflate the bill even when pruning works.
A Glue job running with an admin role and no bookmark causes nightly full reprocessing — the reviewer's own worked example.
production_notes: Keep the task histogram and the scanned-bytes metric in every review; both are the fastest signals that sizing or layout is wrong.
Treat resource-creating MCP tools as requiring human confirmation, and rotate short-lived SSO credentials on a schedule.
resources.why: Cloud bills are silent until the invoice — every gotcha here has a metric or a diff that catches it the day it lands.
resources.diagram:
cloud production gotchas
   |
   |- workers sized by habit --> over-provisioned --> most common Glue cost leak
   |
   |- renamed prefix --> bookmark silently resets --> full reprocess
   |
   |- files < 16 MB --> per-file overhead dominates --> compact
   |
   |- admin role on a job --> nightly full reprocess + IAM overreach
   |
   |- AWS_REGION unset --> resources land in the wrong default region
   |
    --> billable queries (BigQuery): custom quota + maximum_bytes_billed

code.title: The Glue review checklist
code.code:
- Start worker sizing at 2x the number of input files' partitions; watch the task histogram.
- A bookmark only helps if the input path layout is stable.
- A renamed prefix silently resets the bookmark → full reprocess.
- Diff the Glue Data Catalog schema against the file footer.

code.title: The billable surface
code.code:
Queries are billable. Grant `bigquery.dataViewer` + `bigquery.jobUser` only,
set a custom quota, and consider `maximum_bytes_billed` on every job.

code.title: Agent credential binding
code.code:
Bind to a dedicated AWS profile with least privilege, use short-lived SSO
credentials, and never attach an admin role. Treat resource-creating tools
as requiring human confirmation.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Production gotchas — the configs and capacities that break streams
resources.description: The five causes of consumer lag on one card, the two destructive shortcuts that must never happen, and the capacity trap of scaling past the partition count. Ends with the alert that matters — lag slope, not absolute lag — and the sampling rules that keep PII out of agent contexts.
when_to_use: A config change is being proposed as the fix for lag
A new stream goes to production and needs its failure modes listed
learning_objectives: Map a lag symptom to its cause before changing any config
Refuse the destructive shortcuts — offset resets and hand-edited offsets
Size consumers to partitions and fix the sink when lag is uniform

steps.text: Keep the five causes on one card — downstream sink (DB/warehouse) bottleneck, a hot key routed to a single partition, a rebalance loop stealing consumption time, a poison message retried forever, too few consumers for the partition count.
Read the lag shape before scaling — uniform lag means capacity; one stuck partition means key skew or a poison message.
Respect the capacity ceiling — adding consumers past the partition count buys nothing.
Do not "fix" lag by resetting offsets. That is data loss wearing a hat.
On the ingestion side the same rule holds — never hand-edit offsets; replay from the snapshot point.

Before sampling messages in production, know the risk — sampling can expose production PII in the agent's context; grant a read-only principal, prefer a topic allow-list, and never sample topics containing personal data without masking.
Set the alert that matters — alert on lag slope, not on an absolute lag number, and keep a DLQ for messages failing N times.

what_you_need: A cluster whose lag, DLQ depth, and group state you can read
check_yourself: Scaling from 6 to 12 consumers on a 6-partition topic fixes nothing — uniform lag is a sink-throughput problem.
No incident in this lesson ends with an offset reset or a hand-edited offset — recovery replays from the log or the snapshot point.
gotchas: Never reset offsets to clear lag; that is silent data loss.
Adding consumers past the partition count buys nothing.
Credential rotation can stall a connector with no error on the consumer side.
production_notes: Alert on lag slope, not on an absolute lag number.
Alert on replication-slot retained WAL and on connector task state.
resources.why: Most streaming outages are self-inflicted — a config changed to chase a symptom, a fleet scaled past the partition count, or an offset reset that deleted data.
resources.diagram:
production gotchas
   |
   |- lag uniform --> capacity bound --> fix the SINK, not the fleet
   |- consumers > partitions --> idle members, no gain
   |- PreparingRebalance looping --> session.timeout.ms / max.poll.interval.ms
   |- one offset stuck --> poison message --> DLQ + commit past
   |
   |- never: offset resets, hand-edited offsets
   |- sampling: read-only principal, topic allow-list, mask PII
   |
    --> alert on lag slope, not absolute lag

code.title: The five causes of lag
code.code:
- Downstream sink (DB/warehouse) is the bottleneck
- A hot key routes to a single partition
- Rebalance loop stealing consumption time
- A poison message retried forever
- Too few consumers for the partition count

code.title: The never list
code.code: Do not "fix" lag by resetting offsets. That is data loss wearing a hat.

code.title: Sampling risk in production
code.code:
Sampling messages can expose production PII in the agent's context. Grant a
read-only principal, prefer a topic allow-list, and never sample topics
containing personal data without masking.

resources.title: Production gotchas — topology, timeouts, concurrency
resources.description: The DAG failures that become pages: unbounded concurrency, missing catchup policy, and a backfill that starves the daily run — cap them with max_active_runs and pools, then wire the monitoring and escalation path the backfill runbook prescribes.
when_to_use: Hardening a DAG before it takes production traffic
Planning a backfill that runs beside live schedules
learning_objectives: Cap max_active_runs and pool limits before a backfill starves the daily run
Find unsafe retries, missing catchup policy and unbounded concurrency
Monitor backfill progress, resource contention and validation pass rate

steps.text: Check the DAG for unsafe retries, missing catchup policy, ambiguous catchup/backfill semantics and unbounded concurrency.
Cap max_active_runs and pool limits so a backfill cannot starve the daily run.
Never overlap the production window; never backfill without a rollback path.
Design against the incident — an unmanaged backfill can starve daily production runs and double-write history.
Monitor backfill progress, resource contention and validation pass rate.
Schedule with the platform owner; escalate if the backfill window collides with a golden-hour production run.

what_you_need: The DAGs currently in production
The daily production schedule and golden-hour windows
check_yourself: max_active_runs and pool limits are set on every DAG a backfill could touch.
The escalation path names the platform owner and the golden-hour window that must stay clear.
gotchas: Cap max_active_runs and pool limits so a backfill cannot starve the daily run.
Never overlap the production window; never backfill without a rollback path.
Ambiguous catchup/backfill semantics are a review finding, not a footnote.
production_notes: Monitor backfill progress, resource contention and validation pass rate.
Escalate if the backfill window collides with a golden-hour production run.
resources.why: Unbounded concurrency and a missing catchup policy only surface when a backfill collides with the daily run — cap both first.
resources.diagram:
production topology
   |
   |- max_active_runs + pools --> contention capped
   |
   |- catchup policy --> catchup/backfill semantics explicit
   |
   |- monitoring --> progress, contention, validation pass rate

code.title: Concurrency guard from the checklist
code.code: `max_active_runs` and pool limits prevent a backfill from starving the daily run.

code.title: What the reviewer flags
code.code:
Non-idempotent tasks, unsafe retries, missing catchup policy, ambiguous
catchup/backfill semantics and unbounded concurrency.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Read a Spark event log with the Spark Lens plugin
resources.description: Install the Spark Lens plugin and work its three commands over a Spark event log: /spark-analyze to build a task histogram and flag skew, /spark-explain-plan to check the join strategy, and /spark-baseline to store the cost baseline the guard enforces.
when_to_use: Diagnosing a slow or expensive Spark job from its event log
Storing a cost baseline before the next Spark change
learning_objectives: Turn a Spark event log into a task histogram
Flag skew and shuffle amplification with /spark-analyze
Store a cost baseline with /spark-baseline

steps.text: Install the plugin: `amp plugin add de-agent/spark-lens`.
Point it at a Spark event log — it parses the log into a task histogram and flags skew and shuffle amplification.
Run `/spark-analyze` on the event log.
Run `/spark-explain-plan` before shipping the change.
Run `/spark-baseline` to store the cost baseline.
Wire the guard — shuffle write grows 3.9x after a join change → build fails with the stage id.

what_you_need: A Spark event log or Spark UI metrics
The job source
check_yourself: `/spark-analyze` produces a task histogram from the event log and names skew or shuffle amplification when present.
A join change that grows shuffle write 3.9x fails the build with the stage id.
gotchas: The cost guard needs prior runs to build its 5-run baseline — a cold start has nothing to compare against.
The plugin's permissions are filesystem read-only with no network — it analyzes logs you provide, it does not fetch metrics.
Event-log retention matters — rotated logs close the run-over-run comparison window.
production_notes: Store a baseline per job and compare against the median of the last 5 runs.
The plugin ships the skew-diagnosis and cost-regression-guard skills — use them for the root-cause step.
resources.why: Event logs already contain the cost story — the plugin turns them into a histogram and a baseline the CI guard can enforce.
resources.diagram:
event log
   |
   |- /spark-analyze --> task histogram --> skew / shuffle amplification flags
   |
   |- /spark-explain-plan --> broadcast vs sort-merge
   |
   |- /spark-baseline --> stored baseline --> CI guard fails > 25% growth

code.title: Install the plugin
code.code: amp plugin add de-agent/spark-lens

code.title: The three commands over one event log
code.code:
/spark-analyze        # task histogram; flags skew and shuffle amplification
/spark-explain-plan   # check the join strategy before shipping the change
/spark-baseline       # store the cost baseline the CI guard enforces

code.title: What the baseline guard enforces
code.code:
After the job's test run, read shuffle/spill/scan metrics from the event log,
compare against the stored baseline (median of last 5), and fail if any metric
grew by more than 25%. Emit the offending stage and metric.

Example: shuffle write grows 3.9x after a join change → build fails with the stage id.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Read an EXPLAIN plan and pick the one fix
resources.description: Take the EXPLAIN output of a slow query and read it bottom-up, naming the expensive node before you touch anything. You compare estimated rows to actual rows to catch stale statistics, separate scan cost from compute time with the warehouse runbook, and finish by deciding between an index, a rewrite, or a stats refresh — one change, with a way to measure it.
when_to_use: A query that used to take seconds now takes minutes
Estimated rows and actual rows disagree by an order of magnitude
learning_objectives: Read a plan bottom-up and name the expensive node
Detect cardinality misestimation from stale statistics
Separate scan cost from compute time before choosing a fix

steps.text: Read a plan bottom-up and name the expensive node.
Detect cardinality misestimation from stale statistics.
Separate scan cost from compute time (bytes/partitions scanned vs queue time).
Compare the plan against the clustering/partition key.
Over-scan → fix the predicate or add/adjust the clustering key.
Decide between an index, a rewrite, or a stats refresh.

what_you_need: EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE output for a slow query
The target dialect (postgres/duckdb)
check_yourself: You can point to the single most expensive node and quote its estimated vs actual rows.
The one recommended change states its expected effect and a way to measure it.
gotchas: >10x off between estimated and actual rows means stale stats — refresh them before buying an index.
Bytes scanned and queue time are different diseases — sizing up a scan-bound query buys nothing.
Clustering on a low-selectivity key stops pruning entirely.
production_notes: Alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio.
Review weekly query history for the top-cost queries.
resources.why: Reading the plan bottom-up turns an unreadable dump into one expensive node and one change worth making.
resources.diagram:
query plan read
   |
   |- read bottom-up --> name the expensive node
   |
   |- rows vs actual rows --> >10x off --> stale stats --> refresh
   |
   |- scan cost vs compute --> over-scan --> fix predicate / recluster
   |
   |- one change --> index, rewrite, or stats refresh --> measure

code.title: Read the plan bottom-up, then one recommended change
code.code:
Method
1. Read bottom-up; the deepest node is the first data touched.
2. Compare rows (estimate) to actual rows. >10x off means stale stats.
3. Look for Seq Scan on a large table that should use an index.
4. Look for Sort / Hash spilling to disk (disk usage in the plan).

Output: one sentence per expensive node, then exactly one recommended
change with the expected effect and a way to measure it.

code.title: Partitions scanned vs total in query history (Snowflake)
Pick the fix - over-scan vs queue time
code.code:
Over-scan → fix the predicate or add/adjust the clustering key.
Compute-bound with high queue time → add clusters, not size.
Rebuild clustering on a low-selectivity key.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Respond when a data contract breaks
resources.description: Work the broken-contract runbook end to end: identify which clause broke, bound the consumer impact set from lineage before anything else, decide whether the producer reverts or the consumer adapts, and close with consumer-driven contract tests in the producer's pipeline.
when_to_use: A consumer broke right after a producer deploy
A promised column or semantic changed, or an SLA was breached
learning_objectives: Classify a breach by clause — schema, semantics, or SLA
Bound the consumer impact set from lineage before assigning the fix
Choose between a producer revert and a consumer adaptation

steps.text: Identify which contract clause broke — schema, semantics, or SLA.
Establish the impact set from lineage before anything else.
Determine if the fix is on the producer (revert) or consumer (adapt).
Schema breach → producer reverts or adds a compatibility shim.
SLA breach → negotiate a temporary relaxation and a root-cause fix.
Add consumer-driven contract tests in the producer's pipeline.

what_you_need: The failing consumer's error and the producer's recent deploys
Lineage for the broken asset
The contract document with its SLA and breaking-change policy
check_yourself: The impact-set query returns every downstream consumer of the broken asset before anyone assigns the fix.
A consumer that broke right after a producer deploy traces to a rename that changed semantics, and is treated as a breach.
gotchas: A rename that changed semantics is still a breach, even when it looks safe.
SLA misses can come from unrelated outages — root-cause before pointing at the producer.
Whatever the fix, the consumer impact set comes first, from lineage.
production_notes: Contracts get CI enforcement and a dated deprecation path.
Run consumer-driven contract tests in the producer's pipeline.
resources.why: A broken contract is a negotiation as much as a bug — bound the blast radius from lineage before deciding who reverts and who adapts.
resources.diagram:
contract broken
   |
   |- which clause broke? --> schema / semantics / SLA
   |
   |- impact set from lineage --> consumers listed first
   |
   |- schema breach --> producer reverts or adds a compatibility shim
   |
   |- SLA breach --> temporary relaxation --> root-cause fix

code.title: Bound the consumer impact set from lineage
code.code:
# impact set from lineage
SELECT * FROM lineage WHERE upstream = 'prod.orders' AND direction = 'downstream';

code.title: Classify the breach by clause
code.code:
- Identify which contract clause broke (schema, semantics, or SLA).
- Establish the impact set from lineage before anything else.
- Determine if the fix is on the producer (revert) or consumer (adapt).

code.title: Who fixes it — producer reverts, consumer adapts
code.code:
- Schema breach → producer reverts or adds a compatibility shim.
- SLA breach → negotiate a temporary relaxation and a root-cause fix.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Review a dbt model PR before merge
resources.description: Take a pull request that adds or changes a dbt model and walk the reviewer's pass: read the diff in context, state the model's grain and check it against the unique key test, choose table vs incremental vs view deliberately, and handle late-arriving data in the incremental filter. You finish with findings a reviewer can verify before the model merges.
when_to_use: A PR changes a dbt model's materialisation or incremental filter
A model's unique test does not sit on its declared grain key
learning_objectives: State a model's grain in one sentence and match it to the unique test
Justify table vs incremental vs view for a given source
Add a lookback window so late-arriving rows are not dropped

steps.text: Read the diff and the file context.
Establish the grain of every result set.
State a model's grain and match it to its unique key test.
Choose table vs incremental vs view deliberately.
Handle late data in an incremental model.

what_you_need: A pull request that adds or changes a dbt model
The model's schema.yml with its declared grain
check_yourself: The review states the model's grain in one sentence and the unique test sits on that key.
An incremental model carries a lookback window such as >= max(updated_at) - interval '3 days'.
gotchas: Late-arriving rows older than the watermark are silently dropped — add a lookback window.
is_incremental() must guard the filter or every full run is a full reload.
Deletes never arrive — decide explicitly: soft-delete, or periodic full-refresh.
production_notes: Add a lookback window (e.g. >= max(updated_at) - interval '3 days') to every incremental filter.
Decide soft-delete vs periodic full-refresh explicitly; deletes never arrive on their own.
resources.why: Grain, materialisation, and late data decide whether a model lies, and this pass checks all three before merge.
resources.diagram:
dbt model review
   |
   |- read diff + context --> establish grain per result set
   |
   |- grain statement --> unique test on that key
   |
   |- materialisation picker --> view / table / incremental
   |
   |- incremental --> lookback window --> guard is_incremental()

code.title: Grain first - the unique test on the declared grain key
code.code:
# One row = one ___ ; the unique test goes on that key
models:
  - name: <model>
    columns:
      - name: <grain key>
        tests:
          - unique

code.title: Materialisation picker - view vs table vs incremental
code.code:
view        - cheap, and the model is small or rarely queried.
table       - the source is huge and consumers need speed.
incremental - the source grows monotonically and you can define the watermark.

code.title: Incremental filter with a lookback window, guarded by is_incremental()

resources.title: Review a PySpark transform for silent quality failures
resources.description: Run the five-check pass over a PySpark transform before it merges: null propagation, join fan-out, silent coercion, non-determinism, and missing post-write assertions. Each finding lands as severity, file:line, rule and a suggested patch.
when_to_use: A PySpark transform is about to be merged
A downstream table's row count changed without a code change
learning_objectives: Identify the five classes of silent failure in a Spark transform
Add pre/post row-count and null assertions to a job
Report findings as severity, file:line, rule, patch

steps.text: Run this when a PySpark transform is about to be merged, or when a downstream table's row count changed without a code change.
Null propagation — every outer join introduces nullable right-side keys; confirm downstream code coalesces or filters them.
Join fan-out — assert key uniqueness on the intended 1-side before joining.
Silent coercion — `cast` failures return null, not errors; prefer `try_cast` and count the nulls it produces.
Non-determinism — `dropDuplicates` without a sort key keeps an arbitrary row.
Missing assertions — every write should be followed by a row-count and a null-rate check on the primary key.

what_you_need: A PySpark transform about to be merged
The intended grain of the output table
check_yourself: Every write in the transform is followed by a row-count and a null-rate check on the primary key.
Findings come back as `severity | file:line | rule | suggested patch`.
gotchas: `cast` failures return null, not errors — count the nulls try_cast produces.
`dropDuplicates` without a sort key keeps an arbitrary row.
Every outer join introduces nullable right-side keys — confirm downstream code coalesces or filters them.
production_notes: Every write should be followed by a row-count and a null-rate check on the primary key.
Report findings as `severity | file:line | rule | suggested patch` so they are actionable in a PR.
resources.why: Spark fails silently — nulls propagate, casts return null, and dropDuplicates keeps an arbitrary row, so the review pass is the defense before consumers see it.
resources.diagram:
transform review
   |
   |- null propagation --> outer joins --> coalesce or filter downstream
   |
   |- join fan-out --> assert 1-side key uniqueness
   |
   |- silent coercion --> try_cast + count nulls
   |
   |- non-determinism --> sort key before dropDuplicates
   |
   |- missing assertions --> row-count + null-rate after every write

code.title: The five-check pass, in order
code.code:
1. Null propagation — every outer join introduces nullable right-side keys.
   Confirm downstream code coalesces or filters them.
2. Join fan-out — assert key uniqueness on the intended 1-side before joining.
3. Silent coercion — `cast` failures return null, not errors. Prefer `try_cast`
   and count the nulls it produces.
4. Non-determinism — `dropDuplicates` without a sort key keeps an arbitrary row.
5. Missing assertions — every write should be followed by a row-count and a
   null-rate check on the primary key.

code.title: When to run it, and what comes back
code.code:
Run this when a PySpark transform is about to be merged, or when a downstream
table's row count changed without a code change.

Output: a findings list — severity | file:line | rule | suggested patch

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Review a schema change against its contract
resources.description: Run the Schema Reviewer's four-step pass over a producer's schema diff — classify each field change, resolve consumers from lineage, emit a dated migration plan — and use the schema-drift runbook to separate hard failures from silent nulls before anything merges.
when_to_use: A producer PR touches a column a contract covers
A column appeared, disappeared or changed type upstream without notice
learning_objectives: Classify each schema change as compatible, risky, or breaking
Resolve the consumer impact set from lineage
Emit a migration plan with dates for any breaking change

steps.text: Diff the schemas field by field.
Classify each change: compatible, risky, breaking.
Determine whether the failure is hard (job error) or silent (nulls).
Resolve consumers from lineage.
Emit a migration plan with dates.
Rename/removal is breaking; coordinate with consumers.

what_you_need: Before/after schema for the change
A consumer list or lineage
check_yourself: A diff narrowing decimal(18,2) to decimal(10,2) is classified risky and blocked as data-loss risky.
On a labelled set of 20 schema changes, every classification matches its label.
gotchas: Assume breaking when semantics are ambiguous.
Renames are removals in disguise; treat them as breaking.
A rename + a new column with the old name looks compatible to a schema differ — always diff semantics, not just names.
production_notes: Never approve a breaking change without a dated plan.
Enforce a schema contract with a compatibility policy in CI.
resources.why: A schema change shipped unreviewed is a loaded gun in the pipeline — hard casts break loudly, silent nulls break worse.
resources.diagram:
schema change review
   |
   |- field-by-field diff --> classify compatible / risky / breaking
   |
   |- hard failure or silent nulls? --> silent nulls keep the job green
   |
   |- consumers from lineage --> migration plan with dates --> approve or block

code.title: Diff the old and new schema
code.code:
diff <(parquet-tools schema old.parquet) <(parquet-tools schema new.parquet)
# Glue/Athena: compare catalog columns to the Parquet footer

code.title: Classification — compatible / risky / breaking
code.code:
- **Compatible** — new nullable column, widened type that preserves values.
- **Risky** — narrowing a type, adding a NOT NULL without a default, changing units.
- **Breaking** — rename, remove, or semantic change to an existing column.

code.title: Dated migration skeleton
code.code: Add → dual-write → backfill → announce → migrate consumers → remove (dated).

resources.title: Run an AWS data architecture review pass
resources.description: Point the AWS Architecture Reviewer at an architecture description or IaC and follow its four-step workflow: map the services to a data flow, check IAM for least privilege, estimate dominant cost drivers, and identify single points of failure. The agent is read-only and never creates resources.
when_to_use: A new AWS data architecture needs a cost/IAM/reliability pass before build
An existing platform keeps producing cost surprises or single points of failure
learning_objectives: Map an AWS data platform into a single data flow before judging it
Check IAM roles for least privilege
Name the dominant cost drivers and single points of failure

steps.text: Map the described services to a data flow.
Check IAM for least privilege.
Estimate dominant cost drivers.
Identify single points of failure.
Collect the four outputs — architecture diagram (text), IAM findings, cost drivers, reliability risks.
Hold the guardrails — the agent never creates resources and requires human approval for any IAM recommendation.

what_you_need: An architecture description or IaC
Workload characteristics (volume, freshness, consumers)
check_yourself: The review flags a Glue job running with an admin role and no bookmark, causing nightly full reprocessing — the agent's own worked example.
Every IAM recommendation stops at human approval, and the agent created zero resources during the pass.
gotchas: The agent never creates resources — anything beyond findings needs a human.
IAM recommendations always require human approval; never auto-apply them.
Bind mcp-aws to a dedicated least-privilege AWS profile with short-lived SSO credentials — never attach an admin role.
production_notes: Score each pass against the 30-anti-pattern checklist so reviews are comparable over time.
Keep the review read-only against the account; resource-creating tools require human confirmation.
resources.why: Thirty AWS data-platform anti-patterns repeat across teams, and a fixed four-step review pass turns them into findings instead of incidents.
resources.diagram:
aws architecture review
   |
   |- map services --> one data flow
   |
   |- IAM --> least privilege --> human approval only
   |
   |- cost drivers --> dominant spend ranked
   |
   |- single points of failure --> reliability risks
   |
   --> findings: diagram + IAM + cost + reliability

code.title: Bind the AWS MCP server to a named profile
code.code:
mcpServers:
  aws-core:
    command: uvx
    args: [awslabs.core-mcp-server@latest]
    env:
      AWS_PROFILE: ${AWS_PROFILE}
      FASTMCP_LOG_LEVEL: ERROR

code.title: Four-step review workflow
code.code:
- Map the described services to a data flow.
- Check IAM for least privilege.
- Estimate dominant cost drivers.
- Identify single points of failure.

code.title: Outputs and guardrails
code.code:
Outputs:
- Architecture diagram (text)
- IAM findings
- Cost drivers
- Reliability risks

Guardrails:
- Never creates resources
- Requires human approval for any IAM recommendation

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Run dbt model review and tests from the workbench plugin
resources.description: Install the dbt Workbench plugin and drive one model change through its three commands: /dbt-review-model for the model review, /dbt-write-tests for a proposed test set, and /dbt-impact before you merge. Along the way you apply the same grain and blast-radius checks the plugin's underlying skills use, with the full-refresh guard watching destructive rebuilds.
when_to_use: Review and test generation for a dbt model should live in the agent, not memory
A model change needs a downstream impact check before merge
learning_objectives: Run /dbt-review-model, /dbt-write-tests, and /dbt-impact on a model change
Read the review output against the model's grain and unique key
Rank the generated tests by blast radius before accepting them

steps.text: Run /dbt-review-model.
State a model's grain and match it to its unique key test.
Run /dbt-write-tests.
Rank tests by the cost of the failure they prevent.
Run /dbt-impact.

what_you_need: A dbt project with a dev target in profiles.yml
A pull request or branch that changes a model
check_yourself: /dbt-review-model returns findings that reference the model's grain and materialisation.
/dbt-write-tests proposes tests ordered by blast radius, and /dbt-impact lists the downstream nodes.
gotchas: The plugin holds warehouse credentials through the dbt profile — scope it to a dev target.
Late-arriving rows older than the watermark are silently dropped; keep the lookback window.
is_incremental() must guard the filter or every full run is a full reload.
production_notes: The full-refresh guard hook blocks destructive rebuilds — leave it enabled.
The plugin runs with filesystem read-write and warehouse network access; review its permissions before installing.
resources.why: The workbench turns review, test generation, and impact checks into three commands instead of habits you have to remember.
resources.diagram:
dbt workbench
   |
   |- /dbt-review-model --> grain + materialisation findings
   |
   |- /dbt-write-tests --> tests ranked by blast radius
   |
   |- /dbt-impact --> downstream nodes --> merge with guard hook on

code.title: Install the dbt Workbench plugin
code.code: amp plugin add de-agent/dbt-workbench

code.title: The three workbench commands in review order
code.code:
/dbt-review-model   # model review: grain + materialisation findings
/dbt-write-tests    # proposed test set, ranked by blast radius
/dbt-impact         # downstream nodes before you merge

code.title: Proposed test set ranked by blast radius in schema.yml
code.code:
models:
  - name: <model>
    columns:
      - name: <grain key>
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: <foreign key>
        tests:
          - relationships:
              to: ref('<dimension model>')
      - name: <enum column>
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: [<allowed values>]
