resources.title: Run the Iceberg maintenance routine
resources.description: Work an Iceberg table through the maintenance skill's plan: read the files metadata table to size the problem, rewrite data files to a 128-256 MB target, rewrite manifests when the manifest list is huge, expire snapshots without breaking time travel, and remove orphan files on a schedule with a safety margin.
when_to_use: Average file size is under 32 MB and the file count keeps growing
A scheduled cleanup plan is needed for snapshots, manifests, and orphan files
learning_objectives: Read an Iceberg metadata table to size the problem
Pick a compaction strategy and rewrite interval
Expire snapshots without breaking time travel

steps.text: Size the problem from metadata: SELECT count(*) files, avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 avg_mb FROM db.tbl.files; avg_mb < 32 and a growing count means compact.
Run rewrite_data_files with a target size (128-256 MB).
Run rewrite_manifests when the manifest list is huge.
Run expire_snapshots older than the retention window — but keep at least one full snapshot for time travel.
Run remove_orphan_files on a schedule, with a safety margin.

what_you_need: An Iceberg table with a growing file count
Query access to the table's metadata tables
check_yourself: After compaction, db.tbl.files reports an average file size inside the 128-256 MB target and a falling file count.
expire_snapshots leaves at least one full snapshot, so time travel within the retention window still works.
gotchas: Do not run compaction during peak ingestion; it conflicts with concurrent writers.
expire_snapshots must keep at least one full snapshot or time travel breaks.
remove_orphan_files runs on a schedule with a safety margin — never ad hoc.
production_notes: Target 128-256 MB files and alert on file-count growth.
Schedule the whole plan outside the ingestion window so compaction and writers never contend.
resources.why: Small files and manifest bloat tax every query and every planning step, and a fixed maintenance plan restores predictable latency without touching writers.
resources.diagram:
iceberg maintenance
   |
   |- SELECT ... FROM db.tbl.files --> avg_mb < 32 + growing count?
   |
   |- rewrite_data_files (target 128-256 MB)
   |
   |- rewrite_manifests (huge manifest list)
   |
   |- expire_snapshots --> keep one full snapshot for time travel
   |
    |- remove_orphan_files on a schedule --> safety margin

code.title: Size the problem from the files metadata table
code.code:
SELECT count(*) files, avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 avg_mb
FROM db.tbl.files;

code.title: The maintenance plan
code.code:
1. `rewrite_data_files` with a target size (128-256 MB).
2. `rewrite_manifests` when the manifest list is huge.
3. `expire_snapshots` older than the retention window — but keep at least one
   full snapshot for time travel.
4. `remove_orphan_files` on a schedule, with a safety margin.

code.title: Compaction call
code.code: CALL catalog.system.rewrite_data_files('db.tbl');  -- Iceberg

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Schema evolution and time travel — change the table, keep the past
resources.description: Change a table without breaking its readers or its history: the Iceberg spec's schema and partition evolution, Delta time travel, the history metadata table you query to see what happened, and the snapshot-expiry rule that keeps time travel working while storage stays bounded. The immutable raw zone is the floor under all of it.
when_to_use: A consumer asks for last month's numbers exactly as they were
A schema change is pending and you want evolution, not a table rebuild
learning_objectives: Use schema and partition evolution instead of recreate-and-copy
Query the history metadata table and time travel within the retention window
Expire snapshots without breaking time travel — keep one full snapshot

steps.text: Evolution is a spec feature: Iceberg's documentation covers schema and partition evolution alongside the table format, snapshots and manifests, and hidden partitioning.
Delta's side of the bargain: its official docs cover ACID transactions on object storage, time travel, OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER clustering, Delta Live Tables, and Unity Catalog integration.
See the past with SQL: for Iceberg/Delta, query the metadata tables (files, history).
Bound the past safely: expire_snapshots older than the retention window — but keep at least one full snapshot for time travel.
Evolution without loss starts at the bottom zone: raw/ — immutable, exactly as received; never edited; schema-on-read.
Reprocessing needs the original bytes — that force is why raw is immutable and why an evolved table can always be rebuilt from its source.
Schedule expiry like compaction: Lakehouse Guard is a guard that blocks compaction or snapshot expiry during peak ingestion windows.

what_you_need: A Delta or Iceberg table with a schema you are tempted to change
Metadata-table access (files, history)
An ingestion window expiry can be scheduled around
check_yourself: You can time travel to a snapshot inside the retention window after expiry ran.
A schema change on curated/ required no rewrite of raw/ — the original bytes were never edited.
The history metadata table answers what changed and when without leaving SQL.
gotchas: expire_snapshots must keep at least one full snapshot or time travel breaks.
Schema and partition evolution are spec features — the format, not a copy job, is the mechanism.
Snapshot expiry is maintenance with a window: the guard blocks it during peak ingestion.
production_notes: Set the snapshot retention window deliberately — it is the knob that trades storage for time-travel depth.
Keep raw/ immutable and schema-on-read so every evolution has an original to return to.
resources.why: Snapshots make the past addressable and evolution makes change cheap; the retention window and the immutable raw zone decide how far back both reach.
resources.diagram:
schema evolution & time travel
   |
   |- spec: schema evolution | partition evolution | hidden partitioning
   |
   |- db.tbl.history --> what changed, when
   |
   |- time travel --> snapshot inside the retention window
   |
   |- expire_snapshots --> keep one full snapshot
   |
   raw (immutable, schema-on-read) --> curated (evolved) --> serving

code.title: The snapshot expiry rule
code.code:
`expire_snapshots` older than the retention window — but keep at least
one full snapshot for time travel.

code.title: The raw zone contract
code.code: raw/       — immutable, exactly as received; never edited; schema-on-read.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Split a batch into quarantine and publish
resources.description: Build the pipeline-dq-quarantine starter the way the Quarantine then Publish pattern prescribes: a quality contract splits each batch into a published set and a quarantine with reasons. You finish with a test that proves no row is ever lost and an alert on the quarantine rate.
when_to_use: External/partner data or any table with an SLA
High-value downstream metrics that one bad batch could poison
learning_objectives: Express a quality contract as executable checks
Design a quarantine table with a reason
Alert on the quarantine rate, not just on failure

steps.text: Split every batch into publish and quarantine on a quality contract.
Validate the contract offline against fixtures with `make test`, then run `make run`.
Load the contract and compile rules to SQL (DuckDB) or Spark expressions.
Split into pass/fail with a stable `failure_reason`.
Publish the pass set; write the fail set to quarantine with provenance.
Alert when the quarantine rate > 1% for 2 consecutive runs.

what_you_need: The pipeline-dq-quarantine starter (contract/orders.yml, src/validate.py, src/publish.py)
DuckDB or PySpark to compile the contract rules to SQL
A batch with ~5% deliberately invalid rows (nulls, dupes, out-of-range)
check_yourself: Every row is either published or quarantined — never lost; the quarantine contains exactly the seeded bad rows, and a clean batch produces an empty quarantine.
A quarantine rate above 1% for 2 consecutive runs fires the alert with the failure_reason breakdown attached.
gotchas: A quarantine nobody reviews is just a slower data loss.
Contract too strict → quarantine rate explodes; tier rules and loosen with evidence.
Alert on quarantine rate, not just on a hard failure — a rising rate is the early signal of an upstream problem.
production_notes: Alert when quarantine rate > 1% for 2 consecutive runs.
Ship a reprocess command that re-runs the quarantined rows after a fix.
resources.why: A row never disappears — it is either published or quarantined with a reason, so one bad batch cannot poison the table.
resources.diagram:
batch
   |
   |- [contract check] --> pass --> published/ (SLA-bearing)
   |
   |- [contract check] --> fail --> quarantine/ (+reason, +source_file)
   |
   |- quarantine rate > 1% x2 runs --> alert --> review + reprocess

code.title: Split every batch — pass publishes, fail quarantines with a reason
code.code:
Split every batch into publish and quarantine on a quality contract.
  pass ─▶ published table (SLA-bearing)
  fail ─▶ quarantine table (retained, alertable, reprocessable)
A row never disappears: it is either published or quarantined with a reason.
Alert on quarantine *rate*, not just on a hard failure — a rising rate is the
early signal of an upstream problem.

code.title: Starter layout — contract, validate, publish
code.code:
pipeline-dq-quarantine/
  contract/orders.yml       # rules: not_null, unique, range, enum
  src/validate.py
  src/publish.py
  tests/test_quarantine.py

code.title: Validate the contract offline, then run the batch
code.code:
make test  # validates against the fixtures offline
make run

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Stream changes, not tables — CDC from Postgres into the lakehouse
resources.description: The intermediate pattern that replaces nightly extraction: read the write-ahead log through Debezium, stream through Kafka, dedupe by LSN, and MERGE into Delta/Iceberg. Covers tombstones, decimal handling, and what a dropped replication slot costs you.
when_to_use: OLTP → lakehouse with freshness < 15 min
You need deletes/updates
learning_objectives: Read the write-ahead log instead of polling source tables
Order events by LSN and dedupe before merging
Handle tombstones without losing history

steps.text: Name the gap batch extraction leaves — it loads the data and still misses deletes and mid-day changes.
Read the write-ahead log, not the tables — WAL → Debezium → Kafka → [dedupe by LSN] → MERGE into lakehouse.
Configure Debezium with `decimal.handling.mode=string` to avoid precision loss.
Read the stream, keep the latest event per key by (lsn, ts_ms); MERGE on the primary key; `op='d'` → soft delete with `_deleted_at`.
Treat deletes as events — a delete is an event with `op = 'd'`; choose hard delete on merge, or soft delete + `_deleted_at` (required if you need history or audit).
Configure a logical replication slot safely.
Know the watch item before going live — a dropped replication slot forces a full re-snapshot.

what_you_need: A Postgres source with logical replication available
check_yourself: A row deleted in Postgres shows up in the lakehouse as an event with `op = 'd'` — applied as a hard delete or a soft delete with `_deleted_at`, not as a missing row.
Replaying the same batch produces an identical table, because events are ranked by (lsn, ts_ms) and deduped before the merge.
gotchas: Replication slot dropped / WAL purged → full re-snapshot required.
Out-of-order events flip a value back → ordering used arrival time.
Never read the source tables on a schedule.
production_notes: Alert on slot retained WAL and connector task failures.
Monitor source-vs-target row counts continuously.
resources.why: Batch extraction from an OLTP database loads it and still misses deletes and mid-day changes — the WAL carries every change with an order you can rank on.
resources.diagram:
postgres cdc pipeline
   |
   |- Postgres WAL --> Debezium --> Kafka topic
   |
   |- dedupe by LSN --> latest event per key
   |
   |- MERGE on primary key; op='d' --> soft delete (_deleted_at)
   |
    --> Delta/Iceberg; alert on slot retained WAL + task failures

code.title: Bring up the CDC stack
code.code:
make up  # postgres + kafka + connect + minio
make register-connector
make seed-mutations  # insert/update/delete

code.title: Check the replication slot
code.code: SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn, confirmed_flush_lsn FROM pg_replication_slots;

code.title: The pipeline in one line
code.code: Postgres WAL ─▶ Debezium ─▶ Kafka topic ─▶ stream dedupe ─▶ MERGE ─▶ Delta/Iceberg

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Table format mechanics — snapshots, manifests, and the metadata tables
resources.description: Open the hood on an Iceberg table: the spec's layers (snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning), the files and history metadata tables you query with plain SQL, and the manifest list as a maintenance target in its own right. One catalog then spans Iceberg, Delta, Hudi, and Hive.
when_to_use: You are about to maintain or debug an Iceberg table and want to know what the engine actually reads
Multiple engines touch the same table and you need the ground truth
learning_objectives: Name the layers the Iceberg spec defines — snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning
Query the files and history metadata tables with plain SQL
Explain when manifests need rewriting and why the spec outranks engine docs

steps.text: A table format is a specification: the spec is the ground truth when tools disagree.
The spec defines the layers: the table format, snapshots and manifests, hidden partitioning, schema and partition evolution, and maintenance procedures like compaction and snapshot expiry.
Metadata is queryable SQL: for Iceberg/Delta, query the metadata tables (files, history).
Start with files: SELECT count(*) files, avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 avg_mb FROM db.tbl.files; — avg_mb < 32 and a growing count means compact.
Metadata itself needs maintenance: run rewrite_manifests when the manifest list is huge.
One format is not the whole story: Amazon EMR's multi-catalog queries Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi, and Hive tables through a single catalog and joins data across AWS accounts without copying it.

what_you_need: An Iceberg table you can query (any engine that reads the format)
Read access to the table's metadata tables (files, history)
No installs — the spec and the metadata tables are the materials
check_yourself: db.tbl.files returns a count and an average file size on your table, and you can say which layer of the spec it reads.
You can explain what rewrite_manifests fixes and when to run it — when the manifest list is huge.
You can say why the spec, not any engine's docs, settles a disagreement between two engines over the same table.
gotchas: The spec is the ground truth when tools disagree — do not settle format questions from an engine's blog post.
A huge manifest list is its own problem: rewrite_manifests, not just data-file compaction.
Metadata tables (files, history) are queried like tables — no special tooling required.
production_notes: Read the spec once end to end: it covers snapshots, manifests, hidden partitioning, evolution, and the maintenance procedures your skills automate.
Multi-engine shops share tables through catalogs; verify which catalog each engine resolves before comparing query plans.
resources.why: Every query plan and every maintenance decision walks the metadata tree first; knowing snapshots, manifests, and the files/history tables turns magic into reading.
resources.diagram:
iceberg metadata mechanics
   |
   spec: snapshots | manifests | hidden partitioning | evolution
   |
   |- db.tbl.files  --> count, avg file size --> compact trigger
   |
   |- db.tbl.history --> what happened, when
   |
   |- manifest list huge --> rewrite_manifests
   |
   |- one catalog --> Iceberg + Delta + Hudi + Hive

code.title: Read the files metadata table
code.code:
SELECT count(*) files, avg(file_size_in_bytes)/1e6 avg_mb
FROM db.tbl.files;

code.title: The maintenance plan the metadata implies
code.code:
1. `rewrite_data_files` with a target size (128-256 MB).
2. `rewrite_manifests` when the manifest list is huge.
3. `expire_snapshots` older than the retention window — but keep at least one
   full snapshot for time travel.
4. `remove_orphan_files` on a schedule, with a safety margin.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Triage Kafka consumer lag from per-partition offsets
resources.description: Combine the lag-triage skill's three questions with the lagging-consumer runbook: read per-partition lag to separate capacity from key skew, check the group state history for a rebalance loop, find the one stuck offset that marks a poison message, then apply the matching fix — and never reset offsets.
when_to_use: Consumer-group lag keeps rising and won't recover on its own
Downstream tables are going fresh-to-stale
learning_objectives: Read per-partition lag to separate skew from throughput
Detect a rebalance loop from consumer-group state
Find the poison message from retry counts

steps.text: Ask the three questions — is lag rising, flat, or falling? Is it even across partitions? Is the consumer group stable?
Get per-partition lag — uniform vs skewed tells you capacity vs key skew.
Check the consumer-group state history for `PreparingRebalance`.
Look for one partition whose committed offset is stuck.

Match the signature — lag on one partition only is key skew; all partitions rising with low CPU is a downstream bottleneck; lag resets to zero then climbs is a rebalance loop; one offset stuck while others advance is a poison message.

Fix accordingly — sink-bound: batch/upsert in bulk or scale the sink; key skew: re-key the topic or increase partitions; rebalance: raise session.timeout.ms / max.poll.interval.ms; poison message: route to a DLQ and commit past it.

what_you_need: kafka-consumer-groups CLI access to the cluster
The consumer group's describe output and state
check_yourself: Lag confined to two partitions with the rest flat is diagnosed as key skew and fixed by re-keying — not by scaling the fleet.
Offsets are never reset during the incident; a message that keeps failing lands in a DLQ and the group commits past it.
gotchas: Never reset offsets to reduce lag; that is silent data loss.
Uniform lag means capacity; one stuck partition means key skew or a poison message — read per-partition lag before scaling.
A rebalance loop can look like slowness: check the group state history for PreparingRebalance.
production_notes: Alert on lag slope, not on an absolute lag number.
Give messages that fail N times a DLQ instead of an endless retry.
resources.why: Lag compounds — every minute behind is a minute of stale truth downstream, and the sink silently becomes the bottleneck nobody owns.
resources.diagram:
consumer lag triage
   |
   |- lag rising? uniform? group stable?
   |
   |- lag uniform --> capacity bound --> scale consumers / sink throughput
   |
   |- one partition stuck --> hot key or poison --> re-key, or DLQ + commit past
   |
   |- PreparingRebalance looping --> rebalance storm --> raise session.timeout.ms
   |
    --> never reset offsets

code.title: Per-partition lag and group state
code.code:
kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group $G
kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group $G --state

code.title: Lag signatures
code.code:
- Lag on one partition only → key skew; re-key or increase partitions.
- All partitions rising, CPU low → downstream (DB/API) is the bottleneck.
- Lag resets to zero then climbs → rebalance loop; check `session.timeout.ms`.
- One offset stuck, others advance → poison message in a retry loop.

code.title: Fix by signature
code.code:
- Sink-bound → batch/upsert in bulk, or scale the sink.
- Key skew → re-key the topic or increase partitions (breaks ordering per key).
- Rebalance → raise session.timeout.ms / max.poll.interval.ms.
- Poison message → route to a DLQ and commit past it.
- Never reset offsets to reduce lag; that is silent data loss.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Window a stream correctly — watermarks, dedupe, and late data
resources.description: Stream processing in practice: start from the kafka-streaming template, pick event-time over processing-time windows, set a watermark you can defend, and prove what happens to late data. Checkpointing and an idempotent MERGE sink make the job restartable without duplicating output.
when_to_use: Aggregations over event streams — counts and sums per window
A streaming job that must survive restarts without duplicating output
learning_objectives: Choose event-time vs processing-time windows
Set a watermark and reason about late data
Run a structured-streaming job with checkpointing and an idempotent MERGE sink

steps.text: Start from the template — a structured-streaming job with checkpointing, watermarking, a dedupe stage and an idempotent MERGE sink to Delta/Iceberg.
Decide time semantics first — choose event-time vs processing-time windows.
Follow the reference architecture — Spark SS with watermark 2m and dedupe on event_id, raw_events appended to bronze, agg_5min as a windowed MERGE on the window key.
Read with `startingOffsets=earliest` in dev only; latest in prod.
Dedupe on `event_id` within the watermark; windowed aggregation to 5-minute tumbling windows, appended idempotently.
Prove late-data behavior in tests — a late event beyond the watermark is dropped (documented, not silent), and replaying a batch yields the same aggregate.
Watch the two classic failures — watermark too short means late data silently dropped; checkpoint lost means duplicates, fixed by making the sink idempotent.

what_you_need: The kafka-streaming template (checkpointing, watermarking, a dedupe stage, an idempotent MERGE sink)
A Kafka topic whose events carry an event timestamp and an event_id
check_yourself: An event arriving inside the 2-minute watermark joins its window; one beyond it is dropped — documented in the tests, not silent.
Replaying a batch yields the same aggregate because the MERGE is on the window key.
gotchas: Watermark too short → late data silently dropped.
Read with `startingOffsets=earliest` in dev only; latest in prod.
Skewed key → one partition saturates; re-key.
production_notes: Checkpoints on durable storage with lineage.
Lag + batch-duration metrics; alert on rising batch duration.
resources.why: Windows turn infinite streams into finite, mergeable results — get the watermark wrong and you either drop late data silently or never emit.
resources.diagram:
windowed streaming job
   |
   |- Kafka events (event_id, event time)
   |
   |- watermark 2m --> dedupe on event_id
   |
   |- 5-minute tumbling windows --> aggregate
   |
   |- raw_events --> append (bronze)
   |- agg_5min  --> MERGE on window key (idempotent)
   |
    --> checkpoint on durable storage; alert on rising batch duration

code.title: Bring up the stack and produce events
code.code:
make up
make produce  # emits events, some deliberately late
make stream &

code.title: Implementation rules
code.code:
- Read with `startingOffsets=earliest` in dev only; latest in prod.
- Dedupe on `event_id` within the watermark.
- Windowed aggregation to 5-minute tumbling windows, appended idempotently.
- MERGE aggregates on the window key so replays converge.

code.title: The reference architecture
code.code:
Kafka (events) ─▶ Spark SS [watermark 2m, dedupe on event_id]
                  ├─▶ Delta: raw_events (append, bronze)
                  └─▶ Delta: agg_5min  (windowed, MERGE on window key)

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Window functions — keep the grain, rank the rows
resources.description: A window function computes over a set of rows and hands the answer back to every row, so the result keeps its grain — the property that makes a keep-latest dedupe safe and a bare GROUP BY grain-changing. You find the duplicates first with one GROUP BY query, dedupe on the business key keeping the latest by event time, and learn when a window over the same key is a shuffle that can skew or spill.
when_to_use: Row counts are inflated and the fix must keep one row per key
A ranking or latest-per-key read has to stay at the row grain
learning_objectives: Keep the result grain intact — a window computes over a set without collapsing rows
Find duplicate keys with one GROUP BY query before deduplicating
Deduplicate on the business key, keeping the latest by event time

steps.text: Review the failure modes first — the sql-review skill exists to catch functions that silently change grain, alongside fan-out joins, NULL-unsafe predicates, implicit casts, and non-deterministic ordering.
State the grain of a result set in one sentence — a window keeps the row grain while computing over its partition, a GROUP BY changes it.
Find the duplicate key first — identify the duplicate key and count duplicates per key.
Count duplicates per key with one query: SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 20;
Deduplicate on the business key, keeping the latest by event time.
Treat the group-by (and any window over the same key) as a shuffle — key skew on a join or group-by key is the first cause to check.
Spill to disk from an oversized partition — a window partition that gets too big is a known shuffle failure.

what_you_need: A table with a business key and an event-time column
The local DuckDB from lesson 2 works for all the practice queries
check_yourself: The deduped table has one row per business key, and the GROUP BY duplicate count proves it.
You can say in one sentence what the window preserved that a GROUP BY would have collapsed.
The window's PARTITION BY key is the same key you checked for skew.
gotchas: A window keeps the grain, a GROUP BY changes it — pick by the grain you owe the consumer.
Dedupe on the business key, keeping the latest by event time — not by insertion order.
A window over a skewed key is a shuffle with a hot partition — it can spill to disk.
production_notes: Keep the GROUP BY duplicate-count query next to the dedupe job as its check.
Check the write mode before dedupe — append vs merge/overwrite decides what the rewrite touches.
resources.why: Windows are the tool that computes over a set without changing the grain — which is why dedupe and rankings go through them.
resources.diagram:
window functions and grain
   |
   |- GROUP BY --> new grain (one row per key)
   |
   |- window --> same grain, value computed over the partition
   |
   |- dedupe --> business key --> keep latest by event time
   |
   |- at scale --> window = shuffle --> skew / spill to disk

code.title: Find the duplicate keys the window dedupe will remove
code.code:
SELECT k, count(*) c FROM t GROUP BY k HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT min(dt), max(dt) FROM (SELECT dt, k, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY dt, k HAVING count(*)>1);

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Wire task dependencies and retries that survive failure
resources.description: Model the pipeline as task groups and give every task deliberate retries with backoff, a timeout and a pool — the skeleton's guarantees, verified the way the DAG reviewer verifies them before the DAG ships.
when_to_use: Wiring task dependencies and retry settings in a new or inherited DAG
A task retries instantly and hammers a downstream system
learning_objectives: Model task structure with task groups from the idempotent skeleton
Choose retries and timeouts deliberately, with backoff
Pass the reviewer's retry and concurrency check

steps.text: Scaffold from the idempotent DAG skeleton — task groups, retries and backoff, SLA, pools, and a sensor using reschedule mode are built in.
Choose retries and timeouts deliberately.
Retries have a backoff; a task that retries instantly will hammer a downstream.
Check retry, timeout and concurrency settings for every task.
Run the reviewer over the DAG — it flags unsafe retries, missing catchup policy and unbounded concurrency.
Make every task safe to re-run before adding the next one.

what_you_need: A scaffolded DAG or any DAG file under review
The pipeline's SLA
check_yourself: Every task in the DAG declares retries with backoff, a timeout and a pool.
Running the reviewer over the DAG returns no unsafe-retry or unbounded-concurrency findings.
gotchas: Retries have a backoff; a task that retries instantly will hammer a downstream.
The reviewer checks for non-idempotent tasks, unsafe retries, missing catchup policy and unbounded concurrency.
production_notes: SLA, pools and backoff come from the template — keep them instead of stripping defaults.
Make every task safe to re-run before adding the next one.
resources.why: Dependencies decide what runs with what, retries decide what happens when it fails — take both from the skeleton instead of rediscovering them per task.
resources.diagram:
dependencies + retries
   |
   |- task groups --> pipeline structure
   |
   |- retries + backoff --> failure handling
   |
   |- timeouts + pools + SLA --> bounded resource use

code.title: What the reviewer checks
code.code:
Checks a DAG for non-idempotent tasks, unsafe retries, missing catchup
policy, ambiguous catchup/backfill semantics and unbounded concurrency.

code.title: Scaffold with the guarantees
code.code: amp template new de-agent/airflow-dag ./dags

resources.title: Capstone — the guarded agent checklist
resources.description: Run the whole series against one agent setup: skills that load on demand, tools scoped at the connection, least-privilege credentials, audited tool contracts, hooks that fail closed, and a human gate on anything irreversible. Prove each box with an attempted violation, not a promise.
when_to_use: Before calling any agent setup production-ready
Periodically re-auditing an agent that already runs
learning_objectives: Run the series checklist against a complete agent setup
Prove each guard with an attempted violation, not a promise
Know which artifacts to keep — config, classification table, approval log

steps.text: Skills in place — SKILL.md with front-matter (name, description, version), plus references/, scripts/, and examples/ directories that the agent loads on demand.

Tools scoped at the connection — the filesystem server grants read/write within the directories you pass as arguments, so scope it to a single working directory and never pass a home directory or a mount containing secrets.
Credentials least-privilege — a fine-grained GitHub token limited to the target repositories, read-only unless the task must open PRs; never org-wide admin.
Contracts audited — tools that can write, delete, spend money or exfiltrate data flagged, and a least-privilege connection recommendation produced.
Hooks active — destructive statements are denied by default, and a DELETE/UPDATE without a WHERE clause is always denied.
Secrets gated — staged diffs scanned for high-confidence secret patterns; pattern matches block the commit.
The pattern underneath — separate read/recommend from write/execute, execute scoped and logged, and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible.

what_you_need: The agent setup from lessons 2 through 9
A non-production database and repository
The DE Data Toolkit plugin and the contract-auditor skill installed
check_yourself: A write against a production target is suspended pending an approve-once token scoped to the single call.
A staged connection string with a password is blocked at commit; a DROP TABLE is denied before any database call.
The agent's permissions read like the review agent's — filesystem read-write, network none, credentials none.
gotchas: Prove each guard with an attempted violation — a promise in config is not a hook firing.
Destructive statements are denied by default — if yours went through, the hook was not on the tool path.
Blast radius can be production — re-check scope after every new tool or credential.
production_notes: Keep the tools-by-class table, the connection configs and the approve-once log together as the agent's audit pack.
The starter plugin is the baseline — SQL/Spark review skills, the destructive-SQL guard, a secret scanner and the file/git MCP servers, wired together.
resources.why: A guarded agent is a checked list — skills that load on demand, scoped tools and tokens, audited contracts, hooks that fail closed, and a human gate on anything irreversible.
resources.diagram:
guarded agent checklist
   |
   |- skills --> SKILL.md + references + examples, loaded on demand
   |
   |- tools --> one dir, one repo, one scoped token
   |
   |- contracts --> Read/Write/Destructive/Spend/Exfiltrate classified
   |
   |- hooks --> destructive denied, prod writes approve-once, secrets blocked
   |
   |- pattern --> read/recommend vs write/execute --> human gate

code.code:
A SKILL.md file with front-matter (name, description, version), plus
references/, scripts/, and examples/ directories that an agent loads
on demand.

code.code: read ─▶ recommend ─▶ human approves ─▶ execute (scoped, logged)

code.code:
Destructive statements are denied by default; a DELETE/UPDATE without a
WHERE clause is always denied. Failure behavior: block.

resources.title: Production gotchas — untrusted content, destructive actions, permission scope
resources.description: An agent executes with your credentials, so its context and config are an attack surface. Read the MCP security model, treat fetched content as untrusted input, keep destructive statements deny-by-default, and scope every credential to the role and repositories the task needs.
when_to_use: Before an agent touches production data or credentials
Reviewing an agent setup that someone else configured
learning_objectives: Treat fetched content as untrusted model input and scope its network path
Bound destructive actions with deny-by-default hooks
Scope every credential to the role and repositories the task needs

steps.text: Read the MCP specification's security section before connecting any MCP server to real data — it is the definitive reference for transports (stdio, SSE, HTTP), tool definitions, resource templates, prompts, and the security model.
Anything fetched becomes model context — the fetch tool retrieves a URL and converts it to markdown for the model.
And fetch is network egress to arbitrary URLs — it can reach internal endpoints (SSRF risk), so in a corporate environment route it through an allowlisting proxy.
Destructive actions are denied by default — intercept DROP / TRUNCATE / DELETE-without-WHERE before the agent executes it.

Scope warehouse credentials — the reference SQL server issues raw SQL: connect with a role that only has SELECT on the schemas intended, prefer a replica, and do not point it at production with a superuser.
Scope repository credentials — use a fine-grained GitHub token limited to the target repositories, read-only unless the task must open PRs; never grant org-wide admin.
Audit the contracts before connecting — flag tools that can write, delete, spend money or exfiltrate data, and produce a least-privilege connection recommendation.

what_you_need: The MCP specification's security section
The tool list and schemas of every server you connect
A non-production database role with SELECT only
check_yourself: Every MCP server connected has had its tools classified — none can write, delete, spend or exfiltrate beyond what the task needs.
The database role has SELECT only, the GitHub token is fine-grained and read-only, and fetch runs behind an allowlist.
gotchas: Network egress to arbitrary URLs can reach internal endpoints — SSRF risk; allowlist the proxy.
Never point a raw-SQL server at production with a superuser — SELECT-only role, prefer a replica.
Never grant org-wide admin on the GitHub token — scope it to the target repositories.
production_notes: Treat MCP registry entries as discovery, never as a trust signal.
Classify every tool — write, delete, spend or exfiltrate — before the first connection, and keep the table with the config.
resources.why: An agent executes with your credentials — untrusted content in its context and unscoped tools in its config turn one bad task into an incident.
resources.diagram:
production agent
   |
   |- fetched page --> untrusted model context --> allowlisted egress only
   |
   |- SQL tools --> SELECT-only role, replica --> never prod superuser
   |
   |- repo tools --> fine-grained read-only token
   |
   |- destructive SQL --> denied by default
   |
   |- spend/exfiltrate tools --> classified before connect

The security section of the MCP specification is required reading before
connecting any MCP server to real data: transports (stdio, SSE, HTTP),
tool definitions, resource templates, prompts, and the security model.

code.code:
The reference server issues raw SQL. Connect with a role that only has

code.code:

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: The 3am batch incident path
resources.description: The nightly job is crawling or dead under memory pressure or skew. Follow the incident path: collect the four pieces of evidence, read p50 vs p99 and the spill bytes, decide revert vs fix, escalate on golden-hour SLAs, and record the skew/spill/scan signature so the next run is faster to diagnose.
when_to_use: A batch job's runtime jumped and no code changed
Executors idle while a few tasks run long
A nightly run failed or blew past its SLA
learning_objectives: Collect the four pieces of evidence a failing Spark run needs
Decide between revert, a config change, and a code fix
Record the skew/spill/scan signature for the cost-per-run history

steps.text: Symptoms — job duration rose sharply with no code change, one or a few tasks dominate the stage, and executors idle while a handful run long.
Collect the evidence — Spark UI stage summary p50/p99 task durations, shuffle read/write and spill bytes per task, input bytes scanned vs the expected partition size, and the run's event log.
Skew if p99 >> p50 (10x+), uniform slowness if p50 is high; check input bytes scanned vs table size.
No code rollback — the job is unchanged. Revert only if a config change (AQE flags, executor sizing) preceded the regression.
Fix — skew gets AQE skew join or a salted hot key; spill gets more partitions or executor memory; over-scan gets a partition predicate. Never repartition(1).
Page the on-call data engineer if the job sits on a golden-hour SLA; otherwise file it and let the owning team run diagnosis in hours.
Follow up — record the skew/spill/scan signature in the run's cost-per-run history, and add the partition-filter lint or CI metric guard that would have caught it.

what_you_need: The affected run's event log and Spark UI stage summary
The job source and its recent config changes
check_yourself: The evidence packet is attached: p50/p99 durations, shuffle/spill bytes per task, input bytes scanned, and the event log.
The decision — revert vs AQE/salt/spill fix — cites a config change or a metric, not a hunch.
gotchas: Spill shows up as slow tasks, not failures — check spill bytes before paying for bigger executors.
repartition(1) serialises the stage — never reach for it to 'fix' slowness.
p99 much greater than p50 means skew; uniformly high p50 means capacity. Salting helps the first, not the second.
production_notes: Monitor task duration p99/p50 ratio, shuffle read/write bytes per run, spill bytes per stage.
Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics so CI fails a regression before the SLA does.
resources.why: 3am is the wrong time to start instrumenting — the incident path runs symptoms, evidence, rollback-or-fix, and leaves a signature behind.
resources.diagram:
3am incident
   |
   |- symptoms --> runtime jumped, no code change, few tasks dominate
   |
   |- evidence --> p50/p99 + shuffle/spill bytes + bytes scanned + event log
   |
   |- decide --> config change? revert : AQE / salt / partitions / predicate
   |
   |- escalate --> golden-hour SLA? page on-call
   |
   |- follow up --> record signature, add the CI guard

code.title: Evidence to collect
code.code:
- Spark UI stage summary: p50/p99 task durations for the slow stages
- Shuffle read/write and spill bytes per task
- Input bytes scanned vs the expected partition size
- The job's event log for the affected run

code.title: Rollback and escalation rules
code.code:
No code rollback — the job is unchanged. Revert only if a config change
(AQE flags, executor sizing) preceded the regression.

Page the on-call data engineer if the job sits on a golden-hour SLA;
otherwise file it and let the owning team run diagnosis in hours.

code.title: Turn the event log into a histogram
code.code:
amp plugin add de-agent/spark-lens
/spark-analyze        # task histogram; flags skew and shuffle amplification

resources.title: Tune a slow job — memory, partitions, baselines
resources.description: Run the tuning loop on a slow batch job: parse task-duration and shuffle metrics, classify the stage as skew, partition count, spill or scan, apply the single highest-impact change, and verify it against a stored baseline the CI guard enforces.
when_to_use: A batch job's runtime jumped and no code changed
Before paying for bigger executors
learning_objectives: Classify a slow stage into skew, partition count, spill, or scan
Apply the single highest-impact fix with an expected effect
Verify the change against baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics

steps.text: Parse task-duration and shuffle metrics.
Classify the stage — skew, partition count, spill, or scan.
Spill → increase partition count or raise executor memory.
Over-scan → add the partition predicate; confirm with bytes scanned.
Propose the single highest-impact change with expected effect, then verify against the baseline metrics.
Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics and fail CI on regression, and add a partition filter lint on source reads.

what_you_need: The job's event log or Spark UI metrics
A stored cost baseline for the job
check_yourself: You can name which of skew, partition count, spill, or scan was the cause, with the metrics to prove it.
The change you shipped is the single highest-impact one, and the stored baseline shows no regression.
gotchas: repartition(1) serialises the stage — never reach for it to 'fix' slowness.
Spill shows up as slow tasks, not failures — check spill bytes before paying for bigger executors.
AQE skew-join healing does not fix over-scan; check bytes scanned separately.
production_notes: Baseline shuffle/spill/scan metrics and fail CI on regression.
Monitor task duration p99/p50 ratio, shuffle read/write bytes per run, spill bytes per stage.
resources.why: Tuning without a classification loop is guessing — parse, classify, fix one thing, and verify against a baseline.
resources.diagram:
slow job
   |
   |- parse --> task-duration + shuffle metrics
   |
   |- classify --> skew | partition count | spill | scan
   |
   |- fix --> single highest-impact change
   |
   |- verify --> baseline metrics --> CI guard fails on regression

code.title: The tuning loop
code.code:
1. Parse task-duration and shuffle metrics.
2. Classify: skew, partition count, spill, or scan.
3. Propose the single highest-impact change with expected effect.
4. Verify against the baseline metrics.

amplification, and compares against a stored cost baseline.

- Add a partition filter lint on source reads.

resources.author: de-agent

resources.title: Warehouse production gotchas — cost, full refreshes, late data
resources.description: The three ways a healthy warehouse model hurts production: a full-refresh that rebuilds a 4B-row table unannounced, a lookback window too short to catch late-arriving orders, and cost drift nobody reviews. Guard the destructive command, harden CI, and put the cost query on a weekly cadence.
when_to_use: Before the first full-refresh of a large production model
Cost or reliability reviews of an existing warehouse model
learning_objectives: Gate full-refreshes on row thresholds and criticality before they run
Size lookback windows against real late-arriving data
Keep warehouse cost visible with weekly top-cost query reviews

steps.text: See the blast radius concretely — `dbt run --full-refresh --select fct_orders` on a 4B-row model is the command the guard pauses for confirmation.

Understand the gate — the hook inspects dbt commands for `--full-refresh`; if any affected model exceeds a row threshold from the manifest's stats or is tagged `critical`, it requires an explicit confirmation token and logs the operator identity.
Late data is the silent drop — a late-arriving order missed means the lookback window was too short.
Environments lie too — CI green but prod differs means CI ran on a different target/schema.
Deletes never arrive on their own — decide explicitly between soft-delete and a periodic full-refresh.
Watch the bill — review weekly query history for the top cost queries and alert on the partitions_scanned/partitions_total ratio.
Harden the loop — CI builds to a per-PR staging schema and runs full tests, source freshness checks watch raw, and exposures are declared for dashboards.

what_you_need: A dbt project with at least one incremental model in production
The manifest stats the guard hook reads row thresholds from
Install: npx de-agent-platform add dbt-model-review
check_yourself: A full-refresh of your largest model now requires a confirmation token and is logged with the operator identity.
Your lookback window is sized from observed late-arriving data, not guessed.
Top-cost queries are reviewed weekly and the partitions ratio has an alert.
gotchas: Late-arriving order missed → lookback window too short.
CI green but prod differs → CI ran on a different target/schema.
Deletes never arrive. Decide explicitly: soft-delete, or periodic full-refresh.
production_notes: Leave the full-refresh guard hook enabled — it pauses destructive rebuilds on models over the row threshold or tagged critical.
Run CI to a per-PR staging schema with full tests, source freshness on raw, and declared exposures.
resources.why: The commands that fix warehouses are also the ones that can destroy them — cost, full-refreshes, and late data are where models meet production.
resources.diagram:
production gotchas
   |
   |- --full-refresh --> row threshold / critical tag --> confirmation + logged identity
   |
   |- incremental --> lookback window sized for late data
   |
   |- deletes --> soft-delete or periodic full-refresh, decided explicitly
   |
   |- cost --> weekly top-cost review + partitions-ratio alert

code.title: The command the guard pauses
code.code:
dbt run --full-refresh --select fct_orders
# on a 4B-row model this is paused for confirmation

code.title: Production hardening checklist, from the starter project
code.code:
CI builds to a per-PR staging schema and runs full tests
Source freshness checks on raw
Exposures declared for dashboards

resources.title: When an agent does the wrong thing — contain, audit, postmortem
resources.description: An agent merged a change it should not have. Roll back first, use the scoping you configured to contain and reconstruct what happened — diffs, logs and approve-once records — walk the incident workflow, and close with a blameless postmortem whose action items name the missing gate.
when_to_use: An agent merged, wrote or executed something it should not have
After any agent action a human did not explicitly approve
learning_objectives: Contain the damage before diagnosing — rollback first
Reconstruct what the agent did from the audit trail
Produce a blameless postmortem with dated, owned action items

steps.text: Roll back first — a deploy broke production: correlate the signal with the change and roll back before diagnosing.
Containment was designed in — the git server can commit and create branches in the scoped repository, but cannot push unless credentials are also present in the environment.
Reconstruct the change from the tools the agent had — git_status, git_diff_unstaged, git_diff_staged, git_log, git_commit.
Pull the approval record — any write-class tool against a production target was suspended for an approve-once token scoped to the single call, so the log names the human who approved it.
Walk the incident workflow in order — establish impact and start time, check for a correlated deploy, walk the matching runbook, capture the timeline for the postmortem.
Keep the assistant's own guardrails on during response — it suggests, never executes, production changes, and escalates to a human before any destructive step.
Close with the postmortem — timeline, impact, detection gap, contributing factors, and action items with owners and dates.

what_you_need: The scoped, logged execute path your agent writes through
The repository the agent worked in
check_yourself: You can list every tool call the agent made — read-only tools leave diffs and logs, writes leave approve-once records.
The postmortem separates trigger from contributing factors, and every action item has an owner and a date.
gotchas: Roll back first — correlate the signal with the change before diagnosing.
The git server cannot push unless credentials are also present — if the agent pushed, a credential was in scope.
Mitigation runs under the same guardrails — suggest, never execute, production changes.
production_notes: Keep the approve-once token log with the postmortem — it is the audit record of who approved the write.
Feed the detection gap back into the hooks — the postmortem's action items should name the gate that was missing.
resources.why: The scoping that bounded the blast radius — no push credentials, approve-once tokens, a logged execute path — is what makes the incident auditable and the rollback cheap.
resources.diagram:
agent incident
   |
   |- rollback first --> correlate signal with change
   |
   |- contain --> no push credentials --> wrong commit stays local
   |
   |- audit --> git log/diff + approve-once token log
   |
   |- respond --> impact -> correlated deploy -> runbook -> timeline
   |
   |- close --> blameless postmortem -> owned, dated action items

resources.title: dbt Test Writer
resources.tagline: Generate the minimum test set that actually protects a model.
resources.description: Proposes dbt tests ranked by blast radius: uniqueness/not-null on the grain key, accepted values on enums, relationships on foreign keys, and freshness on sources.
learning_objectives: Rank tests by the cost of the failure they prevent
Write a custom singular test
Wire freshness on a source
resources.body:
# dbt Test Writer

## Rank by blast radius, not by effort
1. `unique` + `not_null` on the grain key — the model is meaningless without it.
2. `relationships` on every foreign key — catches broken joins upstream.
3. `accepted_values` on low-cardinality enums — catches upstream renames.
4. `freshness` on sources — catches a stalled extractor, the #1 silent outage.

## Avoid
- Row-count equality tests on raw sources: they flake.
- Testing a column nobody reads.
- `warn` severity on a correctness test nobody will see.
